en: When about to enter upon the vow, standing between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires and facing eastward, he touches water. Now, as to why he touches water: man is indeed impure in that he speaks untruth; by that he becomes foul within.
"The waters are pure; having become pure, I shall enter upon the vow," he thinks; "The waters are a means of purification;
purified by the means of purification, I shall enter upon the vow. Therefore, he touches water.
Then, looking toward the fire, he enters upon the vow.
"O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow;
may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me. Agni indeed is the Lord of Vows among the gods; to him he thus says: "I shall perform the vow;
may I be able to do it; may it be successful for me. There is nothing here that is obscure. 1.1.1 [3]
Then, when the sacrifice has been completed, he releases [the vows]:
"O Agni, lord of vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; may that be successful for me.
He says this because he was indeed able, having reached the conclusion of the sacrifice; for it has been successful for him who has reached the conclusion of the sacrifice.
"By this [path], indeed, most people enter upon the vow; however, one should enter by this very [other] path.
For there are these two, and no third exists: truth and untruth. The gods are truth, and untruth..."
"Human beings [say], 'I am departing from untruth and entering truth'; thus he departs from humans and approaches the gods.
He should indeed speak only the truth; for this is the vow that the gods observe, namely truth. Therefore they possess glory; glory..."
He who, knowing thus, speaks the truth, becomes such.
1.1.1.[6] Then, when the sacrifice is completed, he releases his vow, saying:
"I am now who I truly am. For previously, he was as it were non-human.

Whatever vow one undertakes, it is not appropriate for one to say, "I am now entering into untruth from truth," for by doing so, one indeed becomes merely human; therefore, one should release the vow with the words, "I am now who I truly am. 1.1.1 [7]

Now, therefore, regarding eating and fasting: Āṣāḍha Sāvayasa, however, considered fasting alone to be the vow. For the gods indeed know the mind of a human being; they know him when he approaches this vow, [thinking], "Tomorrow morning..."
Thinking, "He will sacrifice," all the gods come to his house; they fast in his house—that is the *upavasatha*.
But that is indeed improper:
for what man would eat before others among men have eaten, let alone one who [is about to perform a sacrifice]?
"If the gods do not eat, one should eat first; therefore, one should certainly not eat.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:
"If he does not eat, he belongs to the ancestors (pitṛ-devatya); if, however, he eats..."
"He eats beyond [the portion of] the gods. Therefore, he should eat that which is both eaten and uneaten. That for which no sacrificial oblation is taken is indeed "eaten and uneaten.
When he eats this, he does not become one whose deity is the ancestors; and when he eats that for which no oblation is taken, he thereby does not eat beyond the portion of the gods. 1.1.1 [10]

He should indeed eat only forest food—either wild herbs or things growing on trees. Regarding this, Barku Vārṣṇa used to say: "Cook for me for a month; they do not take the sacrificial oblation from these. But that is not so.
Or he may prepare this [mixture] with rice and barley; whatever cultivated grain there is, that is rice and barley, and by this he makes rice and barley more abundant.
Therefore, one should eat only forest-grown food.
On that night, he should sleep in the chamber of the Āhavanīya fire.

He who undertakes a vow approaches the gods; he lies down in their very midst when he lies in the Gārhapatya fire-hall. He should lie on the ground, for the service toward one’s superior is as if from below. 1.1.1 [12]
In the morning, he indeed first undertakes the waters as his first act; he leads forward the waters. The waters are indeed the sacrifice;
thus, by this first act, he undertakes the sacrifice itself. He leads them forward; he thereby extends the sacrifice. 1.1.1 [13]
He leads it forward with these undefined vyāhṛtis:
"Who yokes thee? He yokes thee. For whom does he yoke thee? For him he yokes thee.
Prajāpati is indeed undefined.
The sacrifice is Prajāpati; thus he yokes this very Prajāpati, the sacrifice. Furthermore, as for why he brings forward the waters:
by water indeed all this [universe] is pervaded; therefore, by this first rite, he [commences] with that which is already attained.
He obtains everything. 1.1.1.[15] Or rather, whatever [is his] here—
the Hotṛ, or the Adhvaryu, or the Brahman, or the Āgnīdhra, or the sacrificer himself— [he obtains all that].
He does not cause [them] to be taught; by this very act, everything of his becomes attained.
Furthermore, as for why he brings forward the water:
when the gods were sacrificing with the sacrifice, the asuras and rakṣases [attacked] them.
They did not guard them, thinking, "You shall not sacrifice. Because they did not guard them, therefore they are called *rakṣāṃsi* (demons).
Then the gods saw this thunderbolt: namely, the waters. The waters are indeed a thunderbolt, for the waters are a thunderbolt; therefore, by means of these...

They flow downward, they take their stand where they do so, and they burn; therefore, having raised this thunderbolt, they performed the sacrifice in that place which was free from fear, free from destruction, and sheltered from the wind. In the very same way, he now raises this thunderbolt and performs the sacrifice in that place which is free from fear, free from destruction, and sheltered from the wind. Therefore, he leads forward the waters. 1.1.1 [18]
Having poured them out, he places them to the north of the Gārhapatya fire.
Water is indeed female and Agni is male; the Gārhapatya is the home.
Thus, this procreative union is brought about right within the home. He who raises it up wields the thunderbolt.

"He who leads forward [the oblation], or he who raises the thunderbolt while being without a firm foundation, is unable to raise it; indeed, it destroys him. 1.1.1.[19] Now, as for why he places it on the Gārhapatya fire:
The Gārhapatya fire is indeed the home; the home is indeed a firm foundation, and thus he stands firmly established.
Moreover, this thunderbolt does not strike him; therefore, he places [the water] upon the Gārhapatya fire.
He leads them northward past the Āhavanīya fire.
The waters are indeed female and Agni is male; thus a productive union is brought about.
For such is the arrangement of a union: for the woman lies on the left side of the man.
They should not walk between them.

"One should not move them between while they are being used as a pair; one should not set them down after having moved them too far away, nor should one set them down before they have reached their place. For if he were to set them down after moving them too far away—since there is indeed a certain rivalry between fire and water—it would happen to the fire exactly as it happens wherever water touches it, for [the water] is upon the fire."

If he were to carry it beyond [the usual limit] and set it down, he would cause his rival to prosper; if he were to set it down before it has reached its destination, he would not attain that desire for which they are led forward. Therefore, he leads it forward precisely along the path, to the north of the Āhavanīya fire.
Then he strews around with grass.
He brings forward the vessels in pairs: the winnowing basket and the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle;
the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the potsherds; the yoke-pin (*śamyā*) and the black antelope skin; the mortar and pestle, and the large and small grinding stones—that makes ten.

The *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is indeed the *virāj*; thus he brings this sacrifice into correspondence with the *virāj*. Now, as for the pairing: a pair is indeed vigor; when two people join together, then there is vigor.
A pair is indeed a productive union; thus a productive union is thereby brought about. 1.1.2. [1]

Then he takes up the winnowing basket and the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle with the formula: "For the work of you two, for the service of you two. Sacrifice is indeed "work," for it is for the sake of sacrifice; therefore he says, "for the work of you two. "For the service of you two": for he indeed serves the sacrifice. 1.1.2. [2]
Then he restrains his speech.

The sacrifice is indeed speech; [he does so thinking,] "May I extend the sacrifice without disturbance. Then he heats [the implements], saying either, "The Rakṣas is scorched away! Scorched away are the enemies! The Rakṣas is burnt out! Burnt out are the enemies! 1.1.2.[3]

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases; thus, right from the beginning of the sacrifice, he drives away the destructive spirits and the Rakṣases. 1.1.2 [4]
Then he goes forth, saying,
"I follow the wide atmosphere. Indeed, it is along the atmosphere that the Rakṣas roams— rootless and severed on both sides— just as this man here is rootless and severed on both sides.
When it has been fully prepared, it moves through the intermediate space; thus, by means of that very *brahman*, he makes the intermediate space free from fear and free from destruction.
He should indeed take [the milk] from a cart.
In the beginning, indeed, this [world] was like a cart; whatever he intends to do first, thinking "I shall do that," therefore one should take it from a cart. A cart, moreover, is abundance. 1.1.2.
[6] A cart, moreover, is abundance.
The cart, indeed, is abundance; therefore, when there is much, they say, "It has become as much as can be carried by a cart.
Thus, one approaches that very abundance. Therefore, one should take [the water] from a cart alone.
The sacrifice does not dwell in a leather bag, nor in a jar, nor in a water-skin; for it was from a cart that the seers took [the water].
Those *yajus* formulas which were formerly for the bellows in relation to the sages have now become ordinary; "let us fashion sacrifice after sacrifice," he thought.
Therefore, one should take [the ghee] from the cart itself.
Or rather, one should take it from the pan; having spread it out there, one should take it from where they yoke [the oxen], for from where they yoke, thence they unyoke.
Of this very cart, Agni indeed is the pole, for Agni is the pole;
and when they drive it, their draft-animal becomes as if scorched by fire. Now, that which is behind the pillar—
The *uga* is indeed his altar; the *nīḍa* is his *havirdhāna*.
He touches the pole:
"Thou art the pole (*dhūḥ*). Strike down the striker; strike down him who strikes us."
"May we injure him; we shall injure him. This Agni is indeed the draft-animal (*dhurya*); he is about to pass beyond him when he is about to take the oblation.
It is for him that he thus makes amends. Thus Agni, the draft-animal, does not injure him as he passes beyond. 1.1.2. [11]
Regarding this, Āruṇi indeed said:
"Verily, with my teeth of *adharmas* I shall crush my rivals"—this is what he said concerning that.
Then, having touched the yoke-pole behind the post, he mutters:
"Thou art the best carrier of the gods,
the most liberal, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the most excellent invoker of the gods."
"You are unswerving;
O oblation-holder, stand firm, do not waver!"—he thus praises the cart; [thinking], "From one who has been praised and is well-disposed, I shall take the oblation.
"May your lord of the sacrifice not waver"—the lord of the sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer; thus he invokes freedom from harm for the sacrificer. 1.1.2. [13]

Then he steps upon it with the words, "May Viṣṇu step upon you. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he strode this stride across these worlds for the sake of the gods—this very stride which is here, with his first step.
With the second [step], he strode across this intermediate space;
with the highest, the sky. Indeed, Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, strides this very stride for him.
Then he gazes.
"Wide for the wind"—the wind is indeed the vital breath; thus, by means of the Brahman, he makes a wide passage for the vital breath, the wind. Then he throws it away.
"Struck away is the Rakṣas!"— if anything has been damaged there, or even if he does not touch it at all, he thereby strikes away the destructive Rākṣasas from that place.
Then he takes hold of it.
"Let them beg; fivefold is this [world], for these fingers are five; the sacrifice is indeed fivefold; thus he places the sacrifice itself here. 1.1.2. [17] Then he takes [the milk].

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee, acceptable to Agni"—for Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it. "With the arms of the Aśvins"—the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryu priests—"with the hands of Pūṣan"—Pūṣan is [the deity].
The tax-collector is food, and he who places it near with his hands is truth; the gods are the end and humans are the means.
By means of that very truth, he thus takes this.
Then he assigns it to the deity.

All the deities indeed attend upon the Adhvaryu when he is about to take the oblation, thinking, "He will utter my name; he will utter my name. He thus creates harmony among them while they are together. 1.1.2 [19]
Moreover, as for why he announces the deity:

for as many deities as the oblations are taken, they consider themselves to have a debt toward him; thus, whatever desire he may have for which he takes the oblation, they fulfill that desire for him.
Therefore, indeed, he assigns [the portions] to the deity. Having taken the oblations in this very manner as before, he then touches them with the formula:
"For existence, thee, not for non-existence! Thus, he causes that very thing from which he took them to swell again.
Then he looks toward the east, saying, "May I behold the light.
For this cart-pole becomes as if enveloped, and its eye, as it were, becomes seized by evil. The light is indeed the sacrifice; the gods are the days.
By means of its very sound, the sun beholds this from here. 1.1.2.
[22] Then he descends with the formula:
"May the dwellings on earth be firm. The dwellings are indeed the *duryās*; for these houses are liable to collapse.
Whichever Adhvaryu of this sacrificer performs the sacrifice, as he moves forward, [the sacrificer's] prosperity may follow him and flow away;
it is possible that his family will be thrown into disorder. Therefore, he makes them firm upon this earth;
thus they do not fall away, and thus they are not thrown into disorder. That is why he says: "May the dwellings be made firm."
"On the earth"—this is the meaning; then he says, "I go along the wide mid-air"; that has the same significance as before.
Now, for whomsoever they cook the sacrificial oblations on the *gārhapatya* fire, they set down the vessels on that *gārhapatya* fire.
Then he should set it down behind the *gārhapatya* fire-altar for one whose sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are cooked on the *āhavanīya*, and whose vessels are arranged around the *āhavanīya*;
then he should set it down behind the *āhavanīya*, saying:
"I set thee on the navel of the earth. The navel is indeed the center, and the center is free from danger; therefore he says, "On the navel of the earth."
"I set thee down," he says; "in the lap of Aditi," he says. For they say that when they guard something well-concealed, it is as if they place it in a lap;
therefore he says, "in the lap of Aditi. "O Agni, protect the offering," he says;
thereby he entrusts this oblation both to Agni for protection and to this earth; therefore he says, "O Agni, protect the offering. 1.1.3. [1]
He makes two strainers with [the formula], "You two are strainers, belonging to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "You two belong to the sacrifice.
These two are indeed [made] as a pair.
This indeed is the purifier: he who blows here [the wind]. He blows as if he were one;
yet he has entered within the person as these two, the outward-breath (*prāṇa*) and the inward-breath (*udāna*), moving forward and backward.
Therefore, according to the measure of this very [purifier], there are two [strainers]. 1.1.3. [3]
Or there may even be three;
for the *vyāna* is the third. But there are indeed only two; having purified these sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*) with those two, he sprinkles with them.
Now, as to why he purifies them with those two... 1.1.3 [4]
Vṛtra indeed lay here having encompassed all this—that which is between heaven and earth. Because he lay there having encompassed all this, he is named Vṛtra. 1.1.3.5
Indra slew him.

Being slain, he flowed out as stench toward the waters on every side; for this ocean flows out from every side. Therefore, some of the waters were repelled by it; they overflowed one over the other, and from that [came] these [waters].
These *darbha* blades are indeed water that has not turned putrid; for in other waters there is something as if mixed together, namely the stench which Vṛtra flowed out upon them.
He removes that very thing from these [waters] by means of these two purifiers; then he sprinkles with the pure waters. Therefore, he purifies by means of these two. 1.1.3. [6]
He purifies it with the formula:
"At the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun.
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies it. "With a flawless strainer"—for he who... [is the flawless strainer].
"This one purifies; this is the flawless purifier"—by saying "with the rays of the sun," he means this, for the rays of the sun are indeed the purifiers;
therefore he says, "with the rays of the sun.
Having placed them in his left hand...
With the right hand he points them out; he thus praises them and magnifies them:

"O divine waters, you who go first, you who drink first. For the waters are indeed divine; therefore he says, "O divine waters. As for "you who go first," it is because they go to the ocean that they are called "you who go first. As for "you who drink first," it is because they are the first [to drink] of King Soma...

"Therefore they eat first; [with the words] 'Lead this sacrifice today to the foremost place, lead the lord of the sacrifice to the foremost place, the well-established lord of the sacrifice who seeks the gods,' he thereby says: 'A successful sacrifice, a successful sacrificer!
[And with the words] 'Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra.'"
For it was these very ones that Indra chose when contending with Vṛtra;
for with them he struck him down. Therefore he says, "Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra.
And [he says], "You chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra."
"For these indeed chose Indra when he was contending with Vṛtra; for with these they struck him down. Therefore he says: 'You chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra.
"You are sprinkled," [he says].
He hides it from these [deities], and then he sprinkles the oblation. Indeed, there is one single bond for the sprinkling: he thereby makes it pure.
He sprinkles it, saying, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Agni"; thus, he offers it to whichever deity the oblation belongs.
In this very manner, he makes [the materials] pure, having sprinkled the sacrificial oblations as before. 1.1.3.
[12] Then he sprinkles the sacrificial vessels with [the mantra]:
"Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods," for the sake of the divine rite.

"For it purifies the work for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods; 'that which you have struck while impure, this I now purify for you'—thus, whatever impurity there was among them here, whether a carpenter or someone else who was unclean struck [the wood], that he now makes pure for them with water. Therefore he says: 'That which you have struck while impure, this...'"
"Vastacundhāmīti. Then he takes up the black antelope skin for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice; for the sacrifice indeed fled away from the gods.

Having become black, he moved about; the gods, having discovered him, stripped away his skin and carried it off. Those hairs of his which were white and those which were black are the form of the *ṛg* verses and the *sāman* chants; those which were white are [the form of the *sāmans*].

Those which are black are the form of the *sāmans*, and those which are white are the form of the *ṛcs*; or alternatively, those which are black are the form of the *sāmans* and those which are white are the form of the *ṛcs*, while those which are tawny or golden are the form of the *yajus*. 1.1.4. [3]
This triple Vidyā is the sacrifice;

this black antelope skin is its craft and this its color. That there is a black antelope skin is for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice; therefore they undergo consecration upon the black antelope skin for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice.

Therefore, there is threshing and pounding so that the oblation may not be spilled; whatever grain or flour might be spilled here, it is for the sake of ensuring that the sacrifice remains established within the sacrifice. That is why there is threshing and pounding. 1.1.4. [4]

Then he takes up the black antelope skin with the words, "Thou art a refuge. For this is indeed the skin of the black antelope; that is his human refuge, but among the gods it is a refuge; therefore he says, "Thou art a refuge. He shakes it out with the words, "Shaken off is the Rakṣas, shaken off are the enemies."
Thereby he drives away the destructive powers and the *rakṣas* from here; he shakes out the vessels so as to cast off whatever impurity has come upon them.
Then he spreads [the grass] with its points directed westward.
"You are the skin of Aditi; may Aditi acknowledge you! Aditi is indeed this earth, and her skin is that which is upon her—whatever exists here. Therefore he says, "You are the skin of Aditi.
"May Aditi acknowledge you," he says, for one recognizes one's own. He thus speaks this very recognition to the black antelope skin.
"Let them not harm one another"—thus [the mortar] is placed with the left hand.
Then he brings the mortar with his right hand, thinking, "Lest the destructive *rakṣas* demons enter here before [the sacrifice]," for [it is said in] the Brāhmaṇa: "Indeed..."
Because he is the repeller of the *rakṣases*, he therefore places [the mortar] with his left hand in the "placed" (*abhinihita*) position. 1.1.4.
[7] Then he sets down the mortar, saying either: "Thou art a stone, made of wood; thou art a pressing-stone, broad-based."

Just as they press King Soma with the pressing-stones, even so does he press the Haviryajña with the mortar and pestle and the large and small grinding stones; "stones" (adrayaḥ) is indeed one of their names, therefore he says, "Thou art a stone," and "thou art made of wood."
"Thus, for this pressing-stone is made of wood; 'Thou art a broad-based stone,' for this is indeed a stone and it is broad-based.
'May the skin of Aditi recognize thee!'—he says this to create a mutual understanding between the black antelope skin and the stone, so that they may not harm one another.
Then he pours out the oblation-material with the words, "Thou art the body of Agni, the release of speech. For the sacrifice is indeed the body of Agni; thus it is the release of speech.
For that speech which he restrains when about to take the oblation, he releases here at this point.

Now, as for why they release this speech here: it is because this sacrifice has established itself in the mortar; it is because it has been spread out. Therefore, he says, "the release of speech. If one were to utter human speech before this point, [it would be a fault]. 1.1.4 [9] Sa yadidam purā mānuṣīṃ vācaṃ vyāharet.
In that case, one should mutter either a verse or a sacrificial formula belonging to Viṣṇu;

for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, and thus he recommences the sacrifice. This is its expiation: "I take thee for the feast of the gods," for the oblation is taken while saying, "I invoke the gods. 1.1.4. [10]
Then he takes up the mace with the formula:

"Thou art the great stone, belonging to the trees. For it is indeed the great stone, and it belongs to the trees. He places it down [on the mortar] with the formula: "Prepare this oblation for the gods; prepare it well; prepare it! He prepares this.

"Prepare the oblation for the gods; prepare it well-prepared"—this is what he says. 1.1.4. [11] Then he causes the preparer of the oblation to call out: "O preparer of the oblation, come! O preparer of the oblation, come! Speech, indeed, is the preparer of the oblation.

By this, he releases speech itself; for speech is indeed the sacrifice, and thus he calls the sacrifice back again. These, then, are the four [calls] of speech: "Come! for the Brāhmaṇa; "Come hither! for the Rājanya; "Approach! for the Vaiśya; and "Hasten! for the Śūdra. 1.1.4. [12] Indeed, these are the four. "Come! is for the Brāhmaṇa; "Come hither! is for the Vaiśya. And so on.
And for a member of the royal caste, [he says] "Run hither! For a Śūdra, he says the same as for a Brāhmaṇa;
for this is most worthy of sacrifice, and this indeed is the most peaceful form of speech: "Come here! Therefore, one should say only "Come here. 1.1.4. [13] Now, formerly...

The wife herself used to rise as the preparer of the oblation; even now, whoever rises for that purpose, when he causes the preparer of the oblation to respond, then he alone strikes together the lower and upper grinding stones.
This is why they cause this speech here to respond. 1.1.4 [14]
Manu indeed had a bull;
in it was entered speech that slays Asuras and slays rivals. From its snorting and bellowing, the Asuras and Rakṣasas went away being crushed. Those Asuras said to one another, "Alas, this is evil!"
"This bull does not submit; how indeed might we deceive him? Thus [they thought].
Kilāta and Akuli—these two were the Asura-Brahmins.
They both said: [1.1.4] "We two shall deceive him."
"Śraddhā, the goddess, and Manu indeed did not know [the answer]. They came and said, 'O Manu, let us two perform the sacrifice for you.
He asked, 'By what means? They replied, 'By this bull. He agreed, saying, 'So be it. When that bull was slaughtered, his speech departed. 1.1.4 [16] It entered Manu’s wife, Manāvī.

Wherever they heard her as she spoke, from that very place the Asuras and Rakṣasas would depart, being crushed. Those Asuras then deliberated: "Something worse than this is surely overtaking us, for human speech speaks more abundantly. Then Kilāta and Ākulī said: "He is indeed one whose god is faith (śraddhādeva)."
"Manu surely knows the sound," they thought; so the two came and said, "O Manu, let us sacrifice for you.
"With what? he asked. "With this very wife," they replied. "So be it," he said. When she was being immolated, her speech departed. It entered the sacrificial fire and the sacrificial vessels.
Then they were unable to drive her away;
this very voice, which slays the Asuras, speaks aloud. For him who knows this, if they respond with this same speech here, his rivals indeed become more wretched. 1.1.4 [18]
He strikes it, saying, "Thou art a cock, honey-tongued. For he was indeed honey-tongued for the gods and poison-tongued for the Asuras.
"Be thou that which was for the gods," he thereby says; "proclaim food and strength through thee, we [the sacrificers]."
"We shall conquer each and every battle"— of this there is nothing hidden.
Then he takes up the winnowing basket with the formula,
"Thou art grown by rain," for it is indeed grown by rain, whether it be made of reeds or otherwise.
Just as rain causes the reeds and their stalks to grow, so does he cause these to grow. 1.1.4. [20] Then he pours out the oblation-material with the formula:
"May the rain-grown recognize thee! For indeed, these are rain-grown. If...
"If they are rice or barley, it causes them to grow even more during the rainy season; thus he speaks this greeting to the winnowing basket so that they may not harm one another. Then he winnows.
"Blown away is the Rakṣas; blown away are the enemies," he says. Then he throws out the husks with, "Struck down is the Rakṣas.
Thus he strikes away the destructive Rakṣasas from here. Then he winnows [the rice].

"May Vāyu separate you"—this Vāyu is indeed he who blows here; for he separates everything here that is separated. Thus, it is he who now separates these [grains] at the very moment they reach that point where he winnows them. 1.1.4. [23]
Then he consecrates it with the mantra: "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you with his flawless hand;
may you be well-received. Then he husks it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold. 1.1.4 [24]
Now, some thresh [the grains] while saying, "Be pure for the gods! Be pure for the gods!

But one should not do so; for this oblation has already been assigned to its specific deity, yet by saying "Be pure for the gods," he makes it belong to all the gods (vaiśvadeva). Therefore, he should do so silently.
He should winnow the grain.
One of them indeed sets down the potsherds, while the other sets down the large and small grinding stones; thus these two things are done together.
Now, that which is done—namely, this pair being performed together—is as follows:
[1.2.1.2] The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice. Those [bones] here are the skull-bones of the head;
these very [pieces] are its skull-bones. The ground flour is the brain. Thus, these two parts of the body we shall perform together as one and the same.
Therefore, these two things are performed together.
Now, he who lays down the potsherds takes up the fire-stirring stick (*upaveṣa*) with the formula, "Thou art the bold one. For by means of this, he [stirs] the fire...
Because he approaches it boldly, it is called *dhṛṣṭi* (the bold one); and because with it he reaches out toward the sacrifice, he as if embraces it, therefore it is called *upaveṣa* (the embracer).
With it, he pushes the embers forward.

"O Agni, drive away the raw-eating Agni; expel the flesh-eater!"—for that by which humans eat after cooking this [food] is the raw-eater (āmāda), and that by which they burn a person is the flesh-eater (kravyād). It is these two he thus drives away from here. 1.2.1. [5]

Then he heats the charcoal with the formula: "Bring hither the one who goes to the gods! [The meaning is: "In him who goes to the gods, let us cook the oblations; in him let us extend the sacrifice. For this reason, he heats it. 1.2.1. [6]
He places it down with the middle *kapāla*.
The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were indeed afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases, [thinking], "Lest the destructive spirits [should seize us] from below."
"The Rakṣases are about to rise up," [he thinks], for Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases; therefore he lays it down in this manner.
Now, as to why it is this very one and no other: it is this one that is prepared with the Yajus-formula and is fit for sacrifice; therefore he lays it down over the middle potsherd. 1.2.1. [7]
He lays it down with the formula: "Thou art the firm one; make the earth firm. By means of the very form of the earth, he thus makes this [earth] firm;
by this very act, he repels his hateful rival. "Thee, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility..."

"I place thee with the *sajātavana* brick for the slaying of the enemy"—for the blessing in the *yajus*-formulas is indeed manifold; he thus invokes both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*. "With the *sajātavana*"—the *sajātās* (kinsmen) are indeed abundance; he thus invokes abundance. "I place thee for the slaying of the enemy"—if he does not practice sorcery, [this is the formula]; but if he should practice sorcery, [he says] "of so-and-so."
"Drive them away," he should say; for it remains pressed down by the finger of his left hand.
Then he throws out the charcoal, thinking, "Lest the destructive demons (*nāṣṭrā rakṣāṃsi*) enter here before [the fire is established]," for so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Because he is the repeller of the *rakṣases*, therefore it remains pressed down by a finger of the left hand. 1.2.1 [9] Then he places a coal upon it with the mantra: "O Agni, grasp the sacred formulation (*brahman*)," lest the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) come here before that.
"May the *rakṣases* enter [it]," he says; for Agni is the repeller of the *rakṣases*, therefore he piles it upon this [brick].
Then he lays down that which is behind:
"Thou art the support; make firm the atmosphere," he says; [this is] for the sake of the atmosphere itself.

By form this very [brick] is made firm; by this very [form] he repels the hateful rival. "I set thee down, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility, winner of the kinsmen, for the destruction of the rival"—thus [he says].
Then he sets down that which was in front.
"You are the support; make the sky firm"—by means of the very form of the sky, he thus makes this [earth] firm.
"With this, bind it fast.
Then, that which is on the south, he places there.
"I set thee down for all the quarters," he says;

for whatever there may be beyond these worlds—a fourth or not—it is by that very thing that he repels his hateful enemy. For that which is beyond these worlds—a fourth or not—is indeed uncertain (*anaddhā*).

It is enclosed on all sides because it encompasses all the quarters; therefore he says, "I set thee down for all the quarters. He sets down the other potsherds either silently, or with the formula, "Ye are piled, piled upwards.
Then he covers them over with coals.

"By the ascetic fervor (*tapas*) of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, do you perform your penance"—this indeed is the most brilliant splendor, namely the well-heated [fires] of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases; therefore, he piles it over this.
Now, as for him who lays down the two millstones (*dṛṣad-upale*).
He takes up the black antelope skin with the words, "Thou art a shelter";
he shakes it with the words, "Shaken off is the Rakṣas, shaken off are the enemies"—the significance of this is the same as before.
He spreads it out with the neck toward the west, saying, "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may Aditi recognize thee"—the significance of this is the same as before.
The Kinsman 1.2.1.[15]:
Now he places the lower millstone.
"Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, the mountain-like; may the skin of the Ādityas recognize thee! For she is indeed Dhiṣaṇā.
"For Parvatī, for thee, let the Ādityas know thy skin"—he says this to give a name to the black antelope skin, so that they two may not harm one another; for this earth is indeed that [skin] in form.
Then he places a yoke-pin with its tip pointing northward.

"Thou art the support of heaven," he says; this refers to the intermediate space by its form, for by the intermediate space these two, heaven and earth, are supported; therefore he says, "Thou art the support of heaven.
Then he lays down the pebble.
"You are Dhiṣaṇā, daughter of the mountain; may the mountain recognize you! For she is the younger one, as it were, like a daughter;

therefore he says, "daughter of the mountain. "May the mountain recognize you," he says, for she recognizes her own kin; thus he speaks this mutual recognition to the large and small millstones so that they do not injure one another.

This [upper millstone] is heaven by its form; the two millstones are the jaws; the *śamyā* (wooden pin) is the tongue. Therefore, one strikes together with the *śamyā*, for one speaks with the tongue.
1.2.1. [18] Now he pours out the sacrificial oblation.
"You are grain; refresh the gods," he says, for grain indeed refreshes the gods; thus it is that the oblation is taken. 1.2.1.
[19] Then he grinds it.
"For breath thee, for out-breath thee, for diffused breath thee; may I bestow long extension for life"—with these words he pushes it forward.
"May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you with his flawless hand—for sight thee! Thus [he says].
Now, as to why he grinds it in this manner:
The living being is indeed the oblation of the gods;
the immortal is the oblation of the immortals. Yet, by means of the mortar and pestle, and the lower and upper grinding stones, they slaughter this sacrificial oblation.

When he says, "For out-breath thee, for up-breath thee," he thereby bestows out-breath and up-breath; when he says, "For through-breath thee," he thereby bestows through-breath; when he says, "May I place you along a long extension for the sake of life," he thereby bestows life; and when [he says], "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you with his flawless hand so that they may be well-received," [he says] "For sight thee."

He bestows that eye; for these indeed belong to one who lives. Thus, this living one indeed becomes the oblation for the gods, the immortal for the immortals. Therefore, he grinds it thus; they grind it, and having ground it, they heat the potsherds.
Then one pours out the clarified butter.
Whatever oblation is taken for a specified deity, it belongs to that many deities;
he takes it with another *yajus* formula, for this [butter] does not belong to any single deity.
When taking the oblation, he gives an instruction; since it is clarified butter (*ājya*), he takes it with an undefined *yajus*: "Thou art the milk of the great ones.

For some indeed say that "the great ones" (*mahī*) is the name of cows; this is their milk, therefore he says, "Thou art the milk of the great ones. Thus, indeed, it becomes taken for him by means of the *yajus* itself; for this reason, too, he speaks thus.
"Thou art the milk of the great ones," [he says].
He pours [the grain] into [the vessel] containing the strainers; having placed the two strainers into the bowl, [he says], "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ..."
"With the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour together"—this is the significance of that sacrificial formula (*yajus*).
Then he sits down within the altar (*antarvedi*).
Now one person comes with the secondary waters (*upasarjanī*); he brings them, and [pours them] through the two strainers (*pavitra*).
"He unites with the waters, with the plants"— for indeed, these [doughs] unite with these ground plants; "the plants with their sap"— for indeed,
these ground plants unite with the water, for water is their sap.

"May these wealthy ones be united with the moving ones"—the wealthy ones are the waters and the moving ones are the plants, for it is these two together that are here united. "May the honeyed ones be united with the honeyed ones"—by this he means, "may the sapful ones be united with the sapful ones. 1.2.2. [3]
Then he mixes it, saying, "I mix thee for generation. Just as what has been moistened is born from fire, even so does he mix it. 1.2.2. [4]
Then he divides it into two parts;
if there are two oblations— as there are indeed two oblations at the full moon sacrifice—
then where [he proceeds] again...

When he is about to offer the oblation, he touches it with the words, "This is for Agni; this is for Agni-Soma. For in the beginning they take the sacrificial offerings separately, but then they pound them together and grind them together; he makes them separate again, and therefore he touches it in this manner. He places the cake upon the fire, and that other one [the butter] he places upon the fire as well. 1.2.2. [5]

This, indeed, is done both together; for that which is done here as both together—this clarified butter (ājya) is one half of the self of the sacrifice, and this oblation (havis) is the other half. [The thought is:
"May we cause both that half and this half to go to Agni. Therefore, this is done both together in this manner.
This very self of the sacrifice is being joined together. He places the clarified butter on the fire with the words, "For food (iṣe) thee! By saying "For food thee," he speaks for the sake of rain.
He then removes it with the formula, "For strength, thee! He thereby refers to that vigorous sap which is produced from rain.
Then he spreads the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) over [the potsherds] with the formula, "Thou art dharma"; he thereby makes this very sacrifice into the Gharma, as it were.

"He should extend it; thus he extends it with the words, 'All-life,' thereby bestowing life upon it. He spreads it out with the words, "O wide-expanding one, expand widely!"—thus he indeed causes it to expand widely.
"May the lord of the sacrifice spread out"—the lord of the sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer; thus he invokes this blessing for the sacrificer himself.
He should not, however, make it excessively wide.

If he were to make it broad, he would indeed make it human; and that which is human is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I make the sacrifice a failure," he should therefore not make it excessively broad.
"One should make it the size of a horse's hoof," so some say.
"Who knows how large a horse's hoof is? One should make it however large one personally considers it broad in one's mind; one should do it thus. 1.2.2 [11]

He touches it with water, either once or thrice. Whatever of this [sacrificial food] they here injure while threshing or grinding, or whatever they diminish or tear asunder—that is water, for water is a means of pacification; thus he pacifies it with water, that which is a means of pacification, and he unites it with water.
Therefore, he touches [the horse] with water.
He touches it, saying:
"O Agni, do not harm its skin," for [he does so] by means of Agni.
"Thinking, 'I shall heat him thoroughly,' he says this: 'May this one not harm your skin'—it is for this very purpose that he speaks thus.
He carries fire around it;
he thus encloses it with fire so that no destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) may [enter] it.
"May the Rākṣasas be struck down," [he says], for Agni is the slayer of the Rākṣasas; therefore he carries fire around it.
He cooks it, saying:
"May the god Savitṛ cook thee. Indeed, no human is its cooker; it is a god.

"Truly, it is Savitṛ, the god, who cooks him on the highest firmament. By saying "on the highest firmament," he says this with reference to the gods. He touches it, saying, "I know him. That is why he touches it. He touches it thus:
[1.2.2] "I know him."
"Do not fear, do not tremble"—by saying this, he means: "Do not be afraid, do not tremble, because I, a human being, am touching you while you are as yet non-human.
When it is cooked, he then covers it.

He covers it because he thinks, "Lest the destructive spirits and demons look down upon it from above," and also because he thinks, "Lest it lie as if naked or as if robbed. For this reason, indeed, he covers it.
He covers it.

"The sacrifice shall be unexhausted; may the offspring of the sacrificer be unexhausted"—thinking thus, "lest either the sacrifice or the sacrificer should become exhausted because I am covering this," he covers it in this manner.
Then follows the wiping of the vessel.
He pours out the water used for washing the fingers to the Āptyas; as to why he pours it out to the Āptyas:
in the beginning, Agni was indeed divided into four parts. That Agni whom they first chose for the office of Hotṛ—[he was... 1.2.3.[1]

He ran forward; they covered him, and he ran forward again. He ran forward a second time; they covered him, and he ran forward again. He ran forward a third time; they covered him, and he ran forward again.

Then, that Agni who exists here at present hid himself out of fear; he entered into the waters. The gods, having discovered him, suddenly brought him back from the waters by force. He stood threatening the waters, saying, "You are drenched, you who provide no place of refuge!"
"Stay! Whomsoever among you leads me away from my desire," he said; from that, the Āptyas were born: Trita, Dvita, and Ekata.
They wandered with Indra, just as a Brāhmaṇa follows a king here [in this world]. When [he encountered] the three-headed one...
He slew Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ; even though he was destined for death, they knew this, for Trita had indeed slain him long ago. Indra was released from that [guilt], for he is a god.
Then those [sages] said:
"Let those who have announced this victim of his come right up to this sin," he said. "Why?

[The gods replied,] "So that the sacrifice may be cleansed from them. Thus, the sacrifice is cleansed from them when they pour out for them the rinsing of the vessel and the washing of the fingers. 1.2.3. [4]

The Āptyas said to him: "We have indeed reached this; let us lead it beyond us."—"Beyond whom?"—"Beyond whoever should sacrifice with an oblation that lacks a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Therefore, one should not sacrifice with an oblation that lacks a sacrificial fee; for the sacrifice was wiped away from the Āptyas. And the Āptyas...
"He who sacrifices with an offering that lacks a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is defiled by it.
Then the gods devised this sacrificial fee for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, namely the *anvāhārya* rice; [they did this] so that the offering would not be "without a fee" (*adakṣiṇa*).
He pours it out separately, and thus he creates discord among them. He heats it over the fire, and thus [he provides for] them.
When it has been cooked, he pours it out [with the words]: "For Trita thee! For Dvita thee! For Ekata thee! For this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) which is offered is indeed an animal;
for the gods [sacrificed] the human being.

In the beginning, they immolated a beast; when it had been immolated, its vital essence departed and entered a horse. They immolated the horse; when it had been immolated, its vital essence departed and entered a cow.
They immolated the cow... [it entered a sheep]... they immolated the sheep... [it entered a goat]... they immolated the goat.
When he had not been obtained, his vigor departed.
It entered this earth;
they searched for it by digging and found it—these two [fires].
Therefore, even now, when people dig for rice and barley, they find them as if by chance.

Indeed, as much vigor as all these animals would have possessed had they been sacrificed, so much vigor does his oblation possess for one who knows this. This is the point at which they say, "The animal is fivefold. 1.2.3 [8]
When they are ground, they become hair;
when he pours water, it becomes skin;
when he mixes them, it becomes flesh, for at that time it becomes continuous, and flesh is indeed continuous.

When it has been boiled, it then becomes bone, for at that time it is indeed like wood; "wood" (dāru) refers to bone. Then, when he is about to remove it from the fire, he bastes it; he thereby places marrow into it. This is how it comes to be complete, as they say:
"The animal is fivefold. 1.2.3 [9]
The man whom they sacrificed became a *kiṃpuruṣa*; the horse and the cow which they sacrificed became the *gaura* and the *gavaya* respectively;
the sheep which they sacrificed became a camel; and the goat which they sacrificed became a *śarabha*.
"Therefore, one must not eat of these animals; for these animals have departed from the sacrificial essence. 1.2.4.
[1] When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, it shattered into four pieces upon being struck. Of that—

It was either as large as a wooden sword (*sphya*) or as large as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or as large as a chariot wheel; and where he struck it, a splinter broke off and fell, becoming an arrow (*śara*); therefore it is called *śara*. Thus that thunderbolt (*vajra*) became fourfold. 1.2.4 [2]
Then, with two [implements] the Brāhmaṇas proceed at the sacrifice, and with two the kinsmen of the Rājanya at the piercing:
with the sacrificial post and the wooden sword (sphya) the Brāhmaṇas, and with the chariot and the arrow the kinsmen of the Rājanya.
Now, as for why he takes up the wooden sword:

Just as Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra, even so does he now raise this thunderbolt against evil, against the hater, against the enemy; therefore, indeed, he takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*).
He takes it up [with the formula]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee."

‘To the gods, for the performance of the sacrifice’—Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up. ‘With the arms of the Aśvins’—the two Aśvins are the Adhvaryus; thus, with their very arms he takes it up, not with his own. For this [sacrificial ladle] is a thunderbolt, and no mortal is its bearer; therefore, he takes it up with these deities. 1.2.4. [5]
"I take that which is made for the sacrifice for the gods.

Indeed, the *adhvara* is the sacrifice; thus he says, "I take that which is made for the sacrifice for the gods. Having placed it in his left hand and stroked it with his right, he mutters the prayer.
He indeed sharpens this [sacrificial post] when he mutters [the formula]. He mutters: "Thou art the right arm of Indra. For that which is the right arm of Indra is indeed the most powerful;
therefore he says, "Thou art the right arm of Indra. "Thousand-edged, hundred-fold radiant," he says.
That thunderbolt indeed had a thousand points and was of fierce splendor, which he hurled at Vṛtra; it is that very one he now makes.
"Thou art Vāyu, of sharp splendor"—for this is the most brilliant splendor, namely this wind that blows here. This...

"He blows across these worlds crosswise; he thus sharpens him [the breath] for the slaying of the enemy. If he does not intend to practice sorcery, he says, "For the slaying of such-and-such"; but if he intends to practice sorcery, he says, "For the slaying of that one. With that sharpened [breath], he does not touch himself nor the earth, lest he [injure] either himself or the earth with this sharpened thunderbolt.
"Lest I should kill," he thinks; therefore, he does not touch himself nor the earth.
1.2.4 [8] Now, the gods and the Asuras—both of them being the offspring of Prajāpati—vied with one another. Whenever the gods conquered the Asuras...
Then they used to rise up against them once again. 1.2.4. [9] Those gods said:
"We are indeed conquering the Asuras, yet they rise up against us again; how can this be?"
"Let us conquer them so that we cannot be conquered. 1.2.4 [10] Then Agni said: "If they flee toward the north, they will escape us"; and so they used to escape by fleeing toward the north.
They were released.
Then that Fire said:
"I will search from the north; then you shall surround [the enemy] from here."
"Having restrained them, we shall deposit them within these worlds, so that they will not be gathered together again beyond these four worlds.
Then Agni went around to the north.

Then they hemmed them in from here; having hemmed them in, they confined them within these worlds. And because they did not come together again beyond these four worlds, that is the reason why there is the *stambayajus*. 1.2.4 [13]
He who is that Agnīdh who goes around on the north side is Agni himself by his very nature; the Adhvaryu thus confines them from this side,
and having confined them, he establishes them with these worlds, even beyond these worlds.

The fourth [layer] thereafter they do not lift up again; therefore even now the Asuras do not lift themselves up. For with that very same [power] by which the gods repelled them, with that same *brahman* they repel them even now at the sacrifice. And whoever acts as an enemy toward the sacrificer—

And whoever hates him, him he lays low with these very worlds; and whatever exceeds these worlds, all that he takes away from this [earth] alone, for in her all these worlds are established. For what indeed could he take away, saying, "I take the atmosphere," or "I take the sky"?
"Therefore, he takes away everything from her. 1.2.4. [15] Then, having placed a blade of grass in between, he strikes; [thinking]: "Lest I injure the earth with this sharpened thunderbolt."
Therefore, he strikes after placing a blade of grass in between.
He strikes [it], saying:
"O Earth, place of sacrifice for the gods! May I not harm the root of your plant; [I strike] as if leaving the upper root intact."
Or rather, he does this while taking it up; he says this to it: "May I not harm the roots of the plants.
"Go to the fold, to the cow-pen"—even as he is about to set it down, he thus makes it non-departing, for that which is within the fold is indeed non-departing;
therefore he says, "Go to the fold, to the cow-pen. "May the sky rain for thee"—for wherever there is [a place] for it...
By digging, they make it cruel and destroy it; water is peace, so with water he pacifies it through peace, and with water he joins it together.

Therefore he says, "May the sky rain for you. When he says, "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, upon this furthest earth," he is indeed saying to the divine Savitṛ, "Bind him in blind darkness," when he says "upon the furthest [earth]."

"On the earth with six hundred fetters"—by this he says to Amuṣya: "Whoever hates us and whomsoever we hate, do not release him from this. If he does not intend to practice sorcery, [he says this]; but if he intends to practice sorcery, he should say: "Release so-and-so from this. 1.2.4. [17]
Then he strikes a second time with the formula:

"May I drive away Araru from the earth, the place of sacrifice for the gods. For Araru was indeed the name of an Asura-Rakshasa; the gods drove him away from this earth, and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now drives him away from it.
"Go to Vraja, to the cow-pen; may the sky rain for you. O God Savitṛ, bind him with a hundred nooses upon this furthest earth—him who hates us and whom we hate—and do not release him from there.
(1.2.4) [18] The Agnīdh places it down over that.

"O Araru, do not fly up to heaven!"—for when the gods were striking away the Asura-Rakṣasa Araru, he sought to fly up to heaven; Agni laid him down, saying, "O Araru, do not fly up to heaven! and so he did not fly up to heaven. In the same way, the Adhvaryu now separates him from this world.
"The Agnīdh [priest] [comes] from heaven; therefore he acts in this way.
Then he strikes the third [brick], saying:
"May thy drop not spill onto the sky. This [drop] which belongs to her is indeed her drop.
"Upon this sap the creatures subsist; may it not fall from heaven for you"—this is what he says with these words. "Go to the fold, O cow...
[he says]. He indeed carries it three times with the *yajus* formula.
There are indeed these three worlds; with these very worlds he thus lays him down.
For these worlds are manifest (addhā), and that which is the *yajuṣ* is manifest; therefore he carries it thrice with the *yajuṣ*. 1.2.4.
The fourth [syllable] is silent.
Whether there is anything beyond these worlds or not, by that very fact he strikes down his hateful rival; for it is indeterminate whether there is anything beyond these worlds or not.
[The fourth layer is] covered over; that which is silent—therefore the fourth is done in silence. 1.2.5.
[1] The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended. Then the gods were, as it were, inferior.
The Asuras thought, "This world indeed belongs to us alone.
They said, "Come, let us divide this earth; having divided it, let us live upon it.
They marched forward from the west toward the east, dividing it with ox-hides.
The gods heard of that:
"The Asuras are indeed dividing this earth; come, let us go to where the Asuras are dividing it. What shall we become if we do not share in it? They [went] to the sacrifice itself.

"Let them come, placing Viṣṇu at their head. They said, "Grant us a share in this earth; let there be a portion for us as well in this [earth]. The Asuras, as if feeling resentment, said, "We shall give you only as much as this Viṣṇu lies upon."
Vishnu was indeed a dwarf.
At that, the gods were not displeased, saying, "A great thing has come to us, they have given us what is commensurate with our sacrifice. 1.2.5 [6]
Having laid Viṣṇu facing eastward, they enclosed him on all sides with the meters: "With the Gāyatrī meter I enclose thee," [he says] from the south;
"With the Triṣṭubh meter I enclose thee," from the west; "With the Jagatī meter... [he says from the north].
"To the north, [he says], 'I enclose thee with the meters. Having thus enclosed it on both sides with the meters and having placed the fire in front, they worship with that."
Exerting themselves, they wandered about and thereby discovered this entire earth. Because they discovered this entire earth with it, it is called the *vedi* (altar).
Therefore, they say: "As great as the *vedi* is, so great is the earth," for with this they indeed discovered this entire earth.
In the same way, one thus appropriates this entire earth from one's rivals and excludes them from it.
One who knows this thus subdues his rivals.
This very Viṣṇu was exhausted;
Agni, surrounded on all sides by the meters, did not depart from his front.
Then he dug up the roots of the medicinal plants.
Those gods said, "Where indeed has Viṣṇu gone? Where indeed has the sacrifice gone? They replied, "He is on all sides with the meters."

"The fire has been taken hold of from the front; there is no moving away from here. Search right here! So they searched for it as if digging, and they found it at a depth of three finger-breadths. Therefore, the altar (vedi) should be three finger-breadths deep.
And indeed, Pāñci also made the altar of the Soma sacrifice exactly three finger-breadths deep.
One should not do it in that way.

He was indeed searching for the roots of the plants; therefore, one should say, "He should dig up the very roots of the plants. And because they found Viṣṇu there, therefore it is called the *vedi* (the sacrificial altar). 1.2.5 [11]
They enclosed it with the subsequent enclosure, saying,
"Thou art subtle and thou art auspicious," whereby they, having found this very earth, made it subtle and auspicious on the south; and saying, "Thou art pleasant and thou art a good seat."

Thereafter, having discerned this very earth, they made it pleasant and comfortable to sit upon with the words, "Thou art full of vigor and full of milk"; and from the north, having discerned this very earth, they made it full of sap and fit for subsistence.
He indeed performs the first enclosure three times.

Three times more than that makes six; there are six seasons in a year, and the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, so much of it he thus encompasses. 1.2.5. [13]
With six *vyāhṛtis* he first encloses the enclosure; with six [more] he encloses the latter. That makes twelve times.
There are indeed twelve months in a year, and the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati. As great as the sacrifice is—

He takes up exactly as much of it as its measure allows. 1.2.5 [14] "It should be a fathom long at the back," they say; for man is of this extent, since he is measured by a man, being three cubits long.
The east is the threefold sacrifice; there is no fixed measure here, one should make it as large as one thinks fit in one's own mind.
On both sides of the fire, he raises the shoulder-bones.

The altar is indeed a woman, and Agni is a man; having embraced the man, the woman lies down, and thus this procreative union is brought about. Therefore, he raises the shoulder-bones on both sides of the fire.
That [altar] should indeed be wider at the back.
Having gathered it together in the middle, they again place it in front, just as people praise a woman thus: "She has broad hips, well-rounded shoulders, and a slender waist.
By doing so, he makes her acceptable to the gods. 1.2.5 [17]
It should indeed slope toward the east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or it may slope toward the north, for the north is the direction of men.
He throws up loose earth toward the south, for that is the direction of the ancestors; were it to slope toward the south, [it would be so].

Quickly indeed does the sacrificer go to that world, and thus the sacrificer lives long; therefore he throws up loose earth from the south and makes it possessed of loose earth. Loose earth is indeed cattle; he thus makes this [altar] possessed of cattle. 1.2.5. [18]
He wipes that [altar].

The gods, indeed, were about to engage in battle; they said, "Come now, let us place that immortal place of sacrifice belonging to this earth upon the moon, so that if the Asuras should come here from there..."

"Let us conquer by worshipping and exerting ourselves from that very place; then we shall overcome them again. Whatever immortal portion of this earth there was as a sacrificial ground for the gods, they deposited it in the moon; that is what appears as the black spot in the moon.
Therefore, they say, "In the moon is the sacrificial ground of this earth. And indeed...
When his sacrifice has been performed upon this sacrificial ground of the gods, he therefore wipes it clean.
He wipes it clean with the words:
"Before the flowing of the cruel one, O mighty one. The "cruel" is indeed battle, for [battle occurs] in combat.

"A cruel deed is done; the man is slain, the horse lies dead"—for indeed, they deposited this [life] from the battles of old; therefore he says, "O Virapśin, before the spreading of cruelty. "Having taken up the earth, the giver of life"—for what life there was for this earth, they deposited it in the moon; therefore he says, "having taken up the earth."

"By means of the *yāma*s they have sent her forth, thinking 'she who grants life,' with the *svadhā* offerings in the moon"—by this he says, "that which the Brahmans have established in the moon. "The wise, pointing to her, sacrifice"—by this they indeed sacrifice while pointing to her.
And truly, for one who knows this, his sacrifice is performed even in this very place of divine worship (*devayajana*). 1.2.5 [20]
Then he says, "Set down the sprinkling waters. The wooden sword (sphya) is indeed a thunderbolt, and the Brahmin has previously guarded this sacrifice; the waters are also a thunderbolt.
Thus, he sets them down for the purpose of protection by means of that thunderbolt. He, indeed...

While the *prokṣaṇī* waters are being held directly above [the altar], he then raises the wooden sword (*sphya*). Now, if he were to set down the *prokṣaṇī* waters while the wooden sword is still lying on the ground, the two thunderbolts would collide; thus, so that the two thunderbolts do not collide, he raises the wooden sword while the *prokṣaṇī* waters are being held directly above. 1.2.5. [21]
Then he utters this speech:
"Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; wipe the spoons; gird the wife;
bring the clarified butter"—this indeed is the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*). If he should so desire, he may say this; but if not...
He might even desire [the result], yet he would not pay heed [to it], for he himself knows: "From this, this rite must be performed. 1.2.5.
[22] Then he hurls the wooden sword (sphya) toward the north, saying:
"I hurl this thunderbolt at so-and-so," if he should practice sorcery; for the wooden sword is a thunderbolt.
Verily, he strews [the grass] with it; thus he indeed strews with it. Then he washes his hands.
For whatever of this [earth] was cruel, that he has taken away from her; therefore [he washes] his hands.
"He rinses his hands" (1.2.5.24).
Now, those who performed sacrifice in the beginning used to perform the *avamarśa* offering;
they became more wretched, while those who did not sacrifice [prospered].

At that time, there were those who were more excellent; then lack of faith took possession of human beings, [thinking], "Those who sacrifice become worse off, while those who do not sacrifice become better off.
Consequently, the sacrificial oblation did not go from here to the gods, for the gods subsist upon what is offered from here. 1.2.5 [25]

Those gods said to Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa: "Lack of faith has indeed seized hold of human beings; teach them the sacrifice. He went to them and said, "Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa, why do you not sacrifice? They replied, "What is desired?"
"Let us sacrifice! Those who sacrifice become worse off, while those who do not sacrifice become better off.
Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa said: "Indeed, that which we have heard as the portion set aside for the gods—that is this sacrifice.
Since you have handled the prepared oblations and the fashioned altar with your hand, you have therefore become worse off."
"Therefore, perform the sacrifice without touching [the ground], for thus you shall become more prosperous. "How far [does this extend]? "Until the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Indeed, by means of the *barhis*, this [earth] becomes pacified. If anything should happen before the spreading of the *barhis*, one should cast it away while spreading the *barhis*. And when they spread the *barhis*, even then...
They tread upon his feet. He who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice without touching it, indeed becomes superior;
therefore, one should perform the sacrifice without touching it. 1.3.1.
[1] He indeed cleanses the offering-spoons.
Now, as for why he cleans the spoons: just as is the practice among the gods, so too is it among humans;
therefore, when the serving of food has been prepared for humans, one then washes the vessels.

Having been prepared by them, he serves [the food]; in this very way, this sacrifice of the gods comes to be, when the oblations have been prepared and the altar arranged. Of these, the ladles (*srucaḥ*) are their very vessels.
When he wipes them, [he does so].

He indeed cleanses them with this thought: "I shall proceed with them once they have been cleansed. He cleanses them for the gods by means of two things, and for humans by means of one: for the gods by means of water and the *brahman* (the sacred formula), for the waters are the *kuśa* grass and the *yajus* is the *brahman*; for humans, however, by means of only one, namely water alone. Thus, in this way, it becomes distinct. 1.3.1 [4]
Then he takes up the *sruva* ladle; he heats it, [saying]: "The *rakṣas* is burnt away, the enemies are burnt away;
the *rakṣas* is scorched, the enemies are scorched. (ŚB 1.3.1.5)

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣasas; thus, right from the beginning of the sacrifice, he drives away the destructive spirits and the Rakṣasas from there. 1.3.1. [6]
He cleanses it on the inside with the tips [of the grass blades], saying:
"Unsharpened art thou, the destroyer of rivals.
He says this so that he may destroy the rivals of the sacrificer without ceasing; thus he says: "I cleanse thee, the vigorous one, for the sake of attaining vigor."
"Thou who art worthy of sacrifice, I cleanse thee for the sacrifice"—this is what he says by this very formula; with this he cleanses all the *sruva*-ladles.
"Thee, the vigorous one"—with this he cleanses the *sruk*-ladle; silently, the *prāśitra-haraṇa* vessel.
He indeed cleanses [the ladles] first with the tips [of the grass-blades] on the inside.
"By the roots on the outside"—thus he places this as *prāṇa* and thus as *udāna*;
it is indeed *prāṇa* and *udāna* that he thereby bestows. Therefore, "thus these [hairs]," "thus these [hairs].
He hands them over after wiping each one and heating each one.
Having washed the lower [ladle] according to its wiping, he should wash the upper one without wiping; in this same way, having heated it again and again, he hands it over.
1.3.1. [9] He indeed first wipes the *sruva* ladle.
Now as for the other spoons: the *sruk* is indeed female and the *sruva* is male;

therefore, even when many women go along together, he who among them is like a young man reaches the destination first, while the others follow behind him. For this reason, the *sruva* alone goes first.
Then he cleanses the other spoons. He should indeed cleanse them in such a way that he does not sprinkle over the fire, nor [over that from which it was taken].

When he is about to bring food, he should sprinkle it with the water used for rinsing the vessel; thus it becomes pure. Therefore, one should wipe [the ladle] in such a way that one does not sprinkle the fire, but rather stepping aside as if toward the east.
Now, some throw the wiping-cloths of the *sruk* ladles into the fire, saying, "The *sruk* ladles have become the Veda; they were purified by these."

They have indeed wiped this [ladle] together; let this not be anything that is too close to the sacrifice. The Brahman priest should bring food and make him drink the rinsing of the vessels; thus he makes it so for him. Therefore, one should indeed cast these away. 1.3.1. [12] Then he girds the wife.
The wife is indeed the hind part of the sacrifice.
[Thinking,] "May my sacrifice proceed forward as it is being performed," he thus yokes her, [thinking,] "May she sit near my sacrifice, being yoked.
He girds her with a cord.

For they yoke what is fit with a yoke-thong; indeed, there is something impure in the wife that is below the navel. Now, she is about to look at this clarified butter; he thus places the yoke-thong between her and it. Then she looks at the clarified butter with the pure upper part [of her body]; therefore [he yokes] the wife.
He girds himself. That which he girds is indeed a garment; for garments belong to Varuṇa, while plants are indeed garments.
He thus interposes these plants between [the girdle and her body]; so this Varuṇa-related cord does not injure her.
Therefore he girds her with an upper garment.
He girds it on.
"For Aditi’s girdle," he says. Aditi is indeed this earth; she is the wife of the gods, and she becomes the wife of this [sacrificer].
He thus makes for her a girdle, not a rope. A girdle (*rāsnā*) is indeed gold;
it is that very thing he makes for her. 1.3.1. [16]
He should not make a knot; for a knot belongs to Varuṇa, and if he were to make a knot, Varuṇa would seize his wife. Therefore, he does not make a knot. 1.3.1.[17]
He pushes it upward only;

[with the words] "Thou art Viṣṇu’s seat. Indeed, she does not sit behind, facing eastward, to attend upon the sacrifice of the gods. This earth is indeed Aditi; she is the wife of the gods, and she sits behind, facing eastward, for the sake of the gods.

He sits beside the sacrifice; therefore, she should mount this [chariot]. If she were to do so, she would quickly go to yonder world; thus, however, the wife lives long. This [mounting] is a substitute for her; thus, indeed, this [earth] does not harm her. Therefore, she should sit as if to the south. 1.3.1. [18]
Then he gazes at the clarified butter.
The wife is indeed the female, and the clarified butter is the seed; thus a productive union is brought about.
Therefore, he gazes at the clarified butter. 1.3.1 [19]
He gazes at it, saying, "I gaze upon you with unerring sight"; by this he means, "I gaze upon you with uninjured sight.
He says, "You are the tongue of Agni," for when they offer oblations into the fire, they arise like tongues of Agni;
therefore he says, "You are the tongue of Agni. He says, "A good bringer to the gods," meaning "one that is effective."

"O gods," he thereby says; "be for me for every station, for every sacrificial formula," he thereby says, which means, "prosper for my entire sacrifice. Then, taking the clarified butter, he holds it up toward the east.

Then he places it over the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "May my entire sacrifice be cooked on the Āhavanīya for those who cook the oblations on the Āhavanīya. Now, as to why he first places it over there (the Gārhapatya): it is because he intends to give space for the wife; for it would not be fitting if she were present [at that point].
He should bring his wife back, thinking, "I shall cause her to participate. Now, if he were not to cause the wife to participate, he would exclude the wife from the sacrifice;

thus, he does not exclude the wife from the sacrifice. Therefore, having melted [the butter] together with her, he brings it forward while the wife is made to participate; however, for one who has no wife, he first pours it into the Āhavanīya fire.
He places it on the fire; he takes that from there and sets it down within the altar (antarvedi).
Regarding this, they say: "One should not set it down within the altar, for from here [within the altar] they perform the offerings to the wives of the gods;
thus he makes the wives of the gods like eunuchs, and his wife will be beyond [the reach of] her husband. But Yājñavalkya said this:

"Let it be as my wife has directed; who would heed that which is contrary? Whether the wife belongs to another man, or whether the sacrifice is on the altar, or the clarified butter is the sacrifice—'O Sacrifice, fashion the sacrifice from the sacrifice! Therefore, one should set it down only within the altar (antarvedi).
There are two strainers (pavitras) in the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇīs).
He takes them from there; with those two he purifies the clarified butter. Indeed, this is the single purpose of the purification: he thereby makes it pure. He purifies it.
"I purify you at the impulse of Savitṛ with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun"—
the significance of this is the same as before.
Then, [he purifies him] with two strainers smeared with clarified butter.
He purifies the *prokṣaṇī* waters with the formula: "At the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify you...
[and so on]. Its connection is this: when he purifies the *prokṣaṇī* waters with two strainers smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*), he thereby places milk into the waters.
He places it; this very milk is placed within the waters. For when it rains, then the plants are born;
having eaten the plants and drunk the water, from that this essence comes into being.
Therefore, it is for the sake of the completeness of the essence. 1.3.1 [25]
Then he gazes at the clarified butter. Regarding this, some have the sacrificer gaze at it; however, Yājñavalkya said:
"How is it that they do not themselves become the Adhvaryus, and how is it that they do not themselves recite the formulas, when there are so many [priests]?"

"Since these blessings (āśiṣaḥ) are thus pronounced, how is it that they have faith in this very [act]? Whatever blessing the officiating priests (ṛtvij) invoke during the sacrifice belongs to the sacrificer alone; therefore, the Adhvaryu priest himself should look [at the ghee].
He looks [at it], saying: "The eye is indeed truth; for the eye is truth. Therefore, even now, when two [people]..."

If two people come disputing, one saying "I saw it" and the other "I heard it," we should place our trust in the one who says, "I saw it. For he makes that [truth] successful by means of truth itself.
1.3.1 [27]. He looks at [the water], saying: "Thou art brilliance; thou art pure; thou art immortality. This very mantra is indeed truth, for this is brilliance and purity.
For this is indeed the immortal, and this is indeed that; by means of truth alone he makes this prosper. 1.3.2.
[1] Man, verily, is the sacrifice;
man is the sacrifice because man extends it—this [sacrifice], while being extended, is indeed he.
"As great as man is, so great is he ordained; therefore, man is the sacrifice.
Of him, this [hand] is indeed the *juhū* (sacrificial ladle);
this [other hand] is the *upabhṛt*; the self itself is the *dhruvā*. Indeed, these [limbs] belong to the self."
All limbs originate from that; indeed, the entire sacrifice originates from the *dhruvā* [ladle].
The *sruva* [small spoon] is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This very vital breath moves through all the limbs; therefore, the *sruva* is all.
He moves along with the offering-spoons (srucaḥ).
Of this [sacrifice], that very sky is the *juhū* spoon;
this intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is the *upabhṛt* spoon; and this earth is the *dhruvā* spoon. Now, regarding this [earth]:
In this very way all these worlds originate from it; therefore, indeed, every sacrifice originates from the *dhruvā* [ladle].
This very wind that blows here is the *sruva* [small dipping-spoon];
it blows along all these worlds, and therefore it is called the *sruva*.
He moves along all the offering-spoons. This very sacrifice, as it is being extended, is extended for the gods, for the seasons, and for the meters; that which is the oblation belongs to the gods.

Whatever is Soma the King and whatever is the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), having designated each of those, he draws [the portions], saying: "I draw thee, acceptable to such-and-such. Such indeed is the case for these.
Now, as for the portions of clarified butter (ājya) that are drawn...

These [portions] are taken from the seasons and from the meters; without specifying each one individually, he takes them in the form of clarified butter alone. He indeed takes four times in the *juhū* ladle and eight times in the *upabhṛt*.
When he takes [the butter] in the four-pronged ladle, he takes it for the seasons; for he takes it for the *prayāja* offerings, and the *prayāja*s are indeed the seasons.

He takes it without specifying them by name, but only in the form of clarified butter (*ājya*), to avoid repetition; for he would commit a repetition if he were to take it specifically for the spring.
He should take [the butter], saying, "Thee for the summer; thee for [the rains]," and so forth. Therefore, without specifying [the season], he takes it in the form of clarified butter alone.
Now, when he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he takes it for the meters, for [it is taken] for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s).
For the after-offerings (anuyājas) are the *candāṃsi* (metres); he draws them without specifying [the metre], in the form of clarified butter alone, for the sake of non-repetition (*ajāmitā*).
For he would indeed commit repetition if he were to draw them saying, "Thee for the Gāyatrī! Thee for the Triṣṭubh! Therefore, he draws them without specifying, in the form of clarified butter alone.

Now, as for that which he draws four times into the *dhruvā*—he draws it for the sake of the entire sacrifice; he draws it without specifying [any particular deity], but rather in the form of the clarified butter (*ājya*) itself. For to whom indeed could he specify it, since he cuts portions from it for all the deities?
Therefore, from the beginningless [tradition], one takes [the portion] in the very form of what is to be offered.
1.3.2.[11] The sacrificer indeed follows the *juhū* ladle;
he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt* ladle. Eating indeed follows the *juhū* ladle.
The *juhū* ladle is indeed food, and the *upabhṛt* is the eater. He takes four portions in the *juhū* and eight times in the *upabhṛt*.
As for why he takes four in the *juhū*:
By this he makes the eater himself more limited and smaller;
but when he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he makes the food itself more unlimited and greater.
For that is successful where the eater is smaller and the food is greater. 1.3.2 [13]
When taking [the butter] with the four-spoon ladle (*juhū*), he takes more clarified butter;
when taking it with the eight-times-dipped *upabhṛt* ladle, he takes less clarified butter. 1.3.2. [14]

When he takes more clarified butter while taking four times in the *juhū*, he thereby makes the eater more limited and smaller, and places vigor and strength within him; then, when he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt*—
Taking up the butter, he takes it in smaller quantities;

thus, by making it more limited and less abundant, he renders it powerless and weak. Therefore, even a king, having settled among a foreign people, conquers them from a single dwelling, and they submit to him however he desires. It is by this means that he does so.
