By that same power, when he takes more clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle, whatever he takes into the *juhū*, he offers that with the *juhū* itself;
and whatever he takes into the *upabhṛt* ladle, he offers that with the *juhū* itself.
Regarding this they say: "Why then does he take [butter] into the *upabhṛt*, since he does not offer with the *upabhṛt*? As for that which he [takes] with the *upabhṛt*...

If he were to offer these separately, these subjects would not be united; there would be no eater and no food. But because he offers them together, having brought them all into one, therefore these commoners remain under the control of the Kṣatriya, and the cattle attend upon the Vaiśya.
And because he offers them together, having brought them all into one, therefore whenever the Kṣatriya so desires—

"Come, O Vaiśya, bring back that which was deposited by you with me," he said; thus he overcomes him, and he follows him however he desires, for by this his virility has been taken away. These, indeed, are those [verses]. 1.3.2. [16] Indeed, these are they.
The *ājya* offerings are taken from the meters. When he takes four portions into the *juhū*, he takes them for the *gāyatrī*;
then when he takes eight times into the *upabhṛt*, he takes them for the *triṣṭubh* and the *jagatī*;
then when he takes four into the *dhruvā*, he takes them for the *anuṣṭubh*. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech, and all this [universe] comes from speech.

Therefore, from the *dhruvā* alone the entire sacrifice originates; for this [earth] is indeed the *anuṣṭubh*, and from her everything here originates. Therefore, from the *dhruvā* alone the entire sacrifice originates.
He takes it up [with the formula]: "Thou art the abode, the dear one of the gods. This, indeed, is the most beloved abode of the gods.
Since it is clarified butter (*ājya*), he therefore says: "Thou art the abode, the name, the beloved of the gods. [And he says: "Thou art the inviolable place of sacrifice for the gods.
For clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt; therefore he says, "Thou art the inviolable place of sacrifice for the gods.
With this *yajus* formula, he... 1.3.2. [18]...he [proceeds].

He takes once in the *juhū* ladle, three times silently; with this same *yajus* formula he takes once in the *upabhṛt* ladle, seven times silently; with this same *yajus* formula he takes once in the *dhruvā* ladle, three times silently. Regarding this they say: "One should take three times each with the *yajus*, for the sacrifice is threefold. But indeed, one should take only once each time, for it is thus here.
It becomes threefold when taken up thrice. 1.3.3.
[1] The Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters;
he first sprinkles the fuel-bundle (idhma), saying: "Thou art black, dwelling in the clefts, for Agni."
"I sprinkle you, who are acceptable," he says; thus he makes this very [sacrificial substance] pure for Agni.
Then he sprinkles the altar:
"You are the altar; I sprinkle you, who are acceptable, for the sacrificial grass."
He thus makes this sacrificial grass pure for the purpose of the *barhis*.
Then he hands the *barhis* to him; he places it down with the knot facing eastward and sprinkles it, saying: "Thou art the *barhis*."
"I sprinkle you, acceptable to the *sruks*"; by this he makes it pure for the *sruks*. 1.3.3.
[4] Now, those sprinkling waters which remain, with them he pours water over the roots of the plants for Aditi.
"Thou art the unloosener. This earth, indeed, is Aditi; thus he thereby covers the roots of the plants upon her.
Therefore these plants have moist roots; hence, even though their tops become dry, their roots remain moist.

Then, having loosened the knot, he takes up the prastara-bunch from the front with the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; this very tuft of his is the crest-lock (śikhā). He thereby places that very thing upon him. He takes it from the front.
For this [child] is indeed born from the front; therefore he takes [the water] from the front.
Then he loosens the girdle, thinking, "A woman shall give birth for him in due order"; therefore [he loosens] the girdle.
He loosens it and places it on the southern hip; this is indeed its *nīvī* (girdle-end), for this *nīvī* is, as it were, on the south side;
therefore he places it on the southern hip. He covers it over again, for this *nīvī* is indeed covered over; therefore he covers it over again. 1.3.3 [7]
Then he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
This *prastara* bundle is indeed the *stūpa*; and those hairs of his which grow downwards are this other *barhis*.
He thus places those very things upon him; therefore he spreads the sacrificial grass. 1.3.3. [8]
The altar is indeed a woman;
her the gods sit around here, as do these Brahmins who have heard the sacred texts and are learned in them.
While they are thus sitting around her, he makes her naked; it is for the sake of nakedness that he [spreads] the sacrificial grass (barhis).
He strews [the sacrificial grass].
As great as the altar is, so great is the earth; [upon it are] the plants.
He thus places the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon this very earth; these plants are established upon this earth, and therefore he spreads the sacrificial grass.
Regarding this, they say: "One should spread it thickly," for wherever its plants are most abundant, that is [the place] of this earth.
"Therefore, one should spread it thickly, for it is most conducive to livelihood. Thus he spreads the *trivṛt* grass over the very place where he brings [the materials];

for the sacrifice is threefold (*trivṛt*). Moreover, he may also spread it with the roots upward; for it is recited in a verse: "They spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) continuously. He spreads it with the roots downward, for these [plants] on this earth have their roots downward.

Plants are established upon the earth; therefore, he spreads [the grass] with its roots downward. He spreads it, saying: "I spread thee, soft as wool, a pleasant seat for the gods. By saying "soft as wool," he means "excellent for the gods"; by saying "a pleasant seat for the gods," he means "a comfortable seat for the gods."
Thus he says this very thing. 1.3.3.
[12] Now he prepares the fire-altar.
The Āhavanīya is indeed the head of the sacrifice; the eastern half is the head.

He thus prepares the eastern half of the sacrifice; holding the *prastara* above [the *sruk*], he prepares it. For this *prastara* is indeed the *stūpa*; he thereby restores that very thing to him. Therefore, holding the *prastara* above, he prepares it. 1.3.3. [13]

Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). Now, as to why he lays down the enclosing-sticks: when the gods first chose Agni for the office of Hotṛ, he said to them, "I am indeed not able to be your Hotṛ, nor to carry your oblation."
"I would carry for you the three eastern [fires] during the rainy season; they have sought to obstruct them, so grant me leave for that.

Or rather, I shall testify to this: that I may be your Hotṛ and that I may carry your oblation. "So be it," they said, and they granted him these very ones; these are the enclosing-sticks (paridhis). 1.3.3. [14]
He said: "The thunderbolt, indeed, has struck them through the *vaṣaṭ*-call. I am afraid of the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call;

lest the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, strike me down, surround me with these very [verses], so that the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, shall not strike me. "So be it," they said, and they surrounded him with these. The thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, did not strike him.
He thus encloses it with armor; for he girds Agni when he clothes him with these [verses]. 1.3.3.[15] They, moreover, said:
"If you employ us here in the sacrifice, let there also be a share for us in the sacrifice. 1.3.3.[16]
"So be it," the gods said.

"Whatever falls outside the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), that shall be offered into you; but whatever they shall offer over and above that, that shall belong to you. Thus, when they offer into the fire, it satisfies them; and then—

In that they offer these [oblations] one after another, thereby they satisfy them; and in that what falls outside the enclosing-sticks is offered into these very fires, therefore it should not be as if it were spilled. For these [fires] have entered this earth; whatever here falls, all that becomes established in her alone. 1.3.3. [17]
He touches what has been spilled, saying:

"To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! These indeed are the names of those fires: namely, the Lord of the Earth, the Lord of the World, and the Lord of Beings.

It becomes for him as if offered with the *vaṣaṭ* call in these fires. Now, some indeed lay these enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) from the fuel-wood itself; but one should not do so in that way, for they would then be improperly prepared for him. Those which he lays from the fuel-wood are intended only for the purpose of being added to the fire; therefore—
These [sticks] are indeed properly prepared for one who brings other [sticks] as the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*);
therefore, they should bring others. They should be made of *pālāśa* wood.
The Palāśa tree is indeed Brahman, and Agni is Brahman; for the fires are [of the nature of] Agni, therefore they should be made of Palāśa wood.
If one should not find Palāśa wood, then they may be of Vikaṅkata wood; if one should not find Vikaṅkata wood, then likewise...

They should be made of *kārṣmarya* wood; if one cannot find those made of *kārṣmarya*, they may be made of *bilva* wood, or of *khadira* wood, or of *udumbara* wood, for these are the trees that are fit for sacrifice; therefore, they are made from these trees.
They should indeed be fresh.
For this is their life; by it they possess splendor, by it they possess vigor; therefore, they should be moist. First, he [should place] the middle one.
He lays the enclosing stick around [the fire], saying: "May the Gandharva Viśvāvasu enclose you for the safety of all; you are the enclosure of the sacrificer; Agni is praised with the *iḍā*.
Then he lays the southern enclosing stick around.
"Thou art the right arm of Indra, for the safety of all;
thou art the enclosure of the sacrificer; Agni is the praised Iḍ. Thus [he says]. Then he lays on the northern enclosing stick.

"May Mitra and Varuṇa enclose you from the north with a firm ordinance for the safety of all; you are the enclosure of the sacrificer; Agni is the praised Iḍ. For these are indeed fires; therefore he says, "Agni is the praised Iḍ. 1.3.4. [5]

Then he places a fuel-stick on the fire. He first touches the middle enclosing-stick; by that he enkindles them first. Then he places it on the fire; by that he directly enkindles the fire itself. 1.3.4. [6]

He adds fuel with this Gāyatrī verse: "O Sage, we kindle thee, the enjoyer of the oblation, the radiant one, O Agni, the great one at the sacrifice. By this Gāyatrī, he indeed kindles the Gāyatrī itself; that is the Gāyatrī.
The kindled *chandases* he kindles further; the kindled *chandases* carry the sacrifice to the gods. 1.3.4.
[7] Now, the second fuel-stick which he places on the fire—with that he kindles the spring; that spring...
Being kindled, he kindles the other seasons; the seasons, being kindled, cause offspring to be born and ripen the plants.
He places a fuel-stick upon the fire with the words, "Thou art fuel," for the spring is indeed kindled.
Having placed it, he mutters:

"May Sūrya protect you from the east against any curse," he says for protection; the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are placed on all sides for protection, and thus he makes Sūrya himself the protector in the east so that no destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) or demons (*rakṣas*) may descend upon him from the front, for Sūrya is the repeller of destructive spirits and demons. 1.3.4 [9]

Now, that very third kindling-stick which he places upon the fire during the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s), by means of it he kindles the Brāhmaṇa; that Brāhmaṇa, being kindled, carries the sacrifice to the gods. 1.3.4 [10]
Then he approaches the strewn altar.

Taking two blades of grass, he places them crosswise with the formula, "Ye are the arms of Savitṛ. For this *stūpa* is indeed the *prastara*; thus he places these two as its eyebrows crosswise. Therefore, these [eyebrows] are so.

The two eyebrows are crosswise. The *prastara* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the other *barhis* grass is the common people (*viś*). It is for the separation of both the nobility and the common people that he places them crosswise; therefore they are called "separators" (*vidhṛti*). He then spreads the *prastara*.

"I strew thee, soft as wool, a good seat for the gods"—by saying "soft as wool," he means "good for the gods"; by saying "a good seat for the gods," he means "a comfortable resting place for the gods. 1.3.4 [12]
He places it down with [the formula]:

"May the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas sit upon you. These indeed are the three classes of gods—the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; thus he says, "May these sit upon you. While it is being placed down, it remains held by his left hand.

Then he takes hold of the *juhū* ladle with his right hand, [thinking], "Lest the destructive spirits and demons enter here before [the sacrifice is complete]"; for the Brāhmaṇa is the repeller of demons; therefore, it remains held down by his left hand. 1.3.4. [14]
Then he takes up the *juhū* ladle with the formula:

"Thou art the ghee-dripping one, named *juhū*. For she is indeed ghee-dripping and named *juhū*. [He continues: "May she sit upon this dear seat with her dear abode. [He takes up] the *upabhṛt* ladle with the formula: "Thou art the ghee-dripping one, named *upabhṛt*. She is indeed ghee-dripping.
[He addresses the *upabhṛt* with: "By name you are the *upabhṛt*; sit here on this dear seat with your dear abode.

[He addresses the *dhruvā* with: "By name you are the *dhruvā*, O *ghṛtācī*. For she is indeed *ghṛtācī* by name; [he says: "Sit here on this dear seat with your dear abode. [Regarding the other oblation: "Sit here on this dear seat with your dear abode"—this refers to whatever other sacrificial offering (*havis*) there may be. 1.3.4. [15]
He places the *juhū* spoon above and the other spoons below. The *juhū* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the other spoons are the common people (*viś*).
He thus makes the nobility superior to the common people; therefore, the nobleman sits above while these subjects remain below.
They wait upon [the fire]; therefore, he places the *juhū* spoon above and the other *sruva* spoons below.
He touches them, saying:
"The steadfast ones have sat down," for they have indeed sat down; "in the womb of Truth (*ṛta*)," for the sacrifice is indeed Truth.

"Thou hast sat down at the womb of the sacrifice; O Viṣṇu, protect them, protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice"—with these words he addresses the sacrificer. "Protect me, the leader of the sacrifice," he says; thus he does not exclude himself from the sacrifice. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he entrusts all this to him for protection. Therefore he says, "O Viṣṇu, protect them. 1.3.5. [1]
The Adhvaryu indeed kindles this fire with the fuel; therefore it is called *idhma*.
The Hotṛ kindles it with the *sāmidhenī* verses; therefore they are called *sāmidhenīs*. 1.3.5. [2]
He says, "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled," for it is indeed for Agni, as he is being kindled, that he recites this. Regarding this, some say:

"O Hotṛ, recite for Agni as he is being kindled"—one should not speak thus; for previously he is not yet the Hotṛ, but only when they formally choose him does he become the Hotṛ. Therefore, one should simply say: "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled. 1.3.5. [4]
He recites verses addressed to Agni; he thus kindles him by means of his own deity. He recites Gāyatrī verses; the Gāyatrī is indeed the metre of Agni;
he thus kindles him by means of his own metre. The Gāyatrī is vigor; the Gāyatrī is sacred knowledge.
By means of vigor alone he thus kindles him. He recites eleven [verses].
The *triṣṭubh* indeed consists of eleven syllables; the *gāyatrī* is the spiritual power (*brahman*), and the *triṣṭubh* is the ruling power (*kṣatra*).
He recites these two verses in the *triṣṭubh* meter; verily, by means of both these powers, he kindles him. Therefore, he recites eleven verses.
He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times, for the *trivṛt* is indeed the beginning.
The sacrifices have a threefold rising; therefore he recites the first verse thrice and the last verse thrice.
These *sāmidhenī* verses thus amount to fifteen. The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is indeed fifteenfold; the thunderbolt is virility.
He thus brings the *sāmidhenīs* to completion as virility. Therefore, while these are being recited, whomever—
If he should hate someone, he should press him down with his two thumbs, saying, "I press this one down. Thus, by means of this thunderbolt, he presses him down.
There are indeed fifteen nights in a half-month.
The year, indeed, consists of half-months; thus, as it proceeds, it attains the nights. Of fifteen *gāyatrī* verses—

There are three hundred and sixty syllables, and there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in a year; thus he obtains the days, and thereby he obtains the year itself. There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.
One should recite the invitatory verses for the sacrifice in a low voice; one sacrifices to that deity for whom he prepares the offering.
There are twelve months in a year and five seasons; this very [sacrifice] is Prajāpati, consisting of seventeen parts.
Prajāpati is indeed everything; thus, by means of everything, he successfully fulfills without fail whatever desire he has.

He offers an oblation for a specific desire; he sacrifices to the deity in a whisper. That which is whispered is indeed unexpressed, and everything is unexpressed; thus, by means of the whole, he successfully attains that desire without fail. For whatever desire he offers this oblation—this is the procedure for the sacrifice. 1.3.5 [11]

"One should recite twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses even at the New and Full Moon sacrifices," they say. "There are indeed twelve months in a year, five seasons, and three worlds—that makes twenty; this one who shines yonder is the twenty-first. This is that [twenty-first]."
This is the goal, this is the foundation; he goes to that goal, to that foundation. Therefore, one should recite the twenty-first [verse].
One should indeed recite these for one who has already attained his goal, for one who thinks, "May I neither become better nor worse," for whatever such a person may be.
Regarding this they say: "He becomes either exactly like that [as he intended] or even worse—namely, for whomsoever, knowing thus, these [verses] are recited.
This is indeed a mere deliberation; however, these [verses] are not actually recited in that manner.
One should recite the first verse three times and the last verse three times without taking a breath.

There are indeed these three worlds; thus he extends these very worlds and sustains these worlds. There are these three vital breaths in man; he thereby establishes this [breath] in him as continuous and uninterrupted. This is the recitation. 1.3.5. [14]

As long as he might have something to say, he should speak accordingly; one should explain this to him: "If, while desiring to speak after having finished speaking, he were to speak out of tune or without breath, his action would be torn asunder—that is the censure. 1.3.5 [15]
If he should not desire this, he may recite each verse singly without taking breath; thus, by means of each single verse, he connects these worlds one by one and satisfies these worlds one by one.
Now, as for the fact that he bestows breath: the Gāyatrī is indeed breath; therefore, he recites the entire Gāyatrī.
He bestows that entire vital breath; therefore, he should recite each verse individually without drawing breath.
He recites them continuously and without interruption; it is thus that he connects the days and nights of the year. These are those very [days and nights].

The days and nights of the year revolve continuously and without interruption; he thus does not offer a standing place to his hateful rival. For were he to recite them without continuity, he would indeed be offering a standing place [to him]. Therefore, he recites them continuously and without interruption. 1.4.1. [1]
He recites after uttering the *hiṃ* sound.
For it is said, "There is no sacrifice without the *sāman*," and "The *sāman* is not sung without the *hiṃ* sound.
When he utters *hiṃ*, the form of the *hiṃ*-sound is thereby produced; by means of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), he approaches the form of the *sāman*: *o3ṃ*.
By this very syllable "Oṃ," his entire sacrifice becomes complete with its Sāmans.
Furthermore, as to why he utters the *hiṃ* sound:
the *hiṃ* sound is indeed breath; for the *hiṃ* sound is truly breath. Therefore, one should not utter it while holding the nostrils closed.
One is able to utter the sound *hiṃ* with speech, or one recites a *ṛc*; for speech and breath are a couple.
Thus, this couple is produced beforehand in relation to the *sāmidhenī* verses; therefore, having uttered *hiṃ*, he recites. He utters *hiṃ* in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Now, if he were to utter the *hiṃ* loudly, he would perform only one of the two;
therefore, he utters the *hiṃ* in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
He recites both with the prefix *eti* and with the prefix *preti*.
Thus he yokes the Gāyatrī both hitherward and thitherward;

thitherward it carries the sacrifice to the gods, and hitherward it protects men. Therefore, he recites both with "iti" and with "pra". Furthermore, as to why he recites both with "iti" and with "pra":
"Prāṇa" indeed goes forward, and "udāna" goes away; it is these two, prāṇa and udāna, that he thereby bestows.
Therefore, he recites both "eti" (he goes) and "preti" (he goes away).
Furthermore, as to why he recites both "eti" and "preti": [the reason follows].
Verily, the seed is cast forth; it comes and is born. Cattle go forth and return. Indeed, all this world goes forth and returns. Therefore, he recites both "it comes" and "it goes.
He recites: "Forward, O strengths, toward heaven..."—this becomes "pra" (forward). Then, "O Agni, come for the feast..."—this becomes "ā" (come).
Regarding this, some indeed say: [1.4.1.8]... "tadu haika āhuḥ" (Regarding this, some indeed say).

"Both of these together become *pra*," he says; thus, "pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ" (Forward, O strengths, toward heaven) is like something beyond comprehension. But "agna āyāhi vītaye" (O Agni, come for the feast) is "pra. 1.4.1 [9] He recites: "pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ. This indeed becomes *pra*; and "vājāḥ"—for *vāja* is food.
This very food has been celebrated in this [verse]: "The sky-ward ones" (*abhidyavaḥ*); for the half-months are indeed the sky-ward ones;
thus, it is the half-months that have been celebrated here. "The possessors of oblation" (*haviṣmantaḥ*); for cattle are indeed the possessors of oblation;
thus, it is cattle that have been celebrated here. 1.4.1. [10]

"O Ghṛtācī! Videgha Māthava was carrying Agni Vaiśvānara in his mouth; the seer Gotama Rāhūgaṇa was his domestic priest (purohita). When the priest was addressed by him, he would not respond, thinking, "Lest it [the fire] enter my..."
"Agni Vaiśvānara was produced from the mouth. [1.4.1.11] He resolved to summon him with *ṛc*-verses:
"O Sage, we kindle you, the radiant one who enjoys the oblation, O Agni."
"O Videgha, [invoke] the Great One at the sacrifice! 1.4.1.[12] He did not respond.
"O Agni, your pure, bright, and radiant flames rise up; your lights and rays [shine forth]."
"Videgha! [1.4.1.13] He did not respond at all;
he merely uttered, "We choose you, whose back is dripping with ghee," and then—
Agni Vaiśvānara blazed forth from the mouth of Ghṛtakīrti; he was unable to sustain him, and he issued from his mouth and reached this earth on foot.
At that time, Videgha Māthava was there.
From that very place, burning eastward along the Sarasvatī, he proceeded across this earth;

Gotama Rāhūgaṇa and Videgha Māthava followed after him as he burned. He burnt all these rivers, but he did not burn beyond the Sadānīrā, which flows out from the northern mountain; indeed, he did not burn it.
"In former times, the Brāhmaṇas did not cross that [river], thinking, 'It has not been sufficiently burnt by the Vaiśvānara fire.
But from that time until now, many Brāhmaṇas have crossed it; indeed, that place has become as it were more fertile."
"It has been made to flow forth as it were, and tasted by the Vaiśvānara fire.
1.4.1.[16] But now, at this time, it is as if even more of a field; for indeed, the Brāhmaṇas have now tasted it through sacrifices. Sāpi.
"In the last month of summer, he makes it as if it were blazing, for it has not yet been sufficiently burnt by the Vaiśvānara fire.
He said, "Videgha Māthava, where shall I be? "To the east of this very place shall be your realm," he replied.
Even now, this remains the boundary between the Kosalas and the Videhas, for they are indeed the Māthavas.

Then Gautama Rāhūgaṇa said, "Why did you not answer when you were being addressed by us? He replied, "Agni Vaiśvānara was in my mouth; he would have fallen out from my mouth, therefore I did not [answer]."
"I shall respond," [he said].
"How did that come to be?
At the very moment you uttered the words, 'We worship her who drips with ghee,' that was precisely for me."
"In Ghṛtakīrti, Vaiśvānara Agni blazed forth from my mouth; I was unable to sustain him, so he flowed out from my mouth. 1.4.1 [20].
"Therefore, whatever [verse] among the *sāmidhenīs* contains the word 'ghṛta'..."
That is indeed the *sāmidhenī*; by that he kindles him completely and bestows vigor upon him. "Now, it is with the verse beginning 'ghṛtācī'... [1.4.1.21]
"He goes to the gods, seeking favor"—the sacrificer is indeed "seeking favor," for he desires to win over the gods; he indeed wishes to overcome the gods.
Therefore he says, "He goes to the gods, seeking favor. This verse, though addressed to Agni, is undefined (*anirukta*); for everything is undefined, and thus he commences with everything. 1.4.1 [22]
"O Agni, come for the feast!"—thus it is said. "For the feast," he says; for these worlds were, as it were, close together at first. Having touched them, indeed, the sky was [separated]. 1.4.1 [23]
Those gods desired:
"How indeed might these worlds become more distant from one another? How might this [universe] become more spacious?
They separated them by means of these very three syllables, *vi-ta-ra-m*. Thus, these worlds became far apart (*vi-tūram*) from that.
"It became more spacious for the gods; indeed, it becomes more spacious for him who, knowing this, recites this [verse]:
'...for the sake of enjoyment' (RV 3.53.1), and 'being praised, for the giving of the oblation' (RV 3.53.2)."
"The sacrificer is indeed the giver of the oblation; by saying 'for the sacrificer,' he says this very thing.

"Sit down as Hotṛ upon the sacrificial grass"—Agni is indeed the Hotṛ and the sacrificial grass is this world; thus he places Agni in this very world. This Agni is thus established in this world. This [verse] refers to this very world; by means of it, he conquers this very world.
For one who knows thus, they recite this verse: "Thee, O Aṅgiras, with fuel-sticks...
For with fuel-sticks the Aṅgirases kindled him; "O Aṅgiras" means Aṅgiras. 1.4.1 [25]
"Truly, we cause Agni to grow with clarified butter"—this is a *sāmidhenī* verse; with it he kindles him completely and bestows vigor upon him.
"O youngest one, shine forth mightily! [1.4.1.26]

"Great indeed shines this one when kindled, O youngest," he says; for Agni is the youngest, therefore he says "O youngest. This verse is recited with reference to that very world, namely the world of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
therefore, although it belongs to Agni, it is undefined (*anirukta*), for this world is undefined. By means of this [verse], he conquers that very world, for him who knows thus.
They recite this verse for the learned man:
"May he grant us that which is broad and worthy of renown. That indeed is "broad" wherein the gods are; and that is "worthy of renown" wherein the gods have acted.
"O God, do thou dispel," [he says]; by this he means, "O God, do thou cause us to go.
"O Agni, [grant] great heroic power"—that which is "great" is yonder [world], and that which is "heroic power" is that in which the gods [dwell]. 1.4.1 [28]
This very world was proclaimed in accordance with this [verse]; indeed, by means of this [verse], he who knows thus conquers this very world when they recite it for him. 1.4.1.
[29] He then says: "Worthy of praise, worthy of homage"—for he is indeed worthy of praise and he is indeed worthy of homage; "may he pierce through the darkness."
"For when kindled, this Agni is seen like one who drives away the darkness; he is kindled as a bull—for he is indeed kindled as a bull;
'Agni, the bull, is being kindled,' for he is indeed being kindled.
'Like a horse that carries the gods'... [1.4.1.30]...so it is said.
"Having indeed become a horse, he carries the sacrifice for the gods.
Because he says "neti" (no) in the Ṛgveda, that becomes "oṃ"; therefore he says, "The horse, the carrier of the gods.
"Him, the possessors of oblations, worship. 1.4.1 [31]
"For men, possessing oblations, indeed praise him; therefore he says, 'Him, possessing oblations, let them praise.
"Thee, O bull, we bulls, O bull, do we kindle. 1.4.1 [32]

"For they kindle him, O Agni, shining mightily"—for indeed, he shines mightily when fully kindled. 1.4.1 [33]. Now, one recites this triplet containing the word "bull" (vṛṣan); for all these *sāmidhenī* verses belong to Agni.
Indra, indeed, is the deity of the sacrifice; Indra is the bull. Thus, these *sāmidhenī* verses of his become accompanied by Indra.
Therefore, he recites a triplet containing the word "bull. He recites: "We choose Agni as the messenger. Now, both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another.

Competing with them, Gāyatrī stood between them. She who was indeed Gāyatrī was this very earth; she stood there between them. Both sides perceived this: "Whichever side this one shall join, they will be the victors, and the others will be defeated. Both sides then made an appeal to her, and Agni [first] did so.
"He was the messenger of the gods, Saharakṣas"—this refers to the Asura-Rakṣasa; he followed after Agni, who belongs to the Asuras.
Therefore, he recites: "We choose Agni as our messenger," for he was indeed the messenger of the gods; and "the invoker, the all-knowing. 1.4.1 [35]
Regarding this, some recite:

"O Hotṛ, you who possess all knowledge. [They do so thinking,] "Lest I speak thus of myself. However, one should not speak in that way; for they perform what is human at the sacrifice, and whatever is human in the sacrifice is indeed a failure of the sacrifice.
"May I not cause failure in the sacrifice," he thought; therefore, the Hotṛ should recite exactly as it was already stated in the Ṛgveda:
"The all-knowing Hotṛ"—for Agni is indeed the wise performer of this sacrifice—thus he says, "the wise performer of this sacrifice. This [Agni] turned toward the gods.

Then the gods prospered and the asuras were defeated. Indeed, he prospers in himself and his rivals are defeated, for whomsoever, knowing this, they recite this [verse]. One should recite that [verse] on the eighth day.
This [verse] is indeed the Gāyatrī by its underlying principle; for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables.
Therefore, one should recite the eighth [verse]. Regarding this, some place the *dhāyyā* verses at the beginning, thinking: "The *dhāyyās* are food; we thus place this food in the mouth."
"Those who say this should not do so; for her (the *dhāyyā*) becomes ill-placed for him who places the *dhāyyās* at the beginning.

For then it becomes either the tenth or the eleventh [verse]. Her place is indeed well-placed for him to whom they recite this as the eighth. Therefore, one should place the *dhāyyās* only after [the first seven verses]. 1.4.1. [38]
"Being kindled, the sacrifice"—the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus he says, "being kindled, the sacrifice.
"Agni, the purifier, worthy of praise"—for he is indeed the purifier and he is indeed worthy of praise. "We entreat him, the flame-haired one."

"For the hair of this [fire] seems to grieve when it is kindled, [thinking], 'O Agni, you are well-kindled; an oblation has been offered! Therefore, he should place all the fuel-wood (idhma) before that point. Whatever else besides the kindling-sticks (samidh) there may be, he should place it on; for that which is other than the kindling-sticks is, as it were, a rejection. And whatever of the sacrifice is redundant, that indeed belongs to his enemy. Thus, he makes it redundant for him who hates him.
That [fuel] exceeds its rival; therefore, one should place all the fuel other than the kindling-sticks (*samidh*) upon it from the eastward direction.
"Sacrifice to the gods at this well-performed sacrifice! [he says].

"The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; 'I shall worship the gods worthy of good sacrifice,' this is what he says thereby. 'For you are the bearer of oblations'—for Agni is indeed the bearer of oblations; therefore he says, 'For you are the bearer of oblations.
'Offer ye, honor ye Agni as the sacrifice proceeds; choose him as the bearer of oblations.'"

With this [verse] he indeed sends forth [the priests], and [they] offer and sacrifice; "Do that for whatever desire you have kindled yourselves," this is what he says by this. "When the sacrifice proceeds toward Agni"—the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus he says, "when the sacrifice proceeds toward Agni. "Choose the bearer of oblations"—for Agni is indeed the bearer of oblations; therefore he says so.

"Choose the bearer of oblations," [he says]. Regarding this very [verse], he recites the *adhvaravat* triplet.
