They were defeated; therefore, sacrifice (*yajña*) is called *adhvara*. An enemy indeed seeks to overthrow him who, knowing this, has the *adhvaravat* *ṛc* recited for him; for he conquers as much as one conquers by performing the Soma-sacrifice (*saumya-adhvara*). 1.4.2. [1]
For indeed, the gods yoked Agni to the most arduous task when they said, "As Hotṛ, carry this oblation of ours.
Having thus yoked him to the most arduous task, they encouraged him, saying, "Truly, you are powerful; truly, you are capable of this," [referring] to his heroic strength.
While concentrating his vigor, he says, "As they now appoint him who is the most eminent among kinsmen, so do they honor him, saying, 'Truly you are vigorous;
truly you are fit for this task. Thus he concentrates vigor upon him.
In that he places fire (*agni*) in him, [he does so]. 1.4.2. [2]
"O Agni, you are great, O Brāhmaṇa, O Bhārata!
For Agni is indeed the Brahman; therefore he says "Brāhmaṇa.
As for "Bhārata," he indeed bears the oblation (*havya*) to the gods; therefore they say, "Agni is Bhārata. And he, moreover, [sustains] these...

"Having become the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he sustains the subjects; therefore, indeed, one says 'Bhārata'. 1.4.2. [3] Then he announces his lineage (*ārṣeya*); he thereby makes this man known to the seers (*ṛṣi*) and to the gods.
"He who attained the sacrifice was one of great heroism"; therefore, he chooses the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*).
He chooses from the further side toward this side, for offspring are born from the further side toward this side, and [he does so] for the sake of the lordship of the elder.
And he conceals this; for first comes the father, then the son, then the grandson;
therefore, one chooses from the further side toward the nearer.

"Kindled by the gods, kindled by Manu"—for the gods indeed kindled him first; therefore he says, "kindled by the gods. "Kindled by Manu"—for Manu indeed kindled him first; therefore he says, "kindled by Manu. "Praised by the seers. 1.4.2. [6]
"For the seers (ṛṣis) praised him first; therefore he says, 'praised by the seers. 'Rejoiced by the sages (vipras)':
these indeed are the sages, namely the seers, for they rejoiced in him; therefore he says so."
"Approved by the Brahmins" (1.4.2.8).
"Praised by the sages" (1.4.2.9).
These indeed are the sages, namely the ṛṣis; for they praised this [sacrifice], therefore he says, "praised by the sages."

"Refined by the Brahman," for he is indeed refined by the Brahman; "one to whom ghee is offered," for he is indeed one to whom ghee is offered. "The leader of sacrifices, the charioteer of rites"—by him indeed they lead forth all sacrifices, both those which... [1.4.2.10]
"Because he is the other *pākayajñas* as well, therefore he says, 'the leader of sacrifices' (1.4.2).
[He says] 'the charioteer of the rites' (*rathīradhvarāṇām*).
For indeed, having become a chariot, he carries the sacrifice to the gods; therefore he says this."
"O charioteer of the sacrifices" (RV 1.4.2.12);
"the unassailable Hotṛ, the swift carrier of oblations.
For the Rakṣases do not overcome him; therefore he says, "the unassailable Hotṛ."
"Swift, the bearer of oblations"—for he indeed crosses over all evil; therefore he says, "Swift, the bearer of oblations.
"The vessel of the mouth, the ladle of the gods"—for Agni is indeed the vessel of the gods; therefore, in Agni [one offers] for all.
They offer to the gods, for he indeed becomes a vessel for the gods. Whoever knows this thus obtains the vessel of him whose vessel he desires.
"The cup is the drinking-vessel of the gods. 1.4.2 [14]
"By this very vessel, the gods indeed consume [the offering]; therefore he says, 'The cup is the drinking-vessel of the gods.
"Like the spokes, O Agni, you are the rim that encompasses the gods. 1.4.2.[15]
"Just as the rim of a wheel encompasses it on all sides, so do you encompass the gods on all sides"—this is what he says by [the words], "Bring the gods for the sacrificer.
1.4.2 [16] "Bring the gods for the sacrificer! he says.

He says, "O Agni, bring hither the gods for this sacrifice," thereby bringing Agni for the butter-portion (ājyabhāga) dedicated to Agni; he says, "Bring hither Soma," thereby bringing Soma for the butter-portion dedicated to Soma;
and he says, "Bring hither Agni," referring to that very Agni cake which is common to both [portions] and never displaced.

Therefore, he says, "Bring Agni," having thereby brought [Agni] forward. 1.4.2.[17] Then, according to the respective deities: "Bring the gods who drink the clarified butter"—this he says, having thereby brought forward the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.

The *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are indeed the gods who drink the clarified butter (*ājyapa*). When he says, "Bring Agni for the office of the *hotṛ*," he has thus brought Agni for the office of the *hotṛ*.
When he says, "Bring [him] his own greatness," he has thus brought his own greatness. Speech, indeed, is his own greatness;
he has thus brought speech. And when he says, "And bring [them], O Jātavedas, and sacrifice with a good sacrifice," he thereby brings those very deities.
The *āvoḍhavā* says this very thing when he says, "Bring them hither and sacrifice with them," which is what he means by saying, "Sacrifice with a good sacrifice. He recites while standing;
for this is a verse of invocation (*anuvākyā*), and thus, having become that very verse, he recites it.
Therefore, he recites the invitatory formula while standing (1.4.2).
He offers the offering verse while seated;
for this [offering verse] is indeed the *yājyā*. Therefore, no one offers the *yājyā* while standing, for this [offering verse] is indeed the *yājyā*.
Having become this very [fire], it performs the sacrifice; therefore, one recites the *yājyā* while seated. 1.4.3.
That fire which has been kindled by the *sāmidhenī* verses—it indeed blazes all the more.
He blazes forth from the other fire, for he becomes unassailable and untouchable. Just as that very fire, kindled by the *sāmidhenī* verses, blazes forth, even so does the Brāhmaṇa.
One who knows the *sāmidhenī* verses and recites them burns [with fervor], for he becomes unassailable and ungraspable.

He recites: "Forward..."—the forward-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the "forward"; by this verse, he kindles the forward-breath. "O Agni, come for the feast"—the downward-breath (*apāna*) is indeed the "come-hither"; by this verse, he kindles the downward-breath. "Greatly shining, O youngest one"—the upward-breath (*udāna*) is indeed the "greatly shining."
By this [verse], he kindles the *udāna* itself:
"May he grant us wide renown. Wide renown is indeed the sense of hearing, for by means of the sense of hearing, this world is vast and wide.

"He hears"—it is the ear indeed that he kindles by this [verse]. "Worthy of praise, worthy of homage"—speech, indeed, is worthy of praise; for speech praises all this, and by speech all this is praised.
"By this [verse], he kindles speech itself:
'Like a horse, the bearer of the gods'— the mind, indeed, is the bearer of the gods, for this [world] belongs to the mindful."
"Most abundantly he carries it about; by this [verse] he kindles the mind alone. (1.4.3.7) "O Agni, shining mightily!"—the eye indeed shines; by this [verse] he kindles the eye alone. (1.4.3.8)

"We choose Agni as the messenger"—this refers to that very central breath; with this [verse], he kindles it. This one is indeed the "intermediate" among the breaths, for from here the other breaths go upward, and from there the others go downward; thus it is intermediate.
"He becomes internal; they consider him to be such as he who thus knows this internality of the vital breaths.
"We long for him whose hair is flame" (*śociṣkeśa*). The penis, indeed, is "flame-haired," for the penis here is most abundant.
With this [verse], he purifies the penis; he kindles it.
"May he enkindle," [he says]; thus he enkindles his entire self, even unto the nails and the body hair.
1.4.3.[11] If someone should address him while this [verse] is being recited as the first *sāmidhenī*, he should reply to him: "The breath, indeed..."
"You have placed this breath of yours into the fire; you will die from the affliction of that breath. It would indeed happen so, if he were to recite [the second verse] for a second person.
He should say to him: "You have placed this out-breath of yours into the fire."
"You will suffer the affliction of your own *apāna*," he should say. It would indeed happen so if he were to recite it over the third [brick].
To him he should say: "The *udāna* indeed... "By the *udāna* indeed... "It would be so. 1.4.3.[14]

If he should utter [the challenge] on the fourth day, one should reply to him: "Verily, you have placed this very hearing of yours into the fire; through the hearing of yourself you will meet with affliction; you will become deaf. And so indeed it shall come to pass. 1.4.3 [15]
If he should speak ill of him on the fifth day, one should say to him: "Having deposited speech into your own fire, you will suffer injury to your speech; you shall become mute. 1.4.3.[16]

If he should speak ill of him in the sixth [case], one should say to him: "Verily, having placed this mind of yours in the fire, you will suffer injury to your mind; seized by mind-stealing demons, you will wander about utterly bewildered. And so indeed shall it be. 1.4.3. [17]

If on the seventh day... [you eat], that which is the eye of the self you have placed in the fire; through the eye of the self you will meet with affliction and become blind. 1.4.3.[18] If on the eighth day... [you eat], that which is the central breath of the self you have placed in the fire; through the center [of the self]...
"You will suffer injury to your vital breath; you will die gasping. And so indeed it would be.
(1.4.3.19) "If on the ninth day... [you eat] yāciṣṇa, this is as if you have placed a member of your own self into the fire; you will suffer injury to your generative organ;
you will become impotent. And so indeed it would be. (1.4.3.20)

If [he were to die] on the tenth day, [the teacher would say]: "Verily, by placing this downward-breathing of yours into the fire, you will suffer harm through that downward-breathing of yours; you will die smothered. And so indeed it would happen. 1.4.3.
[21] If [he were to die] on the eleventh day...

"If you were to cast this entire self into the fire, you would perish with your whole self; you will soon go to that world. And so it would indeed be. Just as with the fire... [1.4.3] [22]...just as with the fire.
One who falls into the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses while they are being kindled comes to grief;
even so, one comes to grief by reviling a Brāhmaṇa who knows the *sāmidhenīs* while he is reciting them after them.
They indeed kindled that very fire.

"Let us offer to the gods when the fire is kindled!"—with these words he offers these two first oblations into it: to Mind and to Speech. For Mind and Speech, being yoked together, carry the sacrifice to the gods. 1.4.4(2)

In that which is performed silently, the mind carries the sacrifice to the gods; and in that which is performed with articulated speech, speech carries the sacrifice to the gods. Indeed, this [sacrifice] is performed in these two ways, and thus these two [carry it].
"In this way he satisfies him; when he is satisfied and pleased, he shall carry the sacrifice to the gods.
(1.4.4.3) He pours that [libation] with the *sruva* spoon.
That which he pours with the mind, for the mind is a bull (*vṛṣan*), and the *sruva* is a bull. (1.4.4.4)
He pours that [libation] with the *sruc* ladle;
for he pours it with speech, and speech is indeed a woman, and the *sruc* is indeed a woman. He pours it silently.
That which he pours out for the mind, he does not say "svāhā," for the mind is undefined; and that which is silent is indeed undefined.
He pours it out with a mantra.
That which he pours out for speech, for speech is articulated and the mantra is articulated.
(1.4.4) He pours it out while sitting;
that which he pours out for the mind, he does so while standing—for both mind and speech [are indeed...]
Speech and Mind are the two yoked [horses] that carry the sacrifice to the gods. Of the two yoked ones, whichever is the weaker, for it they provide a support.

Speech is indeed weaker than Mind—for Mind is, as it were, more unlimited, while Speech is, as it were, more limited—and thus he provides this support for Speech. These two, being yoked together, carry the sacrifice to the gods.
Therefore, while [the fire] is being carried forward, he offers the two Āghāra libations while standing.
1.4.4. [8] The gods, indeed, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack by the Asuras and Rakṣasas.
He offers it on the right side, for strength is, as it were, uplifted;

therefore, standing on the right, he pours the libation. And because he pours the libation on both sides, therefore this mind and speech, though being the same, are yet distinct. Of these two, one indeed is the head of the sacrifice.
One of the two [fires] is the root of the two libations (āghāra).
He pours that one with the *sruva* ladle;
he pours that which is the root of the sacrifice. With the *sruk* ladle he pours the other; he pours that which is the head of the sacrifice.
He offers that silently;
for that which is the root of the sacrifice is, as it were, silent, since here the voice does not speak. 1.4.4 [11]
He offers it with a mantra;
for that which is the head of the sacrifice is speech, and the mantra is indeed speech, since from the head speech speaks. 1.4.4 [12]
He pours the libation while sitting for that which is the root of the sacrifice, for this root stands as if seated;
he pours the libation while standing for that which is the head of the sacrifice, for this head stands as if upright. 1.4.4 [13]

Having first poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva*-ladle, he says, "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire! This is just as one would place a yoke upon [the ox]; for when he pours the first *āghāra*, it is as if he has already placed the yoke upon it.
"They harness [the horse]. (1.4.4.14) Now he cleanses it;
he thereby harnesses it, thinking, "Being harnessed, may it carry the sacrifice to the gods."
Therefore he cleanses; he cleanses while stepping around, for they yoke what is fit by stepping around. He cleanses three times each, for the sacrifice is threefold. 1.4.4 [15] He cleanses it.

"O Agni, winner of the prize, I cleanse you who are about to win the prize; I cleanse you, the winner of the prize"—by this he says, "I cleanse you, the worthy of sacrifice, who are about to carry the sacrifice. Then, afterwards, he does so silently three times.

This is just as if, having yoked [a horse], one were to urge it on, saying, "Go forward! Carry [the load]!"—in the same way, he goads him with the whip, saying, "Go forward! Carry the sacrifice to the gods!"
Therefore, above that, he performs it silently three times; and because this rite is performed between those two, therefore this mind and speech, though being the same, are yet not the same. 1.4.5.
[1] He, about to pour the second libation with the ladle—

To the east, he places his joined palms (añjali) with the two offering-ladles, saying, "Homage to the gods! Svadhā to the ancestors! Thus, intending to perform the priestly office for both the gods and the ancestors, he pays homage to them.
He takes up the two ladles, saying, "May you two be easy for me to control; may you two be easy for me to bear."
"May I be able to support you two"— this is what he says with the words, "May I today collect the clarified butter for the gods without spilling";
"I shall extend the sacrifice for the gods today without agitation"— this is what he says with the words, "O Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you with my foot."
The sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu; it is to him that he makes this submission, saying, "May I not step upon you.
"O Agni, may I honor your earthy form in your lap," he says; by this he means, "O Agni, may I honor your auspicious form in your lap. 1.4.5 [3]
"Thou art the station of Viṣṇu," he says.
Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; for it stands near him, therefore he says, "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu.
"From here Indra performed his heroic deed," he says, for from here, standing on the south side, Indra [warded off] the destructive spirits.
"The Rakṣases drove him away; therefore he said: 'Indra performed a heroic deed. 'He stood upright for the sacrifice'—the sacrifice is indeed the adhvara;
thus he says, 'The sacrifice stood upright.
'O Agni, perform the office of the Hotṛ; perform the office of the messenger.'"
Agni is indeed both of these for the gods: the Hotṛ and the messenger.
"Know both of these, that you are for the gods"—this is what he thereby says. "May Heaven and Earth protect you;
may you protect Heaven and Earth"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were. [He offers] to Sviṣṭakṛt for the gods, Indra, with clarified butter.
"By the oblation, svāhā!"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "O Indra, with ghee!
For he pours this libation for Speech, and they say that Indra is Speech; for this reason also he says, "O Indra, with ghee.
Then, having gone around so as not to let the two ladles touch each other...

He anoints with the *dhruvā* [ladle]. The upper libation (*uttara-āghāra*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the *dhruvā* is the self; thus he places the head back into the self. The upper libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the head is prosperity (*śrī*);
for the head is indeed prosperity, therefore whoever is the most excellent part of a region, he is "the head" of that region.
"The head," they say, refers to the *dhruvā* spoon; it follows the sacrificer himself.
He who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt* spoon; for when [he acts] with the *upabhṛt*, [it is he]. 1.4.5.[6]
He unites [the ladle] with the formula "Obeisance to him who is hostile to the sacrificer"; he thereby bestows strength upon that very person who acts inimically toward the sacrificer;
therefore, he anoints it with the *dhruvā* ladle.
He anoints it as follows:
"May light unite with light"—for in the one [ladle] there is ghee, which is light, and in the other there is light;
thus these two lights meet together. Therefore he unites them in this manner.
Now, therefore, [the procedure] concerning both the mind and speech.
"Ahambhadra, the mind and speech have indeed arisen. "Ahambhadra, we two have arisen.
Then the mind said: [1.4.5.9]

"I alone am superior to you; indeed, there is nothing that you speak which has not been previously understood by me. Since you are merely an imitator and a follower of my path, I alone am superior to you. Then Speech spoke: "I alone am superior to you; indeed, there is nothing that you speak which has not been previously understood by me. Since you are merely an imitator and a follower of my path, I alone am superior to you. 1.4.5 [10] Then Speech said:
"I alone am superior to you;
whatever you know, I understand it and I explain it. They both went to Prajāpati for a decision on this matter.

That Prajāpati spoke in accordance with the mind alone: "The mind indeed is better than speech; for you are an imitator of what is done and a follower of the path by the mind; indeed, one who is worse becomes an imitator of what is done and a follower of the path. 1.4.5 [12]
When she was spoken against, Vāk was struck with wonder;
her fetus fell away, and Vāk said to Prajāpati: "May I become for you one who does not carry the oblation, since you have spoken against me."
Therefore, whatever pertaining to Prajāpati is performed at the sacrifice, that is performed in a whisper; for speech was the carrier of oblations to Prajāpati.
And this, indeed, the gods [performed].
Whether it was on the hide of a ram or on that of a brown one, they indeed asked about that place, saying, "Was it right here?
From there he came into being; therefore, even with a woman of the Ātreya clan, one incurs no sin, for these [sages] were born from this very woman, the goddess Vāc. 1.5.1. [1]
He indeed makes the announcement for the *pravara* (the choosing of the priests). Now, as to why he makes the announcement for the *pravara*: the announcement is the sacrifice;
having thus uttered the sacrifice, he then chooses the *hotṛ*. Therefore, he makes the announcement for the *pravara*. 1.5.1. [2]
Having taken hold of the cord for binding the sacrificial fuel, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*.
For if the Adhvaryu were to call for the *āśrāvaṇa* without having grasped the sacrifice, he would either tremble or meet with some other misfortune. 1.5.1. [3]

Now, some indeed, having reached either the sacrificial grass spread upon the altar or a chip of the fuel-wood, cause the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made, saying, "This is something of the sacrifice; by reaching this, we shall cause the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made for the sacrifice. But one should not do so; for this [fuel-wood] is indeed something of the sacrifice.

When the fuel-bundles have been tied together and they sweep the fire, it is indeed at that very moment that he approaches the sacrifice and calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* response; therefore, he should call for the *śrauṣaṭ* while actually taking hold of the fuel-bundles themselves. Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he first chooses as the Hotṛ of the gods none other than Agni himself; thus [he chooses] Agni for Agni.
And he makes amends to the gods when he chooses Agni first; he makes amends to Agni.
Then, when he chooses him who is the Hotṛ of the gods first, he makes amends to the gods.
He says: "Agni, the god, the divine Hotṛ," for Agni is indeed the Hotṛ of the gods; therefore he says, "Agni, the god, the divine."
"He is the Hotṛ"—by this he pays homage to both Agni and the gods. When he first says "Agni," he pays homage to Agni;
then, when he first mentions him who is the Hotṛ of the gods, he pays homage to the gods: "May he, the knowing one, the wise, worship the gods. (1.5.1 [6])
"Agni, indeed, is one who knows the gods; he, knowing them, shall sacrifice for us in due order"—this is what he says by [the words] "like Manu, like Bharata. 1.5.1 [7]
In the beginning, Manu indeed sacrificed with the sacrifice; imitating him, these creatures sacrifice.
Therefore he says, "Manu-like. They say, "The sacrifice belongs to Manu"; for that reason also he says, "Manu-like. "Like Bharata. 1.5.1 [8] "Like Bharata."

For he indeed brings the oblation to the gods; therefore they say, "Agni is Bharata. Moreover, having become the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he supports these creatures; for that reason also, they say, "[He is] like Bharata.
1.5.1 [9] Now, he chooses the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*).
And he thus announces him to the seers and to the gods, saying, "This one of great heroism has reached the sacrifice"; therefore, he chooses the ancestral lineage (ārṣeya).
He chooses it from the further side towards the near side.
For offspring are born from the further side toward this side; moreover, it is concealed from the superior lord.
For first there is the father, then the son, then the grandson; therefore he chooses from the further side toward this side. 1.5.1 [11]
Having stated his lineage (*ārṣeya*), he says, "Accompanied by the *brahman*.

For Agni is indeed the *brahman*; therefore he says, "accompanied by the *brahman*. And when he says, "and may he bring hither," he thereby refers to those very deities whom he has previously caused to bring [the oblation], saying, "and may they bring hither. 1.5.1[.1]2
"The Brahmins are the promoters of this sacrifice.

These indeed are the Brahmins who are the promoters of the sacrifice—those who are learned in the Vedas—for they extend it and they produce it; he makes amends to them for that, and therefore he says, "The Brahmins are [the promoters] of this..."
"O protectors of the sacrifice," [he says].
"This one is human.
By this, he chooses this human Hotṛ; for he was the Hotṛ in ancient times, and so he is now.
The Hotṛ priest (1.5.1.14): Once he has been chosen as the Hotṛ, he mutters [the formulas] and approaches the deities according to the prescribed order for the sake of the gods.

One should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call according to the rule so that he may carry the oblation to the gods; thus he approaches the deities so that he does not stumble. There he mutters: "O God Savitṛ, this [sacrifice] they choose for you. Thus he approaches Savitṛ for impulsion, for he is indeed [the impeller].

"The impeller of the gods, Agni, for the office of the Hotṛ"—by this he makes atonement both to Agni and to the gods. In that he first mentions Agni, he makes atonement to Agni; and in that he first mentions him who is the Hotṛ of the gods, he makes atonement to the gods.
"Together with the father Vaiśvānara"—the father Vaiśvānara is indeed Prajāpati the year;
thus he makes amends to that very year, to Prajāpati. "O Agni, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, speak forth!"

When he is about to recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) or is about to offer the oblation (*yajati*), he thereby makes a formal request to these very deities: "You recite the invitatory verse; you perform the offering!
[May we be] in the bounty of the Vasus.

"May we be of the Rudras on the earth, of the Ādityas for Aditi, faultless"—these indeed are the three classes of gods, namely the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; "may we be under their protection," this is what he thereby says. "Today may I utter speech pleasing to the gods."
"May I recite today what is pleasing to the gods"—this is what he says; for it is successful for one who recites what is pleasing to the gods. "What is pleasing to the Brahmins. 1.5.1 [19]
"May I today recite what is pleasing to the Brahmins"—this is what he says by this;
for it is successful when one recites what is pleasing to the Brahmins. "To Narāśaṃsa, the pleasing one."
"Men are indeed offspring; thus he has spoken for all offspring. For that is successful:
whether one knows it or not, they are released with the words, 'He has spoken well, he has spoken well. [The verse is:
'If today, at the choosing of the Hotṛ, a crooked eye has flown away, may Agni Jātavedas, who observes all people, bring it back again,' just as..."

"Those who first chose the fires for the office of the Hotṛ perished; by saying, 'Whatever has been exhausted here of mine through this choosing, may that be replenished for me,' he says this very thing, and thus it is replenished for him again. Then he touches both the Adhvaryu and the Agnīdh.
The mind is the Adhvaryu and speech is the Hotṛ;
thus he unites both that mind and that speech.
1.5.1 [22]. There he mutters:
"May the six wide expanses protect me—Agni and the Earth, the Waters and Vāja, Day and Night.
By this he means: "May these deities protect me from misfortune. For indeed, there is no stumbling for one whom these deities protect from misfortune. 1.5.1 [23]
Then he approaches the Hotṛ’s seat.
From the Hotṛ’s seat, he throws away a blade of grass, saying, "Expelled is Parāvasu!
For Parāvasu was indeed the name of the Asuras' Hotṛ; it is him that he thus expels from the Hotṛ’s seat. 1.5.1 [24]

Then he sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat with the formula: "Here I sit upon the seat of Arvāvasu. Arvāvasu, indeed, is the name of the Hotṛ of the gods; it is on his very seat that he thus sits. 1.5.1 [25]

There he mutters: "O Viśvakarman, you are the protector of the body; do not harm me, do not injure me; this is your place. He moves northward between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires; for he stands between these two, and thus he makes amends to them with the words, "Do not harm me, do not injure me. In this way, these two do not harm him. 1.5.1 [26]
Then, looking at the fire, he mutters:
"O All-Gods, instruct me how, having been chosen as the Hotṛ here, I may think upon it;
having sat down, tell me my portion, and by which path I shall carry the oblation to you."

Just as one would say to those for whom food has been cooked, "Instruct me how I shall bring it to you, and how I shall serve it to you," even so he seeks instruction from the gods: "Instruct me how I may offer the *vaṣaṭ* call in due order, and how I may carry the oblation in due order. Therefore, he mutters this prayer. 1.5.2. [1]

"Agni, the Hotṛ, let him know the office of the Hotṛ for Agni"—by this he says, "Let Agni here, as the Hotṛ, know [this]"; "the office of the Hotṛ for Agni," for his is indeed the office of the Hotṛ; "let him know the Prāvitra"—the Prāvitra is indeed the sacrifice; by this he says, "let him know the sacrifice"; "well-pleasing to thee, O sacrificer, is the deity"—by this he says, "Well-pleasing to thee, O sacrificer, is that deity for whom Agni is the Hotṛ."

"O Adhvaryu, place the butter-filled ladle upon the mouth," with these words he gives the impulse to the Adhvaryu. As for why he says it as if it were one [ladle]: the sacrificer follows the *juhū* (sacrificial spoon), while he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt*. And as for why he says it as if there were two...
He should say to the sacrificer: "It would make his hateful rival one who rises against him;
for the *juhū* ladle is food that has been given, and the *upabhṛt* is food to be eaten. If he were to speak as if there were two, he would make the eater rise against the food;
therefore, he speaks as if it were only one. 1.5.2. [3]

"Seeking the gods, possessing all boons"—by saying this, he indeed praises her and magnifies her. "We shall praise the gods worthy of praise; we shall honor those worthy of honor; we shall sacrifice."

"Let us praise those worthy of praise; let us bow to those worthy of bowing; let us sacrifice to those worthy of sacrifice. Now, those worthy of praise are human beings, those worthy of bowing are the ancestors, and those worthy of sacrifice are the gods.
(1.5.2) Indeed, those offspring who are not partaken in the sacrifice [are excluded].

Those indeed are defeated who are thus; likewise, he causes those creatures that are undefeated to participate in the sacrifice: after humans come the domestic animals, after the gods come the birds, the plants, and the trees—whatever exists here, all that is thus made to participate in the sacrifice. 1.5.2. [5]
Now, these are indeed the nine *vyāhṛtis*. There are these nine vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in a person; he thus places these very breaths into him.
Therefore, there are nine *vyāhṛtis*.
Sacrifice, indeed, once fled away from the gods.

The gods addressed him, saying, "Hear us; turn back toward us! He replied, "So be it," and turned back toward the gods. With him having turned back, the gods performed sacrifice. Having sacrificed with him, they became that which the gods are now. 1.5.2 [7]
When he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he thus consecrates the sacrifice with the words, "Hear us! Turn toward us!
And when he responds with the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, the sacrifice turns back toward him with the words, "So be it. By means of that turned-back seed...

The priests perform the ritual transmission for the sake of the sacrificer behind his back; just as they would perform the ritual transmission with a full vessel, so do the priests perform the ritual transmission by means of this [breath].
They perform that ritual transmission by speech alone, for the sacrifice is speech, indeed, for speech is the sacrifice.
This is the seed; by this very means they practice the tradition of handing it down.
Having said, "Recite the invitatory verse," the Adhvaryu should neither speak out of turn nor indeed [interrupt].
If the Hotṛ were to speak out of turn, the Adhvaryu would cause the *āśrāvaṇa* (call for the response); that [error] would then revert to the Agnīdh in the sacrifice.
1.5.2. [9] Therefore, he should not speak out of turn regarding the fire;
until the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* (response), the Agnīdh causes the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, and that [error] reverts back to the Adhvaryu in the sacrifice.
He turns back. That Adhvaryu must not speak out of turn;
when it is time for him to say "Recite! (*yajā*), the Adhvaryu should simply say "Recite! (*yajā*) to the Hotṛ for the sacrifice.
He bestows [the offering]. 1.5.2.[11] That Hotṛ priest must not speak out of turn until the *vaṣaṭ* call; at that *vaṣaṣ*-call, he [the offering] becomes semen in Agni as its very womb.
"Agni, indeed, is the womb of the sacrifice; from him it is born"—thus [it is said] regarding the *haviryajña*. Now, regarding the *saumya* sacrifice (*adhvara*):

having drawn the cup (*graha*), the *adhvaryu* must not speak out until the commencement [of the chant], saying to the *udgātṛ*s, "Come hither!"—thus does the *adhvaryu* [offer] the sacrifice to the *udgātṛ*s.
He hands it over. 1.5.2.[13] Those Udgātṛs should not speak out of turn.
To the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛs [should hand over] the sacrifice with the words, "This is the last; this is the last."
They hand it over. 1.5.2.[14] That Hotṛ priest must not speak out until the *vaṣaṭ*-call;
at the *vaṣaṣ*-call, he [the oblation], having become seed, is indeed cast into Agni as its womb.
Agni is indeed the womb of the sacrifice; from him it is born. 1.5.2.
[15] If he were to utter a cry of protest (*apavyāharet*) against that which has come to the sacrifice, it would be as if one were to pour out a full vessel. Thus indeed...

He would pour away the sacrificer. But wherever the officiating priests proceed with the sacrifice in mutual agreement, everything there succeeds and does not fail; therefore, the sacrifice must be maintained in this very way. Now, these are the five utterances: *o śrāvaya*, *astu śrauṣaṭ*, *yaja*, *ye yajāmahe*.
"Vauṣaṭ"—the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year; this is one measure of the sacrifice, this is its perfection.
There are seventeen syllables in these [formulas].
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; Prajāpati is the sacrifice, for this is one measure of the sacrifice—this is its perfection.
"O, cause [the Hotṛ] to announce!"—thus indeed did the gods [speak].
They released the east wind; with "Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*," they caused the clouds to gather;
with "Sacrifice! (*yaj*), the lightning; and with "We who sacrifice" (*ye yajāmahe*), the thunder; and by the *vaṣaṭ*-call itself, they made it rain.
1.5.2 [19] Now, if one should desire rain:

If he should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, or if he should say at the New and Full Moon sacrifices, "I am desirous of rain," then he should say to the *adhvaryu*: "Meditate mentally upon the east wind and lightning";
[he should say] to the *agnīdh*: "Meditate mentally upon the clouds, and upon thunder and rain."

"He should meditate upon the Hotṛ," [it is said]; "he should meditate upon all these with his mind," [it is said regarding] the Brahman. Indeed, it rains in that place where the officiating priests (ṛtvij) perform the sacrifice in such mutual agreement.
"O, cause [the offering] to be heard!"—thus indeed do the gods [speak].

They invoked the Virāj with "Let there be the Śrauṣaṭ! They released the calf with "OṂ Yaja! They drove [the cows] forward with "We sacrifice! They approached with "We sacrifice! By means of the Vaṣaṭ-call alone, they milked the Virāj.
This earth is indeed the Virāj; this is her milking. Thus, indeed, does this earth yield for him.
The Virāj milks all desires for him who knows this milking of the Virāj.
The seasonal offerings (prayāja) are indeed the seasons;
therefore there are five of them, for there are five seasons.
The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this sacrifice—this Father Prajāpati, the Year—each thinking, "This shall be ours; this shall be ours. 1.5.3. [3]
Then the gods, praising and toiling, wandered about; they saw these fore-offerings (prayāja) and sacrificed with them.
By means of them, they drove forth the seasons and the year; from the seasons and from the year, they excluded their rivals.
Therefore, they are called "fore-offerings" (prajaya)—for this is indeed their name. And in the same way, this [sacrificer] now, by means of these, [drives forth] the seasons and the year.
He offers the fore-offerings; he drives away his rivals from the seasons and the year. Therefore, he sacrifices with the fore-offerings.
They have clarified butter as their oblation; clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt, and by means of this, the gods...

By means of the thunderbolt of clarified butter, they drove the seasons and the year forward, and from the seasons and the year they excluded their enemies; in the same way, this sacrificer now drives the seasons and the year forward by means of this thunderbolt of clarified butter, and from the seasons and the year he excludes his enemies. Therefore, the oblations consist of clarified butter. 1.5.3. [5]
This ghee is indeed the milk of the year;

by means of that very milk of his own, the gods made him their own. In the same way, this sacrificer now makes him his own by means of that very milk of his own; therefore, the oblation consists of ghee.
They come to pass.
1.5.3.[6] Wherever he might stand while calling for the *āśrāvaṇa* for the *prayāja* offerings, from that very spot he should not move away; for this is indeed a battle.
He who performs the *prayāja* offerings is brought into proximity. Of two who are engaged in combat, whichever one is defeated indeed retreats;
the victor, however, advances further. Therefore, he should step forward ever further, and he should offer the oblations ever closer together. 1.5.3. [7]
One should not do it in that way.

One should not move away from the very spot where, while standing, one calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* for the *prayāja* offerings; rather, one should offer the oblations at the very place where one considers the fire to be most kindled, by means of an offering into the well-kindled fire.
Verily, these oblations become successful. 1.5.3.
[8] Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says:
"Recite the offering prayer for the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*). He thus kindles the spring; and the spring, being kindled, [flourishes].
He kindles the other seasons; the seasons being kindled, creatures are procreated and plants ripen.

Indeed, he has thus uttered all the seasons. Then he says "Yaja yaja" (Sacrifice! Sacrifice! for the subsequent ones, to avoid repetition (*jāmitā*). For he would commit a repetition if he were to say "Tanūnapāt, yaja iḍo yaja" (Tanūnapāt, sacrifice! Iḍas, sacrifice!). Therefore, he says "Yaja yaja" for the subsequent ones. 1.5.3 [9]
He offers the *samidh* oblations.

The spring is indeed the *samidh*; it was the spring that the gods thus appropriated for themselves; by means of the spring they drove away their rivals. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now appropriates the spring for himself; by means of the spring he drives away his rivals.
Therefore, he offers the *samidh* oblation. Then he offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation.
*Tanūnapāt* is indeed the summer; for it is the summer that heats the bodies of these creatures.

The gods chose the summer season for themselves; they excluded their rivals from the summer. This sacrificer now chooses the summer season for himself and excludes his rivals from the summer. Therefore, he offers to Tanūnapāt.
Then he offers to Iḍ.

The rainy season is indeed *iḍ*. For these small crawling creatures that are driven out by the summer and the winter wander about during the rains as if seeking food that has been praised (*iḍita*). Therefore the rainy season is *iḍ*. It was during the rains that the gods appropriated [the enemy]; through the rains they drove their rivals away. Thus, the rains...
In this way, he appropriates this for himself; he goes away from his rivals after the rains; therefore, he offers the *iḍā*.
Then he offers the *barhis*; for the *barhis* is indeed autumn, since these plants that are the *barhis* belong to autumn.

They are constantly diminished by summer and winter; they increase during the rainy season. In autumn, they lie spread out as the form of sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Therefore, the sacrificial grass is called *carad-barhis*. By means of that, the gods appropriated the autumn, [and] from the autumn [they gained power].
He indeed appropriates for himself those autumns that his rivals were about to pass through;
therefore, he offers with *barhis*.
Then he offers with "Svāhā! Svāhā! 1.5.3. [13]

The *svāhā*-utterance is indeed the end of the sacrifice, and winter is the end of the seasons, for it follows after spring. By means of the end, the gods thus appropriated the end; by means of the end, they drove their rivals away from the end. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now appropriates the end by means of the end.
"From the end, from the end, from the enemy, from the one who is close at hand—therefore he sacrifices with 'Svāhā!
(1.5.3.14). Now, this very thing: it is in spring that one returns again from winter; for from this [spring] he comes into being again.
And indeed, he who knows this thus comes into being again in this world. (1.5.3.15)
He offers with the words, "May he partake! May he partake!
This is to avoid sameness; for he would commit a repetition if he were to offer with "may they partake, may they partake," or even "may he partake, may he partake.
"May they partake" is feminine, and "may he partake" is masculine; thus, this constitutes a productive union.
"Therefore, it is performed; let them eat, let him eat"—thus he sacrifices. Then, at the fourth fore-offering, he pours [the butter] onto the *barhis* grass.
The *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the clarified butter is seed.
Thus, this seed is poured into the very offspring; by means of that poured seed, these offspring are born again in succession.
Therefore, he pours [the butter] together at the fourth fore-offering upon the *barhis* grass.
Indeed, a battle is thereby brought near.

He who sacrifices with the fore-offerings (prayāja) conquers; for of two who are engaged in combat, he who gains the friend wins. In this case, the ladle (juhū) gains the friend from the supporting ladle (upabhṛt); by that he conquers.
Therefore, at the fourth fore-offering, he pours together [the butter] upon the sacrificial grass (barhis). 1.5.3. [18]
The sacrificer follows the *juhū* ladle;
he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt*.
Thus, for the sacrificer, he makes his hateful rival pay tribute, and he himself eats it.
The *juhū* is food, and the *upabhṛt* is likewise food; thus he causes this food to be offered as a tribute. Therefore, he pours [the butter] together during the fourth *prayāja*.
He pours it together without touching [the ladles].
If he were to touch it, he would touch the sacrificer with his hateful rival;
he would touch the giver with the one to be consumed. Therefore, he pours [the butter] together without touching it.
Then he places the *juhū* ladle over the northern [part of the fire].
He thus places the sacrificer upon his rival who hates him; he places the eater upon the food. Therefore, he places the *juhū* spoon over the *upabhṛt*.
The gods indeed said:
"Come, let us complete the sacrifice as already won; if the Asuras and Rakṣases should attack us, our sacrifice will still be completed.
Thus they [spoke] at the final fore-offering (prayāja). 1.5.3 [22].

By means of the utterance "svāhā," they completed the entire sacrifice. With "Svāhā to Agni," they completed that portion of clarified butter belonging to Agni; with "Svāhā to Soma," they completed that portion of clarified butter belonging to Soma;
and with "Svāhā to Agni," they completed that cake which belongs to Agni and is not displaced from either occasion.
He establishes them in their proper order. Then, according to the respective deities:
"Svāhā to the gods who drink the clarified butter!"
They completed it with the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s; for the gods who drink the clarified butter (*ājyapa*) are indeed the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s.
With the words, "May Agni, pleased, accept the clarified butter," they completed it with Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, for Agni is indeed Sviṣṭakṛt.
Thus, even now, this sacrifice is completed in the same way as the gods completed it; therefore, [it is done] at the final *prayāja*.

He offers with "Svāhā! Svāhā! as many times as there are oblations. Thus he brings the entire sacrifice to completion following victory. Therefore, whatever is done subsequently in the sacrifice that is contrary to the proper order, one should not heed it; one should know: "My sacrifice is completed. For this very sacrifice had already reached its goal, just like an offering made with the *vaṣaṭ* call, offered with the *svāhā* call. 1.5.3 [24]
Those gods desired:
"How indeed might we cause this sacrifice to swell again, make it free from weariness, and perform the ritual with it while it is still unworn? 1.5.3 [25]
Whatever clarified butter remained in the *juhū* ladle,

with which they had completed the sacrifice, with that very same [butter] they sprinkled the oblations as before; they thereby caused them to swell again and made them free from weariness, [rendering them] unfatigued.
Therefore, after having performed the final fore-offering (prayāja), he sprinkles the oblations with clarified butter as before;

thus he causes them to swell again and makes them fresh, for clarified butter is indeed fresh. Therefore, whenever he cuts a portion from any oblation, he sprinkles it with clarified butter once more, specifically for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

He then causes it to swell and makes it fresh; now, when he cuts off the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, he does not pour ghee over it again, for he has no further oblation of the sacrificial food (*havis*) to offer into the fire from that point.
He indeed offers the *samidhs*.

The vital breaths are indeed the fuel; he thus kindles the vital breaths, for by the vital breaths this person is kindled. Therefore, if he should be afflicted by illness, one should say, "Touch it. If it be warm, he should then hope for recovery, for as long as it is warm, it remains kindled. But if it be cold, he should not hope.
He thus bestows life-breaths upon him; therefore, he offers the *samidh* oblation.
Then he offers to Tanūnapāt;
Tanūnapāt is indeed semen; it is semen that he thus pours forth; therefore [he offers] to Tanūnapāt.
He performs the sacrifice. 1.5.4.[3] Then he sacrifices the *iḍā*. For offspring is indeed the *iḍā*; when the seed, once cast, is brought forth as offspring, then...
He moves about desiring that food as if it were already offered; he thus generates it. Therefore, he sacrifices with the *iḍā*. Then he sacrifices with the *barhis*.
The *barhis* is indeed abundance; he thus generates abundance. Therefore, he sacrifices with the *barhis*.
Then he sacrifices with "Svāhā! Svāhā!
Winter, indeed, among the seasons is the utterance of "Svāhā. For winter brings these creatures under its own control; therefore, in winter, the plants wither and the leaves of the trees fall.

They are released like birds from a snare; they become like birds flying downward; they fall like one whose hair has fallen out; the wicked man becomes like one with disheveled hair. Winter indeed brings these creatures under its own control.
He for whom this occurs—on whichever side he may be—brings that side under his own power for the sake of prosperity and the eating of food, provided he knows this thus. 1.5.4 [6]
The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. They did not conquer by means of clubs or bows;
being unable to conquer, they said, "Come, let us seek victory through speech alone, O Brahman! Whichever of us [utters] our speech..."
"If she were to follow after what was uttered by the pair, he would be defeated in everything, and the others would win everything.
"So be it," the gods said. Those gods then said to Indra, "Utter [the word].
Indra spoke.
"Mine is one," said one; "ours is one," said the others.
Thus they found that very pair, for "one" and "one" constitute a pair.
Then Indra said, "Mine are two."
Then the others said, "Two are mine.
Thus they found that very pair, for two and two make a pair.
"Three are mine," said Indra. (1.5.4)
Then the others said, "Three for us!
And thus they found that very pair; for three and three indeed constitute a pair.
Then Indra said, "Four for me! 1.5.4. [10]
Then the others said, "Four for us.
Thus they found that very pair, for four males and four females constitute a pair.
"Five for me," said Indra.
Then the others did not find a mate, for there is no mate beyond five; indeed, these two [sets] together become "five, five.
Thereupon the Asuras were utterly defeated from everything, while the gods [prevailed].
They conquered the Asuras and excluded the Asuras from everything.
Therefore, when the first *prayāja* has been offered, he should say: "One for me; one for him whom I hate. 1.5.4. [12]
"If he does not hate [us]," he should say, "he who hates us and whom we hate. At the second *prayāja* offering, he says, "Two for me," and "Two for him who hates us and whom we hate."
"Three for me" at the third fore-offering;
"three for him who hates us and whom we hate" [at the fourth].
"Four for me" at the fourth fore-offering.
"Four for him who hates us and whom we hate," [he says] at the fourth *prayāja*;
"Five for me," at the fifth *prayāja*.

"Nothing belongs to him who hates us or whom we hate"—thinking thus, he becomes "five and five," and so he perishes; for one who knows this, it gathers everything together and excludes all rivals from him. 1.6.1. [1]
The seasons indeed sought a share in the sacrifice among the gods, saying:
"Give us a share in the sacrifice; do not exclude us from the sacrifice; let there be a share for us in the sacrifice as well. 1.6.1 [2]
The gods did not perceive that.
While the gods remained unaware, the seasons turned toward the Asuras—the enemies of the gods, their hateful rivals. 1.6.1 [3]
They indeed made for themselves that wisdom which they now still hear recited; for in former times, some went about plowing and sowing,
while others went about reaping and threshing, yet for them the plants always ripened even without being tilled.
1.6.1.[4] That indeed was the offense against the gods: "He who hates us more, he acts as an enemy toward us."

"But do you know only this much—that this [world] is otherwise than this? They said, "Let us address the Seasons. He asked, "By what means? They replied, "We shall worship them as the very first ones in the sacrifice.
Then Agni said:

Then [they said], "Since you previously sacrificed to me first, where am I? Do not cause me to fall from my abode! When they called upon the seasons, they did not cause Agni to fall from his abode; therefore Agni is immovable, for he indeed does not fall from his abode.

In whatever sphere one exists who thus knows this imperishable Agni—[this is the seventh section]. Those gods said to Agni: "Go, you yourself must consecrate them. Having gone, Agni said: "O Ṛtavas, I have indeed found a share for you among the gods at the sacrifice. "How did you find us? [they asked. "As the very first ones at the sacrifice," [he replied].
"They shall sacrifice," [they said]. 1.6.1.[8] Those seasons spoke to Agni:
"We shall allot you among us, you who are our [share] in the sacrifice among the gods."
"He who knows his portion"—this very Agni is thus apportioned among the seasons. [With the words] "O Agni, fuel; O Agni, Tanūnapāt; O Agni, Iḍ;

O Agni, sacrificial grass; O Agni, Svāhā! he becomes one who has received his share in that meritorious act which his fellow-student performs. Indeed, for him who possesses Agni, the seasons possessed of Agni cause the plants to ripen here.
"Whoever knows this Agni thus distributed among the seasons [attains everything].
Regarding this they say: "Since they invoke the *prayāja* offerings last, why then do they sacrifice them first? For they assigned these to the end of the sacrifice, yet they are the first for you.
They said, "Let us sacrifice! Therefore, they invoke the last [of the fore-offerings] first and perform the first [of the after-offerings] last.
With the fourth fore-offering, the gods attained the sacrifice; with the fifth, they reached its completion.
Then, by establishing that which was not yet established above that point, they attained the heavenly world of the sacrifice. As they were going to the heavenly world— 1.6.1 [11].
As they were going to the heavenly world—
They were afraid of attachment from the Asuras and Rakṣases;

they placed Agni in front as a slayer of Rakṣases, a repeller of Rakṣases; they placed Agni in the middle as a slayer of Rakṣases, a repeller of Rakṣases; they placed Agni behind as a slayer of Rakṣases.
[He is] the repeller of the *rakṣases*.
If the Asuras and *rakṣases* had hemmed them in from the front, Agni himself, the slayer of *rakṣases*, repelled them.

If they were to perish in the middle, Agni—the slayer of *rakṣases*, the repeller of *rakṣases*—would have repelled them; if they were to perish behind, Agni—the slayer of *rakṣases*, the repeller of *rakṣases*—would have repelled them. Thus, protected on all sides by fires, they attained the heavenly world. 1.6.1 [13]

In the same way, he thus obtains the sacrifice by means of the fourth fore-offering (prayāja) alone; he brings it to completion with the fifth. Now, that part of the sacrifice which remains uncompleted beyond that, he thereby establishes in the heavenly world.
He attains [it]. 1.6.1.[14] When he performs the offering of the *ājyabhāga* to Agni,
he thereby places Agni in front as a slayer of demons.

Now, as for the fact that there is a cake for Agni: he thereby places Agni, the slayer of the Rakṣases and the repeller of the Rakṣases, in the middle. And as for the fact that he sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt: he thereby places Agni, the slayer of the Rakṣases and the repeller of the Rakṣases, behind. 1.6.1. [15]
If the Asuras and Rakṣases should attack him from the front, Agni himself repels them— he who is the slayer of Rakṣases,
the repeller of the Rakṣases. If the Asuras and Rakṣases should attack him from the middle, Agni himself repels them.

The slayer of demons, the repeller of Rākṣasas—if from behind the Asuras and Rākṣasas should seek to harm him, Agni himself repels them, he the slayer of demons, the repeller of Rākṣasas. Thus protected on all sides by fires, he attains the heavenly world. 1.6.1 [16]
If he should recite [the formula] after him at the beginning of the sacrifice, one should say to him in return:
"You will meet with a primary affliction; you will become either blind or deaf. These indeed are the primary [afflictions].

And likewise, there would indeed be misfortune for him (1.6.1.17) if he were to utter a counter-proclamation in the middle of the sacrifice. One should say to him: "You shall be without offspring and without cattle. Offspring...

Cattle indeed are the middle; thus it would surely be so. 1.6.1.[18] If someone should utter a curse at the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should say to him: "He shall be unstable, poor, and quickly [go to] that world."
"You shall go to the world [of Yama]," he says; it will surely be so. Therefore, one should not act as a mere reviler, for even one who knows this becomes superior.
For a year, indeed, one conquers by means of the *prayāja* offerings.
Verily, he conquers him who knows its doors;

for what indeed could he do with those houses if he were not separated from them by the intermediate space? As they belong to him, so the spring is its door, and the winter is its door. This very year is that heavenly world.
The year indeed attains everything; everything, moreover, is imperishable. By this, his good deed becomes imperishable, and his world becomes imperishable.
1.6.1 [20] Regarding this they say: "To which deity do the *ājya* offerings belong? One should say, "They belong to Prajāpati," for he is indeed undefined.

Prajāpati is the undefined *ājya* offerings; these indeed have the sacrificer as their deity, for in his own sacrifice the sacrificer is Prajāpati. For by this [formula], the officiating priests being addressed, they extend [the sacrifice] and produce him. 1.6.1. Having spread a base of *ājya*...

Having twice cut portions from the oblation, he then pours clarified butter over it; thus this offering is made mixed with clarified butter. Indeed, it is offered by the sacrificer himself as mixed with clarified butter, whether he sacrifices while far away or while nearby; for just as if he were sacrificing while present at the end [of the rite], even so does the sacrifice of one who knows this become truly performed.
"Even if one commits much evil, provided he knows this, he does not indeed become an outcast from the sacrifice. 1.6.2.
By means of the sacrifice, the gods won that victory which is this world of theirs. They said, "How can we ensure that this [world]..."

"Let it be unassailable by men," they thought; and having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. Because they obstructed it with that, it is called the *yūpa*. This, indeed, was heard by the seers (*ṛṣi*) in tradition. 1.6.2. [2]

By means of sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [victory] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having extracted the essence of the sacrifice, as bees [extract] honey, they...

"They would have drained the sacrifice by milking it dry and vanished after having obscured it with the sacrificial post (yūpa)," they said; thus they resolved to search for it. They wandered about chanting and toiling.
By toil indeed, the gods won that which was theirs.

The seers were being defeated, and the gods either incited them [to flee] or they themselves took up the cause, saying, "Come, let us go to where the gods attained the heavenly world. They asked, "What do you find pleasing? What do you find pleasing?
They went along, and all of them agreed upon the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as it was crawling about, having become a tortoise; for that which... [they all accepted].

"Regarding the word 'sacrifice' (yajña): 1.6.2 [4]. They said, 'Stand for the Aśvins! Stand for Sarasvatī! Stand for Indra! But he simply crawled away. Then they said, 'Stand for Agni! Thereupon he stood still. Thinking, 'He has indeed stood for Agni,' they enclosed him within the fire."
They offered everything as an oblation, for the oblation is the gods' [portion]. Then the sacrifice became pleasing to them; they created it and they performed it.
This very sacrifice, superior and inferior, is recited, just as a father [recites it] to his son who is a religious student (brahmacārin).
He indeed presented that to them beforehand.
He who caused them to take pleasure in the sacrifice—therefore it is called *puroḍāśa*;
for indeed, "puroḍāśa" is the same as "puro-dāśa" (one who gives first). This very cake, belonging to Agni, consisting of eight potsherds, remains unchanging in both cases.
He does not offer the full-moon oblation nor the new-moon oblation; for the full-moon oblation is indeed the Agni-Soma offering, and the new-moon oblation is the Sāṃnāyya.
This sacrifice is prescribed for both occasions, lest he should depart from the sacrifice. Indeed, it is thus.
It is performed before the full moon sacrifice, and likewise before the new moon sacrifice; this is why it is performed here.
Now, if someone were to entreat him, saying, "Sacrifice for me with an *iṣṭi*," he should sacrifice for him with this very [offering]. For whatever desire the seers had when they [performed] this—

They offered [the oblation], and that desire was fulfilled for them. Whatever desire one sacrifices with this sacrifice, that desire is indeed fulfilled for him. For whatever deity the oblation is taken, it is indeed into Agni that one offers it;
and if he were about to offer into Agni, what other deity could he designate? Therefore, [it is offered] to Agni alone.
Agni, indeed, is all the deities;
for in Agni they offer oblations to all the deities. Just as if one were to run to all the deities together, so it is with that; therefore, [the offering is] to Agni alone. 1.6.2. [9]
Agni is indeed the most manifest among the gods;
one should run to him whom one considers the most manifest.
Therefore, [one should run] to Agni alone. 1.6.2. [10]
Agni is indeed the most soft-hearted among the gods; one should run to him whom one considers the most soft-hearted—therefore, [one should run] to Agni alone. 1.6.2.[11]
Agni is indeed the nearest of the gods.
One should run to him whom one considers the nearest among those to be approached;
therefore, [one should run] to Agni alone. 1.6.2. [12]
If he should perform an *iṣṭi*, he should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; he sacrifices to the deity in a whisper, for that is the characteristic form of an *iṣṭi*.
The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* should be verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhanvatī*), and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings should be *vṛtraghna* verses in the *virāj* meter.
The two *saṃyājyā* verses: 1.6.3.
Tvaṣṭṛ indeed had a son who was three-headed and six-eyed; he had exactly three...
His faces were as they had been; because he was of such a form, he was named Viśvarūpa.
Of him, the drinking of soma was one face; the drinking of surā was another; and for others... [the drinking of water was another].
Indra hated him for that one [head]. He cut off those heads of his.
That which was the drinking of Soma therefrom became the *kapiñjala* bird; therefore it is, as it were, brownish, like brown.
Indeed, King Soma [was there].
1.6.3.[4] Now, as for that drinking of *surā* liquor:
from that the *kalaviṅka* bird came into being; therefore, it is as if it becomes intoxicated.

For he speaks as if intoxicated, for he speaks like one who has drunk *surā* liquor. 1.6.3.[5] Now, that which was left over from his hunger became the *tittiri* bird; therefore, it is, as it were, most multiform in color.
"There are indeed drops of ghee from you, and drops of honey as it were dripping upon your leaves"— for such was the food he consumed by means of him. Tvaṣṭṛ became enraged.

"Has he indeed slain my son? he thought, and he brought Soma that was devoid of Indra. Just as this Soma had been pressed, even so was it devoid of Indra. Then Indra reflected: "1.6.3 [7]" 1.6.3.
