"Verily, he is excluding me from the Soma," [Indra thought]. Just as a stronger man [might act] toward a weaker one, so did he consume the bright [Soma] that was in the *droṇakalaśa* without being invited.
He (the Soma) injured him; it ran forth from all his vital breaths, but it did not run forth from his mouth. Then...

It flowed away from all other vital breaths; that [essence] became the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. In it, that is explained—how the gods healed him. Tvaṣṭṛ was angry, thinking, "Why has he consumed the Soma without inviting me? He himself...

He made a sacrificial vessel out of the remains of the sacrifice; that bright [Soma] which was left over in the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, he caused to flow forth with the words, "O enemy of Indra, prosper! Having reached Agni alone, it came into being;
some say it came into being within Agni alone; it came into being as both Agni and Soma—indeed, all knowledge and all glory.
All food and all prosperity.
Because he became *vartamāna*, therefore he is Vṛtra; and because he became *apāt*, therefore he is Ahi. Him—
Danu and Danāyū, like a mother and a father, nurtured him; therefore they call him a Dānava. Then, because he said, "Indra-śatru, grow!"—therefore Indra himself slew him.

For had he ever said, "O enemy of Indra, grow strong," he would surely have caused Indra to perish forever. But because he said, "Grow strong," [Indra grew]. 1.6.3. [11] Now, as for what he said: "Grow strong."

Therefore, indeed, he grew sideways by the measure of an arrow’s length, and forward by the measure of an arrow’s length; he rushed toward the western ocean and toward the eastern one. As far as he reached, so far did he become an eater of food.
To him, indeed, the gods used to bring food in the forenoon, humans at midday, and the ancestors in the afternoon. 1.6.3 [13]
Indra, thus driven away, as he wandered, called out to Agni and Soma: "O Agni and Soma, you two indeed belong to me, and I belong to you;
this [Dasyu] belongs to neither of you. Why do you not help me against this Dasyu?"
"Make me prosper; turn back toward me," [he said].
They both replied, "What would be ours from that? To them, he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma.

He offered the sacrificial cake; therefore, there is an eleven-potherd sacrificial cake for Agni and Soma. Those two turned back toward him; after them all the gods followed, as did all knowledge and all glory.
By sacrificing with this [offering], Indra obtained all food and all prosperity—namely, that which belongs to Indra here. This indeed is the significance of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*).
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Full Moon sacrifice, attains that very prosperity, becomes possessed of such glory, and becomes an eater of such food. 1.6.3. [16]
Then indeed Vṛtra was slain. He lay there collapsed like an emptied leather bag, or like a bellows from which the flour has been shaken out; Indra rushed toward him, intending to kill him. 1.6.3 [17]
He said, "Do not strike me! You are indeed that very thing which I am now; do not destroy me, lest I become something else. Let me eat food for you. "So be it," he replied. He split him in two.
That which was his gentle essence (*saumya*) he made into the moon; and that which was his demonic essence (*asurya*), with that he created these creatures.
He pierced him with his belly; therefore they say, "At that time Vṛtra alone was the eater of food, and now Vṛtra [is the eater].

For when that [moon] swells, it swells from this very world; and when these creatures desire food, they bring tribute to this very Vṛtra, the belly. He who knows this Vṛtra as the eater of food becomes indeed an eater of food.
It comes to pass.
1.6.3.[18] Then those deities who had followed after Agni and Soma said: "O Agni and Soma, you two indeed [belong to us]..."
"You two have received the greatest share; therefore, let this [share] of yours be distributed among us.
They both said, "What would come of that for us? [They replied,] "Whatever oblation you two offer to whichever deity, that shall be yours."

"Before the butter-offering, sacrifice!"—therefore, for whichever deity they prepare an oblation, they first sacrifice two portions of butter to Agni and Soma. This does not apply at the Soma-sacrifice nor at the animal sacrifice; for they said, "For whichever deity one prepares an oblation [in those cases]. 1.6.3 [20]
That Agni said: "Let them offer to you all into me alone; I shall share that among you within myself.
Therefore, they offer to all the gods into the fire; therefore they say, "Agni is all the deities. 1.6.3 [21]
Then Soma said:
"Let them offer to me alone from among all of you; I shall share that [offering] with you within myself.
Therefore, they offer to Soma from among all the gods; therefore they say, "Soma is all the deities. 1.6.3 [22]
Now, because all the gods were established in Indra, therefore they say, "Indra is all the deities; Indra is the best of the gods.
For in this way, the gods indeed became threefold, each belonging to a single deity; and he who knows this thus becomes one.
Verily, he becomes the best among his own people.
1.6.3 [23] This world is indeed twofold; there is no third: the moist and the dry. That which is dry belongs to Agni.
When it is moist, that is Soma; and as for this duality, why is so much done?
Because the two portions of clarified butter belong to Agni and Soma, the Upāṃśu-sacrifice belongs to Agni and Soma, and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to Agni and Soma.
Since one obtains all this through either one alone, why is so much done? For this extent indeed belongs to Agni and Soma.
Vibhūti (manifestation) is procreation. 1.6.3 [24].
The sun is indeed of the nature of Agni; the moon is of the nature of Soma. The day is of the nature of Agni; the night is of the nature of Soma—namely, that which waxes.

The fortnight that waxes belongs to Agni; that which wanes belongs to Soma. By the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), one obtains the sun and the moon; by the low-voiced sacrifice (upāṃśuyāja) alone, one obtains day and night.
"By means of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) alone, one obtains the two half-months," so some say.
Regarding this, Āsuri said:
"From here on, by means of the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), whichever two [days] it may be."

"By the *upāṃśuyāja* alone he obtains this [day]; by the *puroḍāśa* alone he obtains this [night]. By these two he obtains the half-months. 'May everything be obtained for me; may everything be conquered. With everything may I slay Vṛtra; with everything may I slay my hateful rival!'—it is for this reason that this much is performed. 1.6.3. [27]

Regarding this they say: "What is this repetition (*jāmi*) being performed? For there is the clarified butter of Agni and Soma, and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of Agni and Soma; since one follows immediately upon the other, it is repetitive. But by this very means there is no repetition: the one belongs to the clarified butter and the other to the sacrificial cake;

thus one becomes as if different from the other, and the other as if different from the one. Having recited a *ṛc* verse, he offers with the word "juṣāṇa" (enjoying); having recited a *ṛc* verse, [he offers] with a *ṛc* verse.

When he sacrifices, it becomes as if one thing were different from another, and another were different from that other; but by this very means he avoids discord. He sacrifices the *ājya* offering in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), and the cake (*puroḍāśa*) offering aloud. That which is in a low voice is the form belonging to Prajāpati;
therefore, for that [offering], he recites an *anuṣṭubh* verse as the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*). For the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and Prajāpati is speech. 1.6.3 [28]

By means of this very Upāṃśuyāja, the gods, having approached whichever of the Asuras they desired, struck them down with the thunderbolt at the utterance of "vaṣaṭ. In the same way, he [the sacrificer] now, by means of this Upāṃśuyāja, [strikes down] his evil, hateful enemy.
Having assailed his rival, he strikes him with the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call; therefore he performs the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice.

He recites a *ṛc* verse and sacrifices with the word "juṣāṇa" (enjoying); accordingly, these creatures with teeth on one side are produced, for the *ṛc* is bone and the tooth is bone; for thus he makes bone on one side.
Then, having recited a Ṛc, he sacrifices with a Ṛc.
Accordingly, these creatures with teeth on both sides are born; for the Ṛc is bone, and the tooth is bone, since he thus makes bone on both sides. These, indeed, are the two kinds of creatures.

There are those with teeth on only one side and those with teeth on both sides; he who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice to the procreative power of Agni and Soma, indeed becomes rich in offspring and cattle.
Now, when he is about to fast for the full moon sacrifice:

One should not be fully satisfied with it, for by means of this [food], one swallows this belly of the Asuras with the oblations, while that of the gods is at dawn; this indeed is the procedure for the Full Moon sacrifice.
He should fast only on the very day [of the sacrifice].
"Now I shall slay Vṛtra; now I shall slay my hateful rival," [he thinks].
He should rather fast on the later day alone.
He who fasts at the junction of the two days indeed steps as it were upon a precipice;

for when two things have met, one surely overcomes the other, or the other overcomes it. Now, he who fasts on the later day is like one who would crush someone who has turned away and is fleeing, unable to seize him; he would simply be striking at something else. It is even so with that.
He fasts on the later [day]. Indeed, he should fast at the very moment [the moon has disappeared];
for it is just as if one were to grind what has already been killed by another. Thus it is.
He who fasts on the later [day] merely imitates one thing while fasting after another;
therefore, he should fast only on the [proper] day.
Indeed, when Prajāpati was creating creatures, [he...]
The joints fell apart; he indeed is Prajāpati, the Year, and these are his joints: the junctions of day and night, the full moon, the new moon, and the beginnings of the seasons.
With his joints thus fallen apart...
The gods were unable to heal him with those *havis*-sacrifices;
they healed his joints at the junctions of day and night by means of the *agnihotra*,
and they set them right by means of the *paurṇamāsa* and *amāvāsya* sacrifices on the full-moon and new-moon days respectively.
They healed those joints with the *parvan* sacrifices and joined together the beginnings of the seasons with the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices;
they healed those joints with the *parvan* sacrifices and joined them together. With these combined *parvan* sacrifices... 1.6.3 [37]. He [is] with the combined *parvan* sacrifices.
This food has arisen from that which is the food of Prajāpati.
He who, knowing this, fasts at the proper time, truly heals the joint of Prajāpati at the proper time;
Prajāpati protects him, and he who, knowing this, fasts at the proper time, becomes an eater of food in that very way.

Therefore, one should indeed fast immediately [on that day]. For these two *ājyabhāga* offerings are, as it were, the eyes of the sacrifice; therefore, he offers them in front, for these two are in front.
These two eyes are indeed placed right there in front; therefore, these two eyes are located in the front.
Some, however, offer the butter-portion for Agni in the eastern part of the northern half, and [the other portion] in the eastern part of the southern half.
"This gentle *ājyabhāga* portion, we place these two eyes in front," so they say; but that is somewhat obscure.

Indeed, the oblations are the self of the sacrifice. Therefore, when he offers before the other oblations, he thereby places the two eyes in front. He should offer the oblations at the very moment he considers the fire to be most brightly kindled, for it is by means of an offering into a well-kindled fire [that the eyes are established].
The oblations are successful. 1.6.3.[40] He indeed recites a *ṛc* and then sacrifices with the word *juṣāṇa*.
Therefore, these two eyes, though boneless, are firmly fixed within the bony structure.
Now, if one were to recite a verse and then offer with another verse, he would indeed produce bone, but not sight.
These two, moreover, are dependent upon the very form of Agni and Soma: that which is white belongs to Agni, and that which is black belongs to Soma;
or alternatively, that which is black belongs to Agni, and that which is white belongs to Soma. Whatever...
Then he beholds the fiery form; for when one looks at it, his eyes become as if parched, for the fiery is indeed parched.
That which is sleep is the lunar form; for when one has slept, his eyes become as if moist, for Soma is indeed moist. Verily, until old age, he remains possessed of sight in this world.
He who knows these two eyes, the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), becomes possessed of sight in this world. 1.6.4.
When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, he, considering himself weak, thought as if, "I have not struck him down."
Fearing, he took refuge and went to the farthest distances. The gods indeed came to know: "Vṛtra has been slain; now Indra has hidden himself.
They set about searching for him.
Agni is the deity of the gods, Hiraṇyastūpa is the seer of the seers, and the Bṛhatī is the meter of the meters.
Agni discovered him; with him he came to this night. He indeed is the Vasu of the gods, for he is their hero. 1.6.4.
[3] Those gods said:

"Truly, our Vasu dwells with us today—he who has blown upon us. To these two, they prepared this common oblation, just as one might cook a common mess of rice or a goat for two kinsmen or two friends who have arrived together;
for that is a human offering to the gods. In the same way, they offered this common oblation to these two: the Aindrāgna.
[He offered] a cake on twelve potsherds; therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. 1.6.4.
[4] That Indra said:
"When I hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, I was struck with fear; I am, as it were, emaciated."
"Verily, this delights me; do for me that which will delight me," [he said]. "So be it," the gods replied.
Those gods said, "Nothing other than Soma would delight him; let us collect Soma for him."
For him they brought together the Soma; for this King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon.
When, during that night, he is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he comes to this world.
He enters right here into the waters and the plants. For he is indeed the wealth and the food of the gods, since he is this [moon]. When he...
He dwells here for this night; therefore it is called *amāvāsyā*.
Having caused him to settle among the cows, they gathered [the materials]:
from the plants what he ate as plants, and from the waters...
While he was drinking it, they collected that very substance from those waters, pressed it, and made it strong; then they offered it to him.
He said, "It indeed satisfies me, but it does not settle within me as this [other drink] settles in me. Find a way so that it might settle in me. They caused it to settle by means of boiled milk.
Now, this [curd] is indeed the same as milk; it is the very essence of Indra. Yet they call it by different names:
because he said, "It impels me," therefore it is called *dadhi* (curd); and because they prepared him with boiled milk (*śṛta*), therefore it is called *śr̥ta* (boiled).
Just as a stalk of sugar-cane swells...
Thus he swells with offspring and cattle, drives away evil, and destroys jaundice; this indeed is the significance of the New Moon sacrifice.

He who, knowing thus, performs the *saṃnayya* offering, truly swells with offspring and cattle, drives away evil, and destroys jaundice. Therefore, one should certainly perform the *saṃnayya* offering. 1.6.4. [10]

Regarding this they say: "One who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not bring the *sāṃnāyya* offering; for this is indeed a Soma oblation, and it is not secured for one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice.
Therefore, one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not bring the *sāṃnāyya*.
Nevertheless, he should indeed bring it.
"Now, indeed, we have heard that in this interval he said: 'Do not perform the Soma sacrifice for me;

then you shall prepare this nourishment for me. He said, 'This does not satisfy me; provide me with that which would satisfy me. Therefore, they prepared this nourishment for him; hence, even one who does not sacrifice with Soma [may partake]."
One should lead it in the same way.
1.6.4.[12] The full-moon sacrifice is indeed "Vrtra-slaying," for by means of this, Indra slew Vrtra; thus, this is truly the slaying of Vrtra.
When they performed this replenishment for him as he was slaying Vṛtra on the new-moon day— that indeed is the Vārtraghna [offering] which is the full-moon sacrifice; and that moon is indeed Vṛtra.

When he does not see him either in front or behind during that night, then by means of this [sacrifice] he destroys him entirely; he leaves nothing of him remaining. Verily, he who knows this destroys all evil and leaves nothing of evil remaining. 1.6.4. [14]

Regarding this, some indeed fast after seeing [the new moon], thinking, "The sun will not rise tomorrow; thus the food of the gods remains undiminished, and we shall offer it to them from here. That is indeed successful when, while the previous food is still undiminished, another supply of food arrives; he becomes truly possessed of abundant food. However, this applies to one who does not sacrifice with Soma.
King Soma indeed becomes the giver of milk and clarified butter.
1.6.4.[15] Then, just as before, they eat plants exclusively and drink water exclusively; from those [plants and water], there comes forth milk exclusively.

He indeed milks that very thing. This King Soma, who is the moon, is the food of the gods. When he is not seen either in the east or in the west on that night, he comes to this world; he enters here into the waters and the plants.
Having gathered him from the waters and the plants, they produce him from the oblations. Thus, he is born from the oblations.

Later it was seen: 1.6.4.[16] This very food of the gods indeed circulates without ever being exhausted. For him who knows this, food becomes inexhaustible in this world and his merit becomes imperishable in the other world. 1.6.4.[17]
On that very night, food for the gods falls away from them and comes to this world. Those gods desired: "How indeed might this come back to us? How might it not go away forever and be utterly lost?"

Those who indeed prepare [the offerings] hope for them, thinking, "Having gathered these together, they will give them to us. Truly, both those who are their own and those who are strangers hope for him who knows this; for people hope for one who attains the highest state.
Now, this very one who shines yonder is indeed Indra;
and that which is the moon is indeed Vṛtra. He is his rival, as it were;
therefore, even though he has risen far away in the past, on this night he approaches him.
It plunges into his open mouth;
having swallowed it, it rises up.
It is seen neither in front nor behind; indeed, it swallows one's enemy.
"He has only enemies, he has no rivals," they say of one who knows this.
Having winnowed it out, he throws it away;
that which was winnowed is seen behind him, and it swells up again.

It swells again for his very sake of food. For if an enemy or rival should happen to prosper through trade or by some other means, he indeed prospers again for the sake of his food—provided that one who knows this understands it thus. 1.6.4. [21] Now, some perform the rite saying, "To Mahendra," on the grounds that he was Indra before the slaying of Vṛtra, but after Vṛtra...

Just as a great king becomes [known] as "the Conqueror" after having conquered, so did Mahendra become [known]. Therefore, one should offer it to Indra; that is, one should say "to Indra. Indeed, he was Indra before the slaying of Vṛtra, but having slain Vṛtra, he became Mahendra.
Therefore, one should offer it to Indra; that is, one should say "to Indra. 1.7.1. [1]
He indeed drives away the calves with a *parṇa* branch.
As to why he drives away the calves with a *parṇa* branch:
when Gāyatrī flew toward Soma, as she was bringing it back, her foot was wounded; she stretched out her hand and plucked off a leaf (*parṇa*).
Either for the sake of the Gāyatrī or for King Soma, having fallen, it became a leaf (parṇa); therefore its name is "parṇa.
Thinking, "Whatever part of Soma was spilled there, let that be present here as well," he drives away the calves with a branch of the *parṇa* tree.
He gathers it together.

With the words, "For sap thee! For strength thee!"—when he says this, he speaks for the sake of rain. When he says, "For sap thee," and "For strength thee," he speaks for that vigorous essence which is produced from rain. Then they drive the calves together with their mothers.
He touches the calf with a branch, saying, "Ye are winds.
This indeed is the wind that blows here; for he causes all this to swell—whatever he rains down, he is the sweller of these [cows].
Therefore he says, "Ye are winds. Some, however, say, "Ye are approaching winds," for they are indeed approaching.
"The second [verse] says 'he restrains'; one should not speak thus.
Then, having separated one of the mother-cows with a branch, he touches it with the words: 'May the divine Savitṛ impel you.'"

Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; "impelled by Savitṛ, may I gather the sacrifice"—therefore he says, "May the divine Savitṛ impel you for the most excellent rite. 1.7.1 [5] "For the most excellent rite."
"Sacrifice is indeed the most excellent rite; therefore, for that reason, he says, 'for the most excellent rite.
'Swell up, O inviolable ones, as a portion for Indra. 1.7.1 [6]
Just as one designates the oblation for a deity when taking it up, even so does he designate the deity when he says, "Swell up, O inviolable ones, as a portion for Indra. 1.7.1 [7]

"May you be prolific, free from disease, and free from consumption"—there is nothing here that is obscure. "May no thief master you, may no evil-speaker master you"—by this he means, "may no destructive demons (nāṣṭrā) master you. "Be steadfast under this lord of cattle."
"Many," he says, meaning "may there be many [offspring] for this sacrificer who does not depart. Then, either to the east of the Āhavanīya shed or the Gārhapatya shed,
he hides a branch.

"Protect the cattle of the sacrificer"—by this he entrusts the cattle of the sacrificer to the Brahman for protection. Upon that [strainer], he makes a filter with the formula, "Thou art the filter of Vasu. The sacrifice is indeed Vasu; therefore he says, "of Vasu."
"Thou art a purifier," [he says]. 1.7.1.[10] Then, on that night, he offers the Agnihotra with barley-gruel;
for this oblation has already been assigned to its deity.
If it were milk, and he were to offer that milk, it would be as if one were to offer to one deity a sacrificial oblation that had been taken out for another;
therefore, on that night, he performs the Agnihotra with barley-gruel.
While performing the Agnihotra, the *ukhā* (cooking-pot) is prepared; then he says, "Announce when she has been let loose," and when...
"He said, 'It has been approached'" (1.7.1.11).

Then he takes up the fire-pan with the words, "Thou art heaven; thou art earth. By this he indeed praises it; and when he says, "Thou art heaven; thou art earth," he thereby impels it. With the words, "Thou art Mātariśvan’s cauldron," he thereby performs the sacrifice, just as one prepares the *gharma* (heated milk-offering).

One should indeed perform the *pravargya* in this manner; he performs it [with the mantra]: "Thou art all-pervading with the highest station; be firm, do not falter!"—by this he makes it firm and renders it unshakable. "May thy lord of the sacrifice not falter"—the lord of the sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer; thus he invokes freedom from stumbling for the sacrificer himself. 1.7.1. [12]
Then they place the strainer.
He should indeed place it facing east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or he may place it facing north, for the north is the direction of men. This strainer is indeed he who blows here.
Because he blows across these worlds from the side, one should therefore place it facing north.
Just as they [place] King Soma with the filter—
They purify it; in this very same way, he purifies it. That strainer by which they purify King Soma has its fringe pointing northward; therefore, he should place it facing north.
He places it there.
"Thou art the purifier of wealth," he says; for wealth is indeed the sacrifice, therefore he says, "Thou art the purifier of wealth.
"Hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed"—he thus praises it and magnifies it when he says, "Hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed. 1.7.1 [15]
Then he remains silent until three [cows] have been milked; for the sacrifice is speech, and he does so thinking, "May I extend the sacrifice without disturbance.
He then consecrates the milk being brought with the mantra:
"May the god Savitṛ purify you with the filter of Vasu, with its hundred streams."
"Excellent!"—just as they purify King Soma with a filter, even so does he purify this. 1.7.1.
[17] Then he asks, "Have you milked?"—"That one," she says. "She is Viśvāyu. Then he asks the second one, "Have you milked?"—

"Which one was this? "That one," he says; "She is Viśvakarmā. Then he asks about the third: "Which one did you milk? "This one," he says; "She is Viśvadhāyā. Now, as to why he asks: he thereby bestows heroic powers upon her. He milks three [cows], for these worlds are three;
he thus gathers this [milk] from these very worlds. Then he speaks his desire. 1.7.1. [18]
Then, having caused the best cow to be milked,
he pours a small amount from that vessel with which he milked into this one, mixing it and pouring it back; [he does so] thinking,
"Whatever of the milk was lost there, let that be here too," and for the sake of the completeness of the flavor, for when this— namely, the milk— is present...

When it rains, plants are born; having eaten the plants and drunk the water, this sap comes into being from that. Therefore, for the sake of the completeness of the sap, he pours it out and then besmears it; he thus makes it intense. That is why he pours it out and then besmears it. 1.7.1 [19]

He sprinkles it with the formula: "I sprinkle thee, the portion of Indra, with Soma. Just as when he takes the oblation for a deity he designates it, even so does he designate it for the deity when he says, "thee, the portion of Indra.
By saying, "I sprinkle thee with Soma," he indeed makes it palatable for the gods. 1.7.1 [20]

Then he covers it with a water-filled vessel turned upside down, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits and demons touch it from above. For water is indeed a thunderbolt; thus, by means of that thunderbolt, he drives away the destructive spirits and demons from this place.
Therefore, he covers it with a vessel full of water turned face upwards.
He covers it, saying: "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus, he offers this oblation to the sacrifice itself.
He hands it over for protection; therefore he says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation.
Indeed, one who exists is born as a debt.
As soon as he is born, he is [born] as a debt to the gods, to the seers, and to the ancestors.
From men [1.7.2.2].
Whenever he performs a sacrifice, by that he incurs a debt to the gods; for he does this for them when he sacrifices to them.
When he offers oblations to these [gods],
then, whatever he might recite [afterward],
by that a debt toward the seers (*ṛṣi*) arises; for he thereby performs this service for them, [the debt] of the seers.
"For they call one who has studied the Vedas 'the guardian of the treasure' (nidhigopa). 1.7.2.
[4] Now, when he desires offspring, by that he incurs a debt to the ancestors; for he performs this very service for them when he [procreates] their [lineage].
Offspring becomes continuous and unbroken.
Now, in that he provides clothing, by that he incurs a debt to human beings; for it is this which he does for them.
In that he clothes them and gives them food—that person who performs all these acts has fulfilled his duty;
for him everything is attained, everything is conquered. 1.7.2 [6] He is born as a debt to the gods.
Therefore, when he sacrifices, he thereby gratifies them; and when he offers oblations in the fire, he thereby gratifies them.
Therefore, whatever one offers in the fire is called an *avadāna* (a portion).
That [offering] consists of four portions.

This is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), then the offering verse (*yājyā*), then the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and then that deity for whom the oblation is intended is the fourth. For the deities are thus dependent upon the portions cut off, and the portions cut off are dependent upon the deities. That portion which would be a fifth is indeed redundant; for to whom would it belong?
One should cut that [portion]; therefore, there is a fourfold cutting (caturavatta).
Or rather, it is indeed a fivefold cutting (pañcāvatta);
for the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and the seasons are five.

This is the perfection of the fivefold portion of the year; he indeed becomes rich in offspring and cattle, for whom the fivefold portion is performed while he knows thus. This fourfold portion, however, is well-known among the Kuru-Pañcālas;
therefore, it is made fourfold. 1.7.2. [9]

He should indeed cut off only a moderate amount; for if he were to cut off too much, he would make it human, and that which is human is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I should cause a failure in the sacrifice," he should therefore cut off only a moderate amount. 1.7.2. [10]
Having spread a base of clarified butter, having twice taken a portion of the sacrificial oblation, he then pours clarified butter over it; for there are two kinds of offerings:
one is a Soma-offering, the other is a clarified-butter offering, and thus this [Soma-offering] here is distinct.
In that there is this oblation of Soma and this oblation of clarified butter, in that there is the Havis-sacrifice and the animal sacrifice, he thereby makes all of that into clarified butter;
therefore there is clarified butter on both sides. Indeed, clarified butter is what is dear to the gods;
thus he makes it dear to the gods, and for that reason there is clarified butter on both sides. 1.7.2. [11]
That [world] is indeed the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), and this [world] is the offering verse (yājyā). These two are females; their union is the *vaṣaṭ* call itself.
Now, that which blazes yonder is indeed this *vaṣaṭ* call: when it rises, it impregnates that [world], and when it sets, it impregnates this [world].
That which he assails with this [sacrifice], by means of it he procreates this procreative power of his; for this is the procreative power of these two. 1.7.2.
Having recited the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and having run through the offering verse (*yājyā*), he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call from behind; for having approached from behind, the bull [assails].
He runs toward the woman; having placed those two [the ladle and the cup] in front, he causes them to run forward with the bull-like *vaṣaṭ*-call.
Therefore, one should either offer together with the *vaṣaṭ*-call or once the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
For this *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the vessel of the gods.

Just as one would take up [food] from a vessel and offer it, so it is with that; for if one were to sacrifice before the *vaṣaṭ*-call, it would be like something smeared on the ground below—such would that be.
Therefore, one should sacrifice either together with the *vaṣaṭ*-call or once the *vaṣaṭ*-call has been uttered. 1.7.2. [14]
It is just as if one were to pour semen into the womb;

in the same way, if one were to offer the oblation before the *vaṣaṭ* call, it would be as if that poured semen were to belong to another woman. Therefore, one should offer it together with the *vaṣaṭ* call itself.

Or he should offer at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. That [heavenly world] is indeed the *anuvākyā*, and this [earth] is the *yājyā*; that [heavenly world] is the *gāyatrī* and this [earth] is the *triṣṭubh*. He recites the *gāyatrī*.
Reciting that [verse], he indeed recites this as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for this is the *gāyatrī*.

Then he sacrifices with a *triṣṭubh*; sacrificing with this, this is indeed the offering verse (*yājyā*). He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over that [other verse], for it is that one which is indeed [the *anuvākyā*].

He makes these two [the *anuvākyā* and the *yājyā*] yoked together with the *triṣṭubh* meter; therefore these two enjoy together, and following the enjoyment of these two, all these creatures enjoy together.
He should recite the *anuvākyā* as if bending down.

For that [heaven] is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for it is the *bṛhat* [sāman], and its form is indeed *bārhata*; with the offering verse (*yājyā*) they hasten quickly, for this [earth] is the offering verse, for it is the *rathantara* [sāman], and its form is indeed *rāthantara*.
One summons with the invitatory verse and offers with the offering verse; therefore, one says "I summon" as the form of the invitatory verse.

"We invoke [them]; may they come and sit upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*). For when he calls out, he offers with that; he offers with the *yājyā*. Therefore, the form of the *yājyā* is: "Eat the oblation! Enjoy the oblation! O bull, sprinkle it! Taste it! Drink!
For with that [verse], he indeed impels [the gods]. 1.7.2. [18]

That which has its characteristic mark in front should be the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for that [heavenly world] is the invitatory verse; below that [mark] of hers are the moon, the stars, and the sun. 1.7.2. [19]

Now, that which has its characteristic mark above should be the *yājyā* verse; for this is the *yājyā*, and its characteristic mark above consists of the plants, the trees, the waters, the fire, and these creatures. 1.7.2. [20]
That indeed is a successful invitatory verse (anuvākyā) from whose first word one pronounces the name of the deity;
that indeed is a successful offering verse (yājyā) from whose last word one utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the deity, for the deity is indeed vigor.
Having thus enclosed it on both sides with vigor, he offers it to whichever deity the oblation belongs to.
He indeed utters "vauṣaṭ."

The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed speech; he thus pours forth seed with speech as the precursor. "Six"—the seasons are six; it is thus in the seasons that this seed is poured. The seasons, having received the poured seed, bring these creatures into being.
Therefore, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* in this manner. 1.7.2 [22]

The gods and the asuras—both of them descendants of Prajāpati—approached the inheritance of their father Prajāpati. Of these two half-months, that which waxes, the gods approached; that which wanes, the asuras.
Regarding that, [it is said]: "The Asuras were [powerful]. 1.7.2. [23] Those gods desired:
'How indeed might we also win over this which belongs to the Asuras? They, chanting praises..."
Exerting themselves, they wandered about; they saw this Havis-sacrifice, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsau).
They sacrificed with them, and having sacrificed with them, they also appropriated that which belonged to the Asuras.
1.7.2 [24] That which was theirs, the Asuras'—[they took it].
When these two revolve together, then a month comes into being; by months the year is formed.
The year, indeed, is everything. It was this very thing—the year—that the gods appropriated from the Asuras;
they excluded their rivals, the Asuras, from everything. Verily, he now appropriates everything from his rivals.
He who knows this excludes himself from all rivals.

That which belonged to the gods was *yava* (barley), for by it the gods were joined (*yuvata*); that which belonged to the Asuras was *ayava* (non-barley), for by it the Asuras were not joined. 1.7.2 [25]
They did not choose [it], 1.7.2.[26]. Moreover, they say otherwise: that which belonged to the gods was *ayava*; the Asuras did not choose it. That which belonged to the Asuras was *yava*;
the gods chose it. *Sabdamah* is the day; *sagara* is the night; *yavyā* are the months; *sumeka* is the year.

"Sumeka" is indeed the name for "Sveka," because whether they are *yava* (barley) or *ayava* (non-barley), they are as it were *yavetīva*; and since he is the *hotṛ* of these [deities], they call that the *yāvihotra*. 1.7.3.
By means of the sacrifice, the gods...
Then, as the gods were ascending to heaven, that god who rules over cattle was left behind here; therefore they call him Vāstavya, for he was left behind at the dwelling-place (vāstu). 1.7.3.
[2] By that very same path by which the gods ascended to heaven...

Thus they wandered about, chanting and toiling. Now, that god who rules over cattle and was left behind here reflected: "They are excluding me from the sacrifice. He stepped out after them and followed along on the north side.
That very time for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering arose.
Those gods said, "Do not let it be scattered! Do not let it go out! Prepare for me a portion from the sacrifice and from the oblation that has entered within. 1.7.3 [4]
"So be it," he said; he gathered them together, he did not exclude any, and he did not diminish anything.
Then those gods said, "Of all the oblations that have been taken by us..."
"Consider the oblation so that we may prepare an offering for him.
They said to the Adhvaryu,
"Sprinkle the sacrificial offerings as before, for the sake of one portion."
"Make them swell again and render them fresh; then cut off a single portion from each.
Thus spoke the Adhvaryu, who, as before, sprinkled clarified butter over the sacrificial oblations for the sake of a single portion.

He made them fresh again so that they were no longer stale; then he offered each portion one by one. Therefore they say, "It belongs to the dwelling-place (*vāstavya*)," for that which remains when the oblations have been offered is the dwelling-place of the sacrifice.
Therefore, for whatever deity an oblation is taken, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is everywhere partaken of; for the gods everywhere partook of him. 1.7.3. [8]
Or rather, it is performed with the words "to Agni.
For he is indeed that deity; these are his names: "Śarva," as they call him among the Easterners; "Bhava," as the Bāhīkas [call him]; and "Rudra" and "Agni" [are names] for the lord of cattle.
Those other names of his were indeed not peaceful; "Agni" alone is the most peaceful. Therefore, it is performed as "for Agni," as "Sviṣṭakṛt" (the maker of good sacrifice).
They said: "Since we have sacrificed here in you, who are true, make that for us a well-performed sacrifice. And so it was for them.
"He made the sacrifice well-offered (sviṣṭa)," therefore he is called Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having recited the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), he looks toward [the offering], [saying]:
"Those who thus [have offered] to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; Agni has sacrificed for Agni's dear [shares]."
"His abodes"—with these words he recites for the butter-portion belonging to Agni; "the dear abodes of Soma"—with these words he recites for the butter-portion belonging to Soma;
"the dear abodes of Agni"—with these words he recites for that cake which belongs to Agni and is not displaced from either [offering]. 1.7.3. [11]
Then, according to the respective deities:

"He has sacrificed to the beloved abodes of the gods who drink the clarified butter"—this refers to the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, for the gods who drink the clarified butter are indeed the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. "May he sacrifice to the beloved abodes of Agni, the Hotṛ"—this refers to Agni.

The gods, having prepared this oblation for him, said to the Hotṛ, "With this, let us further appease him; let us invoke him to his own dear abode. Therefore, he perceives it thus. 1.7.3 [12] Now, some perform the mention of the deity before the *ayāṭ* formula, saying, "He has sacrificed to Agni," "He has sacrificed to Soma," and so on. But that is not so.

They would perform the sacrifice in reverse order—those who perform the deity first before the *ayāṭ* call; for when one speaks this [formula] for the first time, one speaks the *ayāṭ* call itself. Therefore, one should perform the *ayāṭ* call first. 1.7.3 [13]
"Manifesting his own majesty"—
for when he invokes those deities there, he also invokes his own majesty; therefore, nothing else whatsoever is done here prior to that, except for [the invocation] of his own majesty.
He thus gratifies him, and so this [oblation] of his becomes not in vain when offered; therefore he says, "May he worship according to his own greatness.
"Bring hither the sacrifices for the sacrifice, O nourishments! [he says].
The *iṣ* is indeed offspring; he thus makes that offspring eager for sacrifice. These offspring, as sacrificers, move about praising and toiling.
"May Jātavedas enjoy the oblations at the sacrifices. 1.7.3 [15]
In this, he indeed invokes the prosperity of the sacrifice itself; for when the gods enjoy the oblation, by that they conquer great things. Therefore he says, "May they enjoy the oblation.
Now, as for these [verses] here—

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are most appropriately assigned; for the third pressing belongs to the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, and the third pressing belongs to the *Viśve Devās*. "Piprīhi devān uśato yaviṣṭha" is the *anuvākyā* pertaining to the *Viśve Devās*; "agne yad adya viśo adhvarasya hotaḥ" is the *yājyā* pertaining to the *Viśve Devās*.

That which these two [verses] are of such a form is the Vaiśvadeva; therefore, these two possess the form of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). For this reason, these two are most appropriately established here as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*. They are indeed both in the *triṣṭubh* meter.

The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is indeed the dwelling-place (*vāstu*) of the sacrifice, and the dwelling-place is devoid of power. The *triṣṭubh* is power and vigor; thus he places that very power and vigor into the dwelling-place, the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Therefore, there are two *triṣṭubh* verses. 1.7.3. [18]
Moreover, they both consist of *anuṣṭubh* verses.
The *anuṣṭubh* is a dwelling-place (*vāstu*), and the *Sviṣṭakṛt* is a dwelling-place; thus he establishes this dwelling-place in a dwelling-place.
A dwelling-place is indeed slippery; he whose [sacrifice] consists of two *anuṣṭubh*s while he knows this slips away from offspring and cattle.
Regarding this,
Bhāllaveya made the *anuṣṭubh* verse the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) and the *triṣṭubh* verse the offering formula (*yājyā*); thus he combined both.

"I am taking hold," he said, and he fell from the chariot; having fallen, he even broke his arm. He reflected, "What have I done that has brought me to this calamity? He thought it was because he had performed something contrary (*viloma*) in the sacrifice. Therefore, one should not perform anything contrary. Both [the verses] should be in the same meter—either both in the *anuṣṭubh* or both in the *triṣṭubh*. 1.7.3 [20]
He cuts from the northern half;

he offers in the northern half, for this is the direction of that deity. Therefore, he cuts from the northern half and offers in the northern half. Indeed, he was born from that direction; from there [he arose].
Thus he pacified him; therefore, he cuts off from the northern half and offers in the northern half.
He offers as if closer to the other oblations, for cattle are produced following after the other oblations.
The Sviṣṭakṛt offering belongs to Rudra; if he were to join it with the other oblations, he would subject the cattle to Rudra, and his household and cattle would depart as if being driven away.
Therefore, he offers it as if it were distinct from the other oblations.
This indeed is that sacrifice.
By means of that [fire], the gods ascended to heaven; this is the Āhavanīya.
Now, that which remained here is the Gārhapatya; therefore, they take it out from the Gārhapatya towards the east.
One should indeed place it at eight steps' distance.
The Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables;
by means of the Gāyatrī, he thus ascends to heaven.
He should establish it on eleven [bricks].
The *triṣṭubh* indeed consists of eleven syllables; by means of the *triṣṭubh*, he thus ascends to heaven.
He should place it on twelve [bricks];
for the *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables; by means of the *jagatī*, he thus ascends to heaven. There is no [other way] here.
Wherever he himself may think with his mind, there he should place it. Even if he draws out [the fire] only a little toward the east, by that very act he ascends to heaven.
Regarding this they say: "One should cook the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) in the Āhavanīya fire; for from there the gods indeed ascended to heaven. 1.7.3 [26] Therefore...
Thus, praising and toiling, they moved about, thinking, "In this [fire] we shall cook the oblations; in this we shall perform the sacrifice.
But that would be as if one were to stumble away from the oblations if they were to cook them on the *gārhapatya* fire; for the *āhavanīya* is the sacrifice.
[Thinking,] "In the sacrifice we shall perform the sacrifice," [they proceeded]. 1.7.3. [27]
Moreover, they cook on the Gārhapatya fire itself.

For this [Āhavanīya] is indeed the Āhavanīya; it is not for that purpose for which they would cook what is uncooked in it, nor is it for that purpose for which they would offer what is cooked in it. Therefore, he may do as he wishes.
One should perform [it]. 1.7.3.[28] That very sacrifice said:
"I am indeed afraid of nakedness. [The gods asked: "What is your protection against nakedness? [He replied: "Let them surround me on all sides."

"Let them strew around," he said; therefore they strew around this fire. "I am afraid of thirst," [he said]. "What is your satisfaction? "I would be satisfied following the satisfaction of the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, when the sacrifice is completed, one should say, "One must satisfy the Brāhmaṇa"; for it is thus that he satisfies the sacrifice itself. 1.7.4.1.
11.7.4.2 Prajāpati indeed set his mind upon his own daughter—either Heaven or Dawn—thinking, "May I unite with her in sexual union. He had intercourse with her. 1.7.4.3.
That indeed became an offense against the gods:
"He who thus makes his own daughter our sister! 1.7.4.
Then those gods said:
"This god who rules over animals acts with excessive deception, he who thus makes his own daughter our sister"—saying "Pierce him!", Rudra rushed at him and pierced him;
his seed was spilled prematurely, and from that, indeed, it surely came into being. 1.7.4 [5]
Therefore, this was declared by the Seer:
"When the father begat his own daughter, uniting with her upon the earth, he shed his seed"— this refers to the *agnimāruta* hymn, and therein it is explained as follows.
The gods generated that seed. When the anger of those gods departed, they treated Prajāpati as a physician and extracted that splinter from him. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice itself.
They said, "Devise a way so that this [offering] does not go away to that [world], but rather becomes something smaller than the oblation."

They said, "Carry this to Bhaga as he sits to the south; Bhaga will consume it, and thus it will become as if it were a properly offered oblation. So they carried it to Bhaga as he sat to the south. Bhaga looked at it, and his eyes were scorched. Therefore, it must have been so then; hence they say, "Bhaga is blind. 1.7.4 [8]
They said, "Surely it has not subsided here; let us offer this to Pūṣan. So they offered it to Pūṣan, and Pūṣan ate it;
he knocked out his teeth. Thus, indeed, it must have been then; therefore they say, "Pūṣan is toothless.
Therefore, when they prepare a sacrificial pap (caru) for Pūṣan, they make it of flour that has been ground, just as if for one who is toothless. 1.7.4 [9]
They said, "Surely we have no hope here; let them carry this away to Bṛhaspati. So they carried it away to Bṛhaspati.

Bṛhaspati then ran to Savitṛ for impulsion, saying, "Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; impel this for me! Then Savitṛ, as the impeller, impelled it for him; and so, being impelled by Savitṛ, it did not wound him. Thereupon...
That which is subsequent is peaceful; this very thing is its cause, namely the *prāśitra*.
When he cuts off the *prāśitra*, he [removes] whatever in this sacrifice is pierced and whatever belongs to Rudra.
He creates that very same thing; then he touches water—for water is peace—and thus he pacifies it with water.
Then he cuts off portions of the *iḍā* and the sacrificial animals.
He should indeed cut off only a moderate amount.
In that way the splinter is extracted;

therefore, one should cut off only as much as is necessary. One should place clarified butter on either side—either below or above—so that it becomes like a wound from which the pus has been removed; in that way it flows out. Therefore, one should place clarified butter on either side.

He should do so either below or above (the oblation). Having spread a layer of clarified butter beneath, he takes two portions of the sacrificial food and then pours clarified butter over it from above; this is just as [in the case of the whole-oblation].
This is the cutting-off of the sacrifice.
One should not carry it around by the front;
for some indeed carry it around by the front, [thinking], "From the east they come westward toward the sacrificer."

The animals wait upon him; for he would surely afflict the animals with the Rudra-element if he were to carry [the fire] around by the front. His house and his animals would go away, being utterly destroyed. Therefore, let him rather move it across transversely; thus he does not afflict the animals with the Rudra-element, and he fashions it outwards across. 1.7.4. [14]
He receives it with the formula:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I receive thee. 1.7.4.[15]
Just as there, Bṛhaspati ran to Savitṛ for impulsion, thinking, "Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods;
let him impel this for me," so Savitṛ, the impeller, impelled it for him; thus, he was impelled by Savitṛ.
It is not so; indeed, he approaches Savitṛ alone for instigation. For Savitṛ is the instigator of the gods;
[he thinks,] "May he instigate this for me. Then Savitṛ, as the instigator, instigates it for him; thus, being instigated by Savitṛ, he does not harm him. 1.7.4. [16]
He eats it with the formula, "I eat thee with the mouth of Agni. For Agni does not harm anything whatsoever, and so he does not harm him either. 1.7.4 [17]
Therefore, one should not chew with the teeth, thinking, "Lest this power of Rudra injure my teeth. Therefore, one should not chew with the teeth. 1.7.4 [18]
Then he sips water;
water is peace, so with that peace he pacifies [himself]. Then, having washed the vessel, they bring him the portion for the Brahman priest.
Brahmā indeed sits to the south of the sacrifice as its protector; knowing this to be his portion, he remains there. They brought him the *prāśitra* (the portion for consumption), and he consumed it.

Then, that portion which they bring to him as the *brahmabhāga* (the portion for the Brahman priest)—by that he becomes a sharer [in the sacrifice]. From that point onward, whatever remains until the conclusion of the rite, [he is entitled to it].
He thus protects that [portion] of the sacrifice; therefore, they bring the *brahmabhāga* (the portion for the Brahman priest) to him.
He should indeed remain restrained in speech.
From the moment he says, "O Brahman, I shall set forth," they tear away from this very word. 1.7.4. [20]

Those who damage the sacrifice in its midst by performing the *iḍā* offering of the domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña*), the Brahman priest—who among the officiating priests is the best physician—reunites it. He would not indeed be able to reunite it if he were to sit there speaking;
therefore, he should remain strictly restrained in speech. 1.7.4 [21]

If he should utter human speech before that time, he should mutter there either a verse or a sacrificial formula belonging to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus he recommences the sacrifice. This is indeed the expiation for that. 1.7.4. [22]

When he says, "O Brahman, I shall set forth," then the Brahman mutters: "This sacrifice, O Savitṛ, the gods have proclaimed to thee. He thus has recourse to Savitṛ for instigation, for he is the instigator of the gods.
"To Bṛhaspati, the Brahman"—for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman of the gods; therefore, it is to him who is the Brahman of the gods that he [offers].

Thus he has said this; therefore he says, "For Bṛhaspati, for the Brahman"; "by that protect the sacrifice, by that protect the lord of the sacrifice, by that protect me"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were.
"May the mind, the impeller, enjoy the clarified butter."
"By the mind indeed all this is attained;

by the mind alone he attains all this. "May Bṛhaspati extend this sacrifice; may he establish this sacrifice unimpaired"—by this, he joins together what has been torn asunder. "May all the gods rejoice here"—for all this is indeed [the sacrifice].

The All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ) thus restore it by means of everything. If he should so desire, he may say, "A firm foundation"; but if he should so desire, he need not even take heed of this. 1.8.1. [1] To Manu, indeed, in the morning...
They brought water for washing his feet, just as they bring it with both hands for the purpose of washing; as he was washing his feet, a fish entered his hands.
He spoke these words to him.
"Support me, and I will carry you across," he said. "Why will you carry me across?

"The flood will sweep away all these creatures; then I shall carry you across. "How will you support me? He replied: "As long as we are small, our danger from predators is great, and likewise for fish."

"In this way, the fish swallows me in its pot. When it grows too large for that, then dig a trench and place me in it. When it grows too large for that, then cast me into the ocean; then indeed I shall be beyond all harm. 1.8.1 [4]

"Kaṣa has always been here. For he grows ever greater; therefore, on such-and-such a year, a flood will come. Prepare a boat for me and wait. When that flood has risen, you shall board the boat, and then I will carry you across. 1.8.1 [5]
Having made him thus, he cast him into the ocean. When that year arrived which he had designated, he prepared a boat and waited; when the flood rose, he boarded the boat, and the fish approached him.
He leaped onto his horn and fastened the boat's rope to it; by means of that, he crossed over to the mountain beyond.
He said: "I have indeed carried you across; bind the boat to the tree, but do not bind it to the mountain."

"If there is water within, you must descend as far as the water extends by means of its convergence. He descended exactly that far. This is why this descent of Manu on the northern mountain is known as such; for the flood carried away all those creatures, and Manu alone remained here. 1.8.1 [7]
Desiring offspring, he performed austerities;
there, too, he sacrificed with a *pākayajña*, offering clarified butter, curd, whey, and curdled milk into the waters. Then, after a year, a woman came into being, and she—
She went forth while being pressed; indeed, clarified butter used to collect in her footprint. Mitra and Varuṇa united with her.
They said to her, "Who are you?"

"Tell Manu, 'I am the daughter of you two,'" she said. "No," he replied, "I belong only to him who begot me. They both sought to possess her; whether he perceived it or did not perceive it, she nevertheless went away. She came to Manu. 1.8.1 [9]
Manu said to her, "Who are you?

She replied, "I am your daughter. He asked, "How so, O Blessed One? How can I be your father? [She answered: "Those oblations of ghee, curds, whey, and clotted milk which you offered into the waters—those have given birth to me; I am that prosperity (Āśīḥ)."

"Incorporate her into the sacrifice; for if you incorporate me into the sacrifice, you will become rich in offspring and cattle. Whatever blessing you shall invoke with her, all that shall be fulfilled for you.
So they incorporated her into the middle of the sacrifice, for that which is between [the two offerings] is indeed the middle of the sacrifice.
[He performed] the fore-sacrifices and after-sacrifices. Wearing himself out with those two [verses], he practiced austerities, desiring offspring.
Through them, he brought forth this progeny which belongs to Manu.
Whatever offspring he had, and whatever blessing he invoked with this *iḍā*, all that was fulfilled for him. This is the *iḍā* according to its origin.
Whoever, knowing thus, performs the rite with the *iḍā*, verily produces that same kind of offspring.
Whatever Manu produced, whatever he impelled, and whatever blessing he invoked—all that is fulfilled for him. 1.8.1 [12] It indeed consists of five portions.
The *iḍā* is cattle; cattle are fivefold; therefore it consists of five portions. 1.8.1 [13]
Having cut off the *iḍā* portion, he breaks off the eastern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and places it in front of the *dhruvā* ladle;
having handed it to the Hotṛ, he passes toward the south. 1.8.1 [14]
He anoints the Hotṛ here;
he anoints the lips of the Hotṛ with [the formula]: "With the Lord of Mind, I eat of what has been offered by thee, for the sake of food and for the sake of breath. 1.8.1.[15]
Then he anoints the Hotṛ here;
he anoints the Hotṛ’s lips with the words: "I eat of what has been offered by thee, O Lord of Speech, for the sake of strength and the upward breath. 1.8.1 [16]
Manu, indeed, was afraid of this:
"This is the most vulnerable point of my sacrifice, namely this *iḍā* belonging to the domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña*);
what if the *rakṣases* should destroy my sacrifice here? He [performed] this [rite] for her before the *rakṣases*.

"Previously from the Rakṣases"—it is thus that he causes her to reach [the gods]; and so indeed does he now cause her to reach them "previously from the Rakṣases, previously from the Rakṣases. Now, as to why he does not eat it visibly: thinking "Lest I eat what has not been invited," it is by this very means that he causes her to reach [the gods], when he smears it upon his lips. 1.8.1 [17]
Then he makes an offering-portion into the hand of the Hotṛ.
Although it is already a collected portion, he thereby places her visibly upon the Hotṛ;
through that which has entered into himself, the Hotṛ invokes a blessing for the sacrificer. Therefore, he makes the offering-portion into the hand of the Hotṛ. 1.8.1 [18]

Then he calls out in a whisper. For Manu, indeed, was afraid of this: "This is the most fragile part of my sacrifice, namely this *iḍā* belonging to the domestic sacrifice; what if the *rakṣases* should destroy my sacrifice here?"

In former times he used to call her out in a whisper, saying, "Away from the Rakṣas! Away from the Rakṣas! And so now he likewise calls her out in a whisper, saying, "Away from the Rakṣas! Away from the Rakṣas! 1.8.1 [19].
He calls out:
"The Rathantara has been invoked together with the earth; may the Rathantara invoke me together with the earth!

The Vāmadevya has been invoked together with the intermediate space; may the Vāmadevya invoke me together with the intermediate space! The Bṛhat has been invoked together with the sky; may the Bṛhat invoke me together with the sky!"
Thus, by invoking this very one, he invokes these worlds and these *sāmans*.
"The cows are invoked together with the bull"—for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus he invokes it cryptically.
"Accompanied by the bulls"— he thus invokes her together with her mate.
"Invoked is the Saptahotr"—
thereby he invokes her by means of the Saptahotr and the Soma sacrifice.
"Upahūtā iḍā taturiḥ.
Thus he explicitly invokes her as "taturi," for she indeed overcomes all evil; therefore he says, "taturi. 1.8.1 [23]
"Invoked is the friend, the draught.
The friend and the draught are indeed the vital breath; thus he invokes the vital breath. "Invoked! Heigh!"—thereby he invokes the body; thereby he invokes it in its entirety. 1.8.1 [24]
Then he proceeds:
"Iḍā, invoked! Invoked Iḍā! May Iḍā invoke us; O Iḍā, invoked!
By this, since she has already been invoked, he invokes her directly. For she who was that [Iḍā] was indeed a cow.
The cow indeed has four feet; therefore, one invokes her four times.
While he is invoking her four times, he then invokes her as if they were distinct, to avoid sameness (*ajāmitā*); for [if he did not do so,] there would be sameness.
If he should perform [the invocation], he should invoke it thus: "O Iḍā, invoked! Invoked! For by saying "O Iḍā, invoked!

he invokes her hitherward; by saying "Invoked Iḍā," he invokes her thitherward; and by saying "May Iḍā call upon us," he does not exclude himself from this, yet it becomes otherwise—namely, "O Iḍā, invoked!"—[which is the correct form].
He then invokes her hitherward; thus he invokes her both hitherward and thitherward.
"Mānavī, Ghṛtapadī"—for Manu first generated her, therefore he says "Mānavī," and "Ghṛtapadī."
Because the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) settled in her footprint, therefore he says, "she whose footstep is butter" (*ghṛtapadī*).
And she is also called "belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa" (*maitrāvaruṇī*);
because she united with Mitra and Varuṇa, that very [animal] is the *nyaṅga* belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa.

"Brahmā, summoned by the gods"—for he is indeed their Brahmā, "summoned by the gods"; "summoned are the divine Adhvaryus, summoned are the human ones"—thereby he summons both the divine Adhvaryus and those who are human. The calves are indeed the divine Adhvaryus, while those others are the human ones. 1.8.1 [2]8.
"May they protect this sacrifice, and may they strengthen the lord of the sacrifice.

For those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred lore indeed protect the sacrifice; for they extend it and they generate it. Therefore, he offers a calf to them as a recompense.
"These indeed cause the lord of the sacrifice to prosper; for he whose [priests] are most numerous is the lord of the sacrifice who prospers.
Therefore he says: 'And those who shall cause the lord of the sacrifice to prosper.
"The two worlds, Heaven and Earth, the first-born, the observers of *ṛta*, the goddesses, the mothers of the gods—thus he addresses these two, Heaven and Earth."

He invokes [the Iḍā], saying, "Of whomsoever this all is, he has been invoked; here is the sacrificer. Thus he invokes the sacrificer. Now, as to why he does not mention his name here: for at this point the sacrificial food has already been consecrated. If he were to mention the name, he would make it human; and whatever is human in the sacrifice is indeed unsuccessful.
"May I not cause failure in the sacrifice"— thinking thus, he does not utter the name.
"Invited to the subsequent sacrifice to the gods"— by this,
he invokes for him a long life in an indirect manner.

"For a man, having sacrificed previously, sacrifices again later. This, they say, is how he cryptically prays for offspring for him; for he who has offspring reaches that [world].* 1.8.1. [31] *The phrase "for he who has offspring reaches that" refers to the attainment of the heavenly world through progeny.
