He attains the world for himself; then, in this world, his offspring performs sacrifice. Therefore, the sacrifice performed by offspring is subsequent to the sacrifice performed by the gods. This, then, he invokes for him in a hidden manner: namely, cattle. For he who possesses cattle, having sacrificed first, sacrifices again later.

"At the offering of more oblations, [I am] invited. By this, he invokes for him a life-span in an indirect manner; for having sacrificed previously, one indeed offers oblations again and again. 1.8.1 [34]

Thus, he cryptically invokes for him offspring itself; for he who has offspring exists as one in his own person, and then, moreover, through his offspring he is made into tenfold oblation. Therefore, offspring is the most extensive preparation of the oblation. Thus, he cryptically invokes for him cattle themselves.
For he who possesses cattle, having sacrificed once, performs the oblation again and again.
This indeed is the prayer: "May I live; may I have offspring; may I attain prosperity. In that he prays for cattle, he prays for prosperity.
For prosperity is indeed cattle; thus, by means of these two blessings, everything is obtained.
Therefore, these two blessings are performed here: "May the gods enjoy this oblation of mine! [1.8.1.37]
"In that [verse], 'they have been invited'—he thereby invokes the prosperity of the sacrifice; for when the gods enjoy the oblation, by that indeed one wins great things.
Therefore he says, 'may they enjoy it. 1.8.1 [38]
They indeed consume it;
they do not offer it into the fire. For the *iḍā* is cattle; [they think], "Lest we should consume the cattle in the fire.
Therefore, they do not offer it into the fire. 1.8.1 [39]
It is offered in the vital breaths themselves:

in the Hotṛ, in the Sacrificer, and in the Adhvaryu. Now, when he has broken off the eastern half of the sacrificial cake and places it to the east of the Dhruvā spoon—the Dhruvā being indeed the Sacrificer—[he thereby places it] in the Sacrificer himself.

Thus, it becomes as if the sacrificer himself has partaken; for when he does not eat in person, thinking, "Lest I should eat before the sacrifice is completed," this very [act] constitutes his eating. All partake, thinking, "May there be offerings for me among all. Five partake, for the *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and cattle are fivefold; therefore, five partake. 1.8.1 [40]
Now, where he proceeds:

having divided that sacrificial cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). This is because it is the vessel for the ancestors; for the ancestors are indeed the intermediate directions, and therefore [the cake] is divided into four.
Having prepared the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis). 1.8.1.
[41] Then, when [the Adhvaryu] says, "The Heaven and Earth are invited," he places it for the Āgnīdhra; the Āgnīdhra then consumes it, [saying] "Invited."

"May Mother Earth call upon me; may Mother Earth call upon me from the Āgnīdhra fire-hearth, svāhā! May Father Heaven call upon me; may Father Heaven call upon me from the Āgnīdhra fire-hearth, svāhā! For this Āgnīdhra fire-hearth is indeed heaven and earth; therefore he eats thus. 1.8.1 [42]
Then, where he invokes a blessing, he mutters:
"May Indra bestow this power upon me;
may the liberal lords attend us with riches; may our blessings be fulfilled; may our blessings be true. This is indeed [the formula] for blessings.

The acceptance [of gifts] is this: whatever blessings the officiating priests here invoke for the sacrificer, those he now takes for himself by accepting them. 1.8.1. [43] Then they purify themselves with two strainers (*pavitra*).
For they have performed this as if with the *iḍā* of a domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña*), being purified by the strainers. What [is the purpose]?...
"May we extend that which was not established above for the sacrifice"—therefore they purify themselves with the two strainers (*pavitra*). Then he joins those two strainers to the *prastara* bundle;
the *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, and the two strainers are the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*udāna*).
He places those two, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the up-breath (*udāna*), in the sacrificer; therefore, he mixes them into the *pavitra* strainers upon the *prastara* grass-bundle. 1.8.2.
[1] They indeed carry forth these two firebrands for the sake of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s). For this fire becomes exhausted for the gods.

For he has carried the sacrifice forward so that it is not stale, thinking, "We shall perform the after-offerings with [the fire] that is not stale. Therefore, they carry these two firebrands forward.
They then touch them together again.
Furthermore, they cause this fire to swell and make it free from weariness;
for [they think], "Whatever part of the sacrifice remains uncompleted beyond this point, may we extend that.
Therefore, they touch it again. 1.8.2 (3)

Then he places a fuel-stick upon the fire. He kindles it for him; and while it is thus kindled, he thinks, "Whatever part of the sacrifice remains uncompleted beyond this point, may we extend that. That is why he places a fuel-stick upon the fire. 1.8.2 [4]
The Hotṛ addresses it with the mantra:
"This is thy fuel-stick, O Agni; through it mayest thou grow and swell, and may we also grow and swell. This is just as before.

He recites the verses for the one being kindled; in this very same way he recites here. This is the duty of the Hotṛ; if he should think, "The Hotṛ does not know [the verses]," then the sacrificer himself should also pronounce the consecratory formulas.
Then he cleanses [the fire].
He thus yokes it; being yoked, he shall carry that part of the sacrifice which remains uncompleted from here onwards.
Therefore, he cleanses it. He cleanses it once each time; for in ancient times they cleansed it thrice for the gods, thinking, "Let us not do as we did for the gods."
Therefore, he wipes it once each time for the sake of non-repetition; for he would indeed commit a repetition if he were to do it three times before and three times after.
Therefore, he wipes it once each time. He wipes it thus: 1.8.2. [6] He wipes it.

"O Agni, winner of booty, I cleanse thee, the winner of booty, who hast run for the booty"—thus he says at first regarding one who is about to run, for at that time he is as if about to run; but here [he says], "who hast run," for here he has indeed run; therefore he says, "who hast run. 1.8.2. [7]
Then he performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*).
Whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, all of them have indeed been worshipped thereby;
and since he now offers these as if they were the sacrificial animal once all those [deities] have been worshipped, therefore they are called *anuyāja*.
Now, as for why he performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*):
the after-offerings are indeed the meters (*candāṃsi*), and the meters are the cattle of the gods.

Just as yoked draft animals carry burdens for humans, so the meters (*candāṃsi*), being yoked, carry the sacrifice for the gods. When the meters satisfied the gods, then the gods satisfied the meters;
from that time on, it was thus that the yoked meters carried [the sacrifice] for the gods.
They have carried the sacrifice when they have fully satisfied them. Now, as for why he performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*):
the after-offerings are indeed the meters; it is thus the meters that he satisfies.

Therefore he performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*). Therefore, with whatever vehicle one would drive [the horse], having unyoked it, one should say: "Let it drink; make it well-fed. This indeed is the concealment of the vehicle. He certainly offers the *barhis* first.
That Gāyatrī, though the smallest of the meters, is joined as the first among the meters;

it was by its very power that the falcon, having become a hawk, brought down the Soma from heaven. People consider this to be out of order, that the Gāyatrī, being the smallest meter, should be the first.

Now, the *candas* (metres) are indeed joined here according to their respective order; the gods fashioned the *candas* for the *anuyāja* offerings so that there might be no confusion of better and worse.
He, moreover, sacrifices to the *barhis* first.
This world is indeed the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), and plants are the *barhis*; he thus places plants in this very world. These plants are established in this world;
this entire moving world (*jagat*) rests upon it, and for that reason this [earth] is the *jagatī*. Thus they made the *jagatī* the first. 1.8.2. [12]
Then he sacrifices to Narāśaṃsa as the second.
Narāśaṃsa is indeed the intermediate space; "men" (nara) are indeed offspring.
These offspring move about, praising along this intermediate space. For when one speaks, it is as if one praises (śaṃsati).
Regarding this they say: "Therefore the Narāśaṃsa is the intermediate space; the Triṣṭubh is indeed the intermediate space. Thus they made the second [verse] a Triṣṭubh.
And Agni is the last."

The fire is indeed the *gāyatrī*; they made the *gāyatrī* the last [verse], so that by this well-ordered arrangement the meters became firmly established. Therefore, this is free from evil and brings prosperity. "Sacrifice to the gods!"—thus the *adhvaryu* says.
"God after god," says the Adhvaryu at all [the offerings]; "god after god," says the Hotṛ at all [the offerings]. Indeed, the gods are the gods of the gods;
the meters are their cattle, for cattle are houses, and houses are a firm foundation; and the Anuyājas are the meters.
Therefore, the Adhvaryu says, "Sacrifice to the gods," while the Hotṛ says, "God after god," at all [the offerings]. 1.8.2. [15]

"In the winning of wealth, of the treasure-store"— thus the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered for the deity itself, and it is offered to the deity; yet here, among the *anuyāja* offerings, there is no deity, because [the mantra] says, "O divine *barhis*," wherein there is neither Agni, nor Indra, nor Soma, nor the deity Narāśaṃsa.

"Truth is one"—this is Agni here, and the Gāyatrī is its corresponding basis. Then, when he offers with the words, "For the winning of wealth, for the bestowing of wealth," Agni is indeed the winner of wealth and Indra is the bestower of wealth; this is so.
The deities for the *candas* are indeed Indra and Agni; thus, it is to a deity that the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, and to a deity that the offering is made.
Then, having performed the final *anuyāja* and having brought [the butter] together, he offers it.
These are indeed the *prayājas* and *anuyājas*; it is just as that [which was previously described].
In the *prayāja* offerings, he causes the sacrificer to pay tribute to his hateful rival; here he causes him to pay tribute as food.
In this very same way, he causes him to pay tribute in the *anuyāja* offerings.
He then separates the two offering-spoons.

"May I win after the winning of Agni and Soma; I push forward with the impulse of strength"—with these words, he holds the *juhū* spoon facing eastward with his right hand. "May Agni and Soma drive away him who hates us and whom we hate;
I push him away with the impulse of strength"—with these words, he holds the *upabhṛt* spoon facing westward with his left hand.
If the sacrificer himself [offers it] with his hand, or if the *adhvaryu* [does so], [he should say]:
"May this sacrificer rise up after the rising of Agni and Soma; may he win the prize (*vāja*) for him."
"By the impulse, I push forward Agni and Soma; may they drive away him whom this sacrificer hates and him who hates him;
by the impulse of strength, I push him away"—thus [he says] at the full moon sacrifice, for the oblation of the full moon belongs to Agni and Soma. 1.8.3. [3]
Then, on the new moon day:

"May I conquer following the victory of Indra and Agni; by the impulse of strength (vāja), I push him forth; may Indra and Agni drive away him who hates us and whom we hate—this one, by means of strength."
"If it is the sacrificer himself, [he says]: 'By the impulse (prasava), I drive away [the enemies]'"; "If, however, it is the Adhvaryu:
'May this sacrificer follow Indra and Agni’s victory with his own victory; by the impulse of strength (vāja), may he [drive them away]'."
"I drive away Indra and Agni; may they drive away him whom this sacrificer hates and whoever hates him.

By the impulse of strength (*vāja*), I drive him away"—thus he says at the new moon sacrifice, for the oblation of the new moon belongs to Indra and Agni. In this way he distributes [the verses] according to the respective deities. As to why he thus distributes them: 1.8.3. [5]
The sacrificer indeed follows the *juhū*;
he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt*.
Thus he raises the sacrificer forward and drives away him who acts with hostility toward him; he is truly the eater.

Following the *juhū* ladle he takes up the eater, and following the *upabhṛt* ladle he pushes away the food; thus he raises up the eater facing forward and drives away the food facing backward. Now, this very act is differentiated within the same ritual action; therefore, from the same person, both the eater and the food are born. For it is said, "We meet in the fourth generation, in the third," and so they sit, playing with dice according to their lineage.
Therefore, [it is said]:
"Then he anoints the enclosing sticks with the *juhū* ladle—
the same [ladle] with which he has offered to the gods and with which he has performed the sacrifice."
By means of this very act of establishing [the fire], he gratifies the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*); therefore, he anoints the enclosing-sticks with the *juhū* ladle.

He anoints them, saying: "For the Vasus thee! For the Rudras thee! For the Ādityas thee! These indeed are the three classes of gods—the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; thus he says, "For these thee!"
Then, having approached the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), he causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*).
For it is to the enclosing-sticks that he makes this announcement; the announcement is indeed the sacrifice (*yajña*);
thus, by means of the sacrifice itself, he visibly gratifies the enclosing-sticks. Therefore, having approached the enclosing-stick, he causes the announcement. 1.8.3 [10]
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled. For these enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are indeed the divine Hotṛs, since they are fires;
thus, when he says, "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled," he means this very thing. By saying, "for auspicious speech," he either [means] himself...

The gods become intent upon him when he speaks what is good and does what is good; therefore he says, "for auspicious speech. When it is said, "the human [priest] is sent for the Sūktavāka," he thereby impels this human Hotṛ for the Sūktavāka. 1.8.3. [11]
Then he takes up the *prastara* (grass-bundle). The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer;
thus, he now sends the sacrificer back to his own place—that is, to the world of the gods—to which his sacrifice has gone.
"By this [verse], he leads the sacrificer to the world of fragrance. 1.8.3.
[12] If he should desire rain, he should take up [the earth] with this very [verse]: 'O Heaven and Earth, agree together! For when..."
Heaven and Earth are in agreement, and then it rains; therefore he says, "May Heaven and Earth be in agreement.

"May Mitra and Varuna protect you with rain"—by this he means, "May he who rules over the rain protect you with rain. Now, he who rules over the rain is this wind that blows here; for though it blows as one, it blows as many.
He has entered within this person as these two, the Prāṇa and Udāna, moving forward and backward;
for Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the Prāṇa and Udāna. "May he who rules over rain protect you with rain"—this is what he says by this.
He should take it up with this very [formula], for whenever it rains, it is as if [the deity] is present.
He thus makes this an oblation; having become an oblation, let it go to the world of the gods.
He first anoints the tip on the *juhū*, the middle on the *upabhṛt*, and the base on the *dhruvā*; for [the sacrifice] is like a plant, with its tip, middle, and base.
The *juhū* is like the middle [of the body], the *upabhṛt* like the root, and the *dhruvā* like the base.
He anoints them with the formula: "May the birds eat, licking what has been anointed.
Having thus become a bird, he causes him to fly up from this world of men to the world of the gods; he then carries it as if low.
It is a pair because he should carry it as if low; for the *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, so he carries it thus for its support, lest he strike it away;
verily, he brings down rain right here.
He carries it [with the words]: "Go to the dappled mares of the Maruts! By saying "of the Maruts," he says, "Go to the world of the gods."
"Go to the spotted ones, O cow; having become the speckled one, go to heaven, and from there bring rain for us.
This "cow" (vaśā) is indeed this earth, for whatever edible food is established upon her—both that which has roots and that which is rootless—by that she is the speckled cow (pṛśni).
"Having become this [earth], go to heaven," he says by this; "and from there bring rain for us," he says. For from rain comes strength, sap, and well-being.
"From that [the rain] is produced; therefore he says, 'Therefore, bring us rain. Then he pulls away a single blade of grass.
The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is indeed the sacrificer; as for that which is the whole...

He should throw the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) into the fire; for if he were to throw it immediately, the sacrificer would quickly go to yonder world. Thus, the sacrificer lives long; indeed, he preserves for him that which is his human lifespan here. Having held it for a moment, he throws it into the fire.

Thus, he causes that very self of his to go to where his other self has gone; for if he were not to throw it down, he would indeed exclude the sacrificer from the world; but in this way, he does not exclude the sacrificer from the world. 1.8.3 [18]
He piles it up facing eastward, for the east is the direction of the gods; or facing northward, for the north is the direction of men.
They should smooth it out with their fingers alone, not with wooden sticks or other pieces of wood; they scatter away the other, the corpse-like part.
"Let us prepare it so that the other corpse [is not affected]," they said; therefore, they should crush it with their fingers alone, not with wooden sticks.
When the Hotṛ recites the *sūktavāka*, then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw [the remains] after! (1.8.3).

"In that his other self has gone there, he says this: 'Make it go there for him. Having silently cast [the fire-wood] into the fire, he touches himself with the words, 'O Agni, you are the protector of sight; protect my sight! By this, he does not cause his own self to enter into the fire. 1.8.3 [20]
Then he says, "Converse with him.
This means, "Make him agree with the gods. [The Adhvaryu] says, "Has the Agnīdh come? This means, "Has he indeed come? The other replies, "He has come. [The Adhvaryu] says, "Make it heard! (śrāvaya).

"Make him hear it by means of the gods; awaken him," this is what he says with the word *śrauṣaṭ*. "They have indeed heard him, or they have awakened him"—this is what he says. In this way, both the Adhvaryu and the Agnīdh lead the sacrificer to the world of the gods. Then he says, "Go happily to the divine Hotṛs. For these enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are indeed the divine Hotṛs, for they are fires.
He thus sends these very ones back to their own abodes; therefore he says, "May it be well with the divine Hotṛs," and "May there be well-being for the human ones.
By this, he invokes safety for the human Hotṛ.
Then he throws the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) into the fire; he first throws the middle enclosing-stick into the fire, that one which—

"O divine Agni, when you were being hidden by the Paṇis, you placed a fence around yourself; I bring this back to you according to your pleasure, lest he should cause you to lose consciousness. With these words, he joins the other two [spoons] together at the place dear to Agni that has been reached.
Then he lifts up both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* spoons.
Verily, he makes this an oblation when he anoints [the ladles], thinking, "Having become an oblation, may it go to the world of the gods. Therefore, he takes up both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*.
He indeed takes them up for all the gods.

Or rather, when an oblation is taken for a deity that has not been specifically assigned, all the deities indeed consider themselves entitled to it; for one does not assign this clarified butter (ājya) as an oblation for any particular deity. Therefore, he takes it up for the Viśve Devas; this is its significance.
In the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, [the formula for] the oblation is: "1.8.3.
[25] He takes it up together with the words, 'You are the sharers of the remnants, great ones,' for indeed the remnant is what remains over."
"Those who stand on the *prastara* and those who are the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), O gods"—for both the *prastara* and the enclosing-sticks have been cast into the fire;

"all of you, singing toward this speech"—he thereby makes it belong to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*); "sitting upon this sacrificial grass, rejoice! Svāhā! Vāṭ!"—thus it becomes for him like an oblation offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call. 1.8.3 [26]
They unyoke it from the pole of that cart from which they take the oblation, saying, "From where we yoke, from there we shall unyoke";
for from where they yoke, from there they unyoke. And as for that [cart] from which they take [the oblation] with the wooden sword from the vessel—[from there they unyoke].
"We shall yoke; then we shall unyoke," for they indeed unyoke from the same place where they yoke. 1.8.3.
[27] These two spoons (*srucau*) are truly the two yoke-horses of the sacrifice. He yokes them when he proceeds with the performance; he [then]—whomsoever...
Having set it down, he should cut [the portion] according to the vehicle; as he unyokes it, so does he do for thee—this is the unyoking at the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
He brings it hither, sets it down, and unyokes it for thee; he employs it again here.
Having performed the *anuyāja* offerings, he comes to this unyoking; he sets it down and unyokes it for thee; he employs it again here.
That which he harnesses, he grasps firmly; whatever goal he yokes toward, having reached that goal, he unyokes it.
Or rather, offspring follow the sacrifice; therefore, this man yokes and then unyokes, and then yokes again;
whatever goal he yokes toward, having reached that goal, he finally unyokes it. He sets them down [with the words]: "Ye two are butter-dripping, ye two are the leaders."
"Ye two are in favor; place me in favor," he says; by this he means, "Ye two are auspicious; place me in what is auspicious. 1.9.1.
When he says, "The divine Hotṛ-priests have been impelled for the utterance of the auspicious word; the human [Hotṛ] has been sent forth for the Sūktavāka," then—

The Hotṛ recites the invitatory verses; he says this as if it were a hymn of praise, and thereby he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer. Now, he invokes this blessing at the conclusion of the sacrifice. There is a twofold reason why he invokes the blessing at the conclusion of the sacrifice: [he does so because] this man indeed generates the sacrifice.

Whoever sacrifices, it is indeed by this [formula] that the officiating priests are told to extend [the sacrifice]; they produce him, and then he invokes a blessing. That blessing which he invokes, the sacrifice bends toward him, thinking, "May the one who produced me obtain the blessing which I have invoked. Therefore, he invokes the blessing at the conclusion of the sacrifice. 1.9.1. [3]

He who sacrifices with this sacrifice indeed gratifies the gods—now by means of the *ṛc*s, now by means of the *yajus* formulas, and now by means of the oblations. Having gratified the gods, he becomes one who has entered into their intimacy; he becomes one who has entered into their intimacy.
Having done so, he then invokes a blessing; the gods incline that blessing toward him, thinking, "The blessing which he has invoked is one which he has sent to us.
Therefore, indeed, he invokes the blessing at the conclusion of the sacrifice. Then he proceeds.

"O Heaven and Earth, this has become auspicious," for it indeed became auspicious that he reached the conclusion of the sacrifice; "we have succeeded in the *sūktavāka* and the *namovāka*," for both the *sūktavāka* and the *namovāka* belong to the sacrifice; "we have accomplished the sacrifice, we have found the sacrifice"—this is what he says; "O Agni, you..."
"Thou art of well-spoken speech, hearkening unto heaven and earth"—by this he says this to Agni:

"Thou art of well-spoken speech, hearkening unto these two, heaven and earth. "May heaven and earth be full of protection for thee, O sacrificer, at this sacrifice"—that is, "may heaven and earth be full of food for thee, O sacrificer, at this sacrifice."
"May they be auspicious for the cow and givers of life"—by this he says, "May they be auspicious for the cow and givers of life to you.
"Without a membrane and without a womb"—by this he says, "Do not cause me harm. 1.9.1 [5]
"Why should you be afraid of anyone? May no one find this prosperity of ours"—this is what he says with these words.
"May they be wide-striding and makers of fearlessness"—he says this so that "they may be wide-striding and free from fear for you. "The rain-givers of heaven... [he says].

"May they be rain-bearing and free from frost"—this is what he thereby says. "May they be auspicious and refreshing"—this is what he thereby says: "May they be auspicious for you and refreshing; and may they be full of vigor."
"May they be rich in milk and rich in sap; may they be fit for you to subsist upon"—this is what he says.
"May she be easy to approach and easy to ascend"—he means:
"May that one whom you approach from below be easy for you to approach."

"May this earth be for you a place of your own to walk upon—that which you shall walk upon above," so he says with this. "Of those two, [I am] the witness"—that is to say, "of those two who do not acknowledge me.
"Agni has enjoyed this oblation; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more glorious"—this he says regarding the butter-portion belonging to Agni.

"Soma has accepted this offering; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more mighty"—thus he says regarding the *ājyabhāga* for Soma. "Agni has accepted this offering; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more mighty"—thus he says regarding that cake for Agni which is common to both [offerings] and never shifts. 1.9.1. [10]
Then, according to the respective deities:
"The butter-drinking gods have enjoyed the clarified butter; they have increased; they have made it greater and more vast.

By this he refers to the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. For the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are indeed the butter-drinking gods. Agni [has performed] this by means of the office of the *hotṛ*.
"He has enjoyed the oblation; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more glorious"—by this he means that Agni has enjoyed [the offering] through his office as Hotṛ.
Thus he takes notice of whichever deities have been sacrificed to, thinking, "This one has enjoyed the oblation; that one has enjoyed the oblation.
He thereby invokes the prosperity of the sacrifice itself; for when the gods enjoy the oblation, by that indeed one wins greatness.
Therefore he says, "He has enjoyed it" and "He has increased it. For when the gods enjoy an oblation, they even make it as large as a mountain;
therefore he says, "He has increased it. "They have made it greater than great. 1.9.1 [11]
"The sacrifice is indeed the greatness of the gods, for they make it as it were greater;
therefore he says, 'Greatness has become greater. 'May there be no failure in this divine-offering Hotṛ-function. 1.9.1 [12]
"In this invocation leading to the gods, may he prosper"—this is what he says. "This sacrificer, so-and-so," he says, pronouncing the name; thus he directly endows him with the blessing. 1.9.1 [13]
"He prays for long life":
that which is the superior sacrifice to the gods in the world beyond, that is here manifest as long life.
"He prays for good offspring. 1.9.1 [14]

That which is the further performance of the oblation there is here the visible attainment of good offspring and sovereignty; he who should act thus would thereby pray for the subsequent sacrifice to the gods—this indeed one should say, for that is life, that is progeny, and that is cattle. 1.9.1 [15]

"He further desires the performance of the oblation. This, indeed, is what he desires through the *sajātavanasyā* formula; for the *sajātās* (kinsmen) are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), since one is born together with the vital breaths.
Thus, he desires the vital breaths.
"He desires the celestial abode," he says.

"May there be for me even in the world of the gods"—thus indeed he sacrifices when he sacrifices; he thereby makes him one who has attained that very world of the gods. "What he hopes for by means of this oblation, may he obtain it, may he prosper in it"—when he says, "Whatever he hopes for by means of this oblation, may all that be fulfilled for him," he says this very thing. 1.9.1 [17]
Now, he makes these five prayers for blessings: three in the *iḍā* [verse]; those make eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables;
the Gāyatrī is vigor. Thus, he brings these prayers for blessings into correspondence with vigor. He should not make more than this.

One should not do more than this; for if one were to perform more [verses], whatever is redundant in the sacrifice, that is left over for his hateful enemy. Therefore, one should not perform more than this.
"May the seven younger ones also grant this to him"—
by this he means, "may the gods grant their approval to him"; "may the god Agni win it from the gods for us"— we [win it] from Agni.
"May Agni, as a god, win this for us from the gods; may we win this from Agni"—this is what he says when he says, "The sacrifice and the wealth.
1.9.1 [20] "And the sacrifice and the wealth."
It was as if they sought this sacrifice and found it; therefore he says, "What has been sought and what has been found.
"May both heaven and earth protect him from distress"—by this he means, "May both heaven and earth guard him from misfortune. 1.9.1 [21]
Regarding this, some say:

"Both for me," thinking that in doing so the Hotṛ does not exclude himself from the blessings. But one should not speak thus; for the sacrifice belongs to the sacrificer—what indeed is there for the officiating priests? Whatever blessing the officiating priests [receive] in the sacrifice...

They pronounce a benediction for the sacrificer alone; indeed, he does not establish that benediction anywhere who says, "And both for me. Therefore, one should say, "And both for him. [1.9.1] "Here is the attainment of the desirable."
Whatever is good in the sacrifice, that he thereby bestows upon him; therefore he says, "May there be here the attainment of what is desirable.
And with the words, "And this homage to the gods," having reached the conclusion of the sacrifice, he thus offers homage to the gods.
Therefore he says, "And this homage to the gods" (1.9.1.24). Then he recites the *śamyor*.
For Śamyu Bārhaspatya indeed directly perceived the completion of the sacrifice; he—
He went even to the world of the gods, and for men that [world] became as if it had vanished.
This was heard by the seers:
Śamyu Bārhaspatya indeed [knew] the direct completion of the sacrifice.

He knew that he had departed for the world of the gods; they then adopted that very conclusion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya had known. They said to Śamyu, "Tell us that [conclusion]. He then adopted that very conclusion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya had known, and what Śamyu said, that is what this sacrificer now adopts. Therefore, one says, "O Śamyu! 1.9.1. [26]
He proceeds with the verse, "We choose that truth of both," by which he means to say: "We choose that conclusion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya discovered. 1.9.1 [27]
"An opening for the sacrifice, an opening for the lord of the sacrifice!
For he indeed seeks an opening for the sacrifice and an opening for the lord of the sacrifice who effects the completion of the sacrifice.
"May there be divine well-being for us; may there be well-being for humans"—may there be well-being for us among the gods!

"May it be well with men"—this is what he says by this. "May the remedy go upward"—this is what he says by this: "May this sacrifice of ours ascend to the world of the gods. "May there be welfare for our bipeds, welfare for our quadrupeds."

All this that exists is only as much as what has two feet and what has four feet; therefore, having reached the conclusion of this sacrifice, he makes it propitious for that very reason. Thus he says: "May it be well with our bipeds, may it be well with our quadrupeds. 1.9.1 [29]
Then he touches it with the words, "Bring her hither. For when one has entered upon the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), he becomes, as it were, non-human;
this earth, indeed, is the foundation. Thus, he establishes himself upon this very foundation. And so, indeed...
He becomes human again; therefore, he touches [the water] with this [formula]. 1.9.2.
Now, when they are about to perform the *saṃyājana* (joint offerings) for the wives, they turn back;
the *adhvaryu* takes up the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles.

The Hotṛ [takes] the Veda; the Āgnīdhra [takes] the butter-melting ladle. Regarding this, some say that the Adhvaryu goes around the front of the Āhavanīya fire; however, one should not do so, for it would be outside [the sacrificial ground].

For he would depart from the sacrifice if he were to go by that [route]. According to some, the Adhvaryu goes behind the wife; however, one should not do so, for the front part is indeed [the proper place].

The Adhvaryu is the hind part of the sacrifice, and the wife is as it were its tail; if he were to place the head [of the victim] there, it would be as if he were to put the head back onto the tail, and thus it would indeed be excluded from the sacrifice if he were to lead it by that way.
Therefore, he leads it between the wife and [the Adhvaryu]. 1.9.2. [4] Between them, indeed, is the wife.
Some say that the Adhvaryu goes [by the front], but one should not do so;

for he would thereby exclude the wife from the sacrifice. Therefore, he should go by the front of the Gārhapatya fire and between it and the Āhavanīya fire. Thus, she is not excluded from the sacrifice, just as when he is performing the ritual, he moves between them. And that [is the way].
This is his procedure for moving about.
Then they perform the *saṃyājana* offerings for the wives.
From the sacrifice, indeed, offspring are produced; being produced from the sacrifice—

They are produced from a pair; being produced from a pair, they are produced at the end of the sacrifice. Thus, he causes these offspring to be produced at the end of the sacrifice from that productive union.
Therefore, these offspring are produced from that productive union at the end of the sacrifice; for this reason, they cause the wives to sacrifice together. 1.9.2. [6]
He sacrifices to four deities.
Four indeed constitute a pair; a pair is indeed a couple, for there are always two by two, and thus a productive pair is thereby created. Therefore, he sacrifices to four deities. 1.9.2 [7]
Now, these indeed have clarified butter as their oblation.
Clarified butter is seed; it is seed that he thus pours forth. Therefore, they have clarified butter as their oblation.
Therefore they proceed in a whisper;
for one proceeds as it were secretly with a mate, and that which is whispered is as it were secret;
therefore they proceed in a whisper. 1.9.2. [9]
Then he sacrifices to Soma.
Soma is indeed seed; it is seed that he thus pours out. Therefore he sacrifices to Soma.
Then he sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the emitted seed; therefore, one sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Then he sacrifices to the wives of the gods.
For the seed is established in the womb of the wives, and from that it is born.
He thus establishes that seed, once poured, in the wombs of their wives; from that it is born.
Therefore, he sacrifices to the wives of the gods. When he sacrifices to the wives of the gods—

He places it across in front; for the deities indeed sit waiting as long as the *sam-iṣṭayajus* oblation has not been offered, thinking, "Let him now offer this to us. He thus places it across from them.
Therefore, these human women desire men as if from behind; as he said, "They are like those [deities]."
Yājñavalkya 1.9.2:
Then he sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati.
This Agni is indeed this world; thus, he [establishes] this world and these creatures.
He causes them to procreate; these creatures are born from this world. Therefore, he sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati.
That [offering] concludes with the *iḍā*.
For here there are no enclosing-sticks (paridhi) and no grass-bunch (prastara);
for when he makes the sacrificer go safely home by means of the prastara over there, then the wife also becomes made to go safely home, since the wife follows her husband.
He should indeed perform that which constitutes the form of the prastara; therefore, it should end with the *iḍā* offering, and thus it is.
The form of the *prastara* itself is being made [of him]. 1.9.2.[15] If he should make the form of the *prastara*,
just as [he previously] protected the sacrificer with the *prastara*—
He makes her go to her own place; in this very same way, he makes the wife go to her own place. 1.9.2.
[16] If he should take the form of the *prastara* [bundle], he plucks a single blade of grass from the *veda* and anoints its tip with the *juhū* ladle.
He places the middle part [of the ladle] in the *sruva* and the base in the pot. 1.9.2.
[17] Then the *Āgnīdhra* says, "Throw it after!
Having thrown it after silently, [he recites]: "O Agni, you are the protector of sight; protect my sight."
Saying "Protect [us]," they both touch themselves; thus he does not exclude himself from the sacrificial portion.
Then he says, "Converse! "The Agnīdh has come," "Make it heard! "Oṣaṭ! "Well-being to the divine Hotṛs!"
"May there be well-being for men; speak auspiciousness!
[1.9.2.19] Then he takes up both the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles together.
In that he anoints them, he thereby makes an oblation; having become an oblation, it [proceeds].
"Go to the world of the gods"—therefore he takes up both the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles.
He takes them up for Agni with the words:
"O Agni, of unimpaired life-force, O cool one! [He is] the immortal.

"Thou art Agni," he says; therefore he says, "for security. "Thou art unassailable," he says; for Agni is indeed unassailable; therefore he says, "thou art unassailable. "Protect me from the lightning-flash," "protect me from bondage," "protect me from ill-offered sacrifice," "protect me from ill-eaten food"—by this he means to say, "guard me from all calamities.
"Make our food free from poison"—food is indeed "pitu"; "free from disease," he says. "Not [poison]," he says.
"Make this food free from blemish"—this is what he says; "in a well-seated womb"—this he says regarding his own self; "Svāhā!
Vāṭ!"—thus it becomes for him as if it were offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
Then the wife unties the *veda* grass-bundle.

The altar (vedi) is indeed female, and the sacrificial grass-bundle (veda) is male; the veda is prepared for the sake of union. Now, when he takes hold of it at the sacrifice, this very act constitutes a productive union. Then, as for why he causes the wife to loosen [the veda]: 1.9.2. The wife is indeed female, and the Veda is male; thus a productive union is brought about.
Therefore, the wife unties the Veda. She unties it: 1.9.2. [23] She unties it.
"You are the Veda; by that [Veda] through which you, O God, became the Veda for the gods, by that may the Veda be mine.
If he wishes to perform [the rite] with the Yajus formula, he should do so with this very one.
He spreads it out from the altar.
The altar is indeed a woman, and the *veda* grass-bundle is a man. For a man, having approached from behind, mounts a woman;
so too, having approached it from behind, he causes her to be mounted by means of the male *veda*. Therefore, he strews [the grass] up to the altar. 1.9.2. [25]

Then he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation, thinking, "May my sacrifice be completed while facing eastward. Now, if he were to perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings after having offered the *samiṣṭayajus*, his sacrifice would indeed be completed while facing westward; therefore, [he offers it first].
Now he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* so that his sacrifice may be completed while still directed forward. And as for why it is called *samiṣṭayajus*:
whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this [sacrifice is performed]...
The sacrifice is performed; indeed, all those [oblations] have been completed. Because he offers this [libation] after all of them have been completed, it is therefore called the *samiṣṭayajus*.
Now, as to why he offers the *samiṣṭayajus*:

Whatever deities he invokes with this sacrifice, for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, they indeed sit waiting, thinking, "Let him now offer this to us. He thus dismisses them each to their proper place, wherever their course lies. Verily, he thereby brings forth the sacrifice.
Having produced that which was not yet produced, he establishes it where its foundation lies;

therefore, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation. He offers it with the words, "O gods, you who know the way (*gātuvidas*)," for the gods are indeed knowers of the way; by saying "having known the way," he means "having known the sacrifice."

With the verse "gātumit," he thus releases [the sacrifice] in its proper manner. With the words, "O Lord of the Mind, O God, place this sacrifice in the wind, svāhā!"—this wind is indeed the sacrifice; having thus gathered this sacrifice together, he establishes it in that very sacrifice.
He unites sacrifice with sacrifice; therefore he says, "Place it in the wind, svāhā! 1.9.2. [29]
Then he offers the *barhis*.
The *barhis* is indeed this world, and the plants are the *barhis*; thus they place the plants in this very world.
These plants are established in this world; therefore, he offers the *barhis*. 1.9.2 [30]
Or rather, he offers that as an extra oblation;
for the *samiṣṭayajus* is indeed the end of the sacrifice.
Whatever comes after the *samiṣṭayajus* is extra; and when he offers the *samiṣṭayajus*, then he offers these [oblations]—therefore, these [worlds].

Excessive and unmeasured herbs are produced. He offers the oblation: "May the sacrificial grass be anointed with the offering, with ghee; may it be united with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, and with the Maruts."
"May Indra together with all the gods anoint it; may that which is offered with 'svāhā' go to the celestial sky.
(1.9.2) Then, having gone around to the south, he pours out the *praṇītā* water.
For when one performs this sacrifice, one indeed yokes it.
If he were not to pour it out, the sacrifice, being turned away and unreleased, would consume the sacrificer;
thus, the sacrifice does not consume the sacrificer. Therefore, having gone around to the south, he pours out the *praṇītā* waters.
He pours them out as follows:
"Who unyokes you? He unyokes you. For whom does he unyoke you? For him he unyokes you—for prosperity.
Thus he pronounces the highest prosperity for the sacrificer. With the very same [water] with which he leads forward [the fire], he pours it out;
for with that by which they yoke a draft-animal, they unyoke it; for it is with a thong that they yoke a draft-animal.
They release [the grain] with the thong; then, with the *phalīkaraṇa* husks, he throws the black antelope skin downward and downward, saying:
"Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases. 1.9.2.[34] Now, the gods and the Asuras...
Both the gods and the asuras, being offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this sacrifice with their father Prajāpati, the year, saying, "This shall be ours; this shall be ours.
Then the gods, having gathered together the entire sacrifice, [set aside] whatever was most defective in the sacrifice.

It was their share; with that they excluded them from the animal sacrifice. "They have been well-excluded by means of the husks," [they said]. He who is excluded while having a share is indeed well-excluded;
but he whom they exclude without a share, he remains silent for so long, for even after obtaining his desire, he says, "What have you given me? Thus it was with him.

Whatever portion the gods assigned to these [beings], that very portion he now assigns to them. Now, when he pushes the black antelope skin down and down, he causes them to enter blind darkness where there is no fire;
and likewise, with the words, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases, O blood," he causes the blood of the victim to enter blind darkness where there is no fire.

Therefore, they do not perform the *tedanī* rite for the animal victim, for that is the portion of the *rakṣases*. When the sacrifice has been completed, having gone around to the south, he pours out the full vessel; thus it becomes directed toward the north.

Therefore, having circumambulated from the right, he pours out the full vessel, thinking, "May there be for me a share in the world of the gods. Indeed, he who sacrifices sacrifices with this thought;
thus his sacrifice goes toward the world of the gods, and following after it, he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Following that fee, the sacrificer proceeds, holding onto it. 1.9.3. [2]

This is that path, either the way of the gods or the way of the fathers; on both sides stand two flaming points of fire, burning intensely. They burn against him who is to be burned, and they let pass him who is to be let pass.
Water is peace; thus he pacifies this very path.
He pours it out full; the full is indeed everything; verily, with everything he pacifies him. He pours it out continuously and without interruption;
verily, by means of that which is continuous and uninterrupted, he pacifies him.

Moreover, as to why he pours out the full vessel: whatever in the sacrifice is performed incorrectly, that they rend and tear apart; water is a means of pacification (*śānti*); thus he pacifies it with water, that which is the means of pacification, and he heals it with water. 1.9.3 [5]
He pours it out full;
for the full is everything—thus he unites it with everything. He pours it out continuously and without interruption;
thus he unites it by means of that which is continuous and uninterrupted. 1.9.3 [6]
Then he receives it with his joined palms, saying:
"We have united with splendor, with nourishment, and with our bodies; we have united with a gracious mind.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, the bounteous giver, bestow wealth upon us and smooth over for us whatever was disjointed," that is, whatever was torn asunder.
He joins that together. 1.9.3.
[7] Then he touches his face;
for there is a twofold reason why he touches his face: the waters are indeed nectar.
They touch it with something dead; he thus makes this ritual action part of his own self; therefore he touches his mouth.
1.9.3 [8] Then he strides the Viṣṇu-strides.
He who sacrifices with this sacrifice gratifies the gods, as if with Ṛg-verses.

As if by means of your *yajus* formulas and as if by means of your oblations, having gratified the gods with them, he becomes one who has entered among them; having become one who has entered among them, he moves forward toward them. Furthermore, as to why he strides the *viṣṇukrama* steps.

Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he strode this stride for the gods, which is this very stride of theirs. With his first step he touched this [earth], with his second this intermediate space, and with his highest [step] the sky. It is for this very purpose that he [performs it].
Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; he strides with a stride, therefore he strides the Viṣṇu-strides. Indeed, from this point onward, they mostly stride away from here.
That is where Viṣṇu strode upon the earth.
By means of the *gāyatrī* metre, he is excluded from that [world]—he who hates us and whom we hate. In the intermediate space, Viṣṇu strode out with the *triṣṭubh* metre;
by that, he is excluded—he who hates us and whom we hate. In the sky, Viṣṇu strode out with the *jagatī* metre.

"May the fierce one exclude from this world him who hates us and whom we hate"—having ascended these worlds in this manner, this is the goal, this is the foundation: he who shines yonder. His rays are the performers of good deeds; and that which is the supreme light is Prajāpati, or else it is heaven.
The world, having thus ascended these worlds, then goes to this goal, this foundation;

but he who wishes to issue a command from here should step downward from above. For that is why he steps downward from above. In the beginning, the gods, by retreating, won what was to be won while conquering.
First [they conquered] heaven,
then this intermediate space, and from there they drove away their enemies so that they could not retreat; in the same way,
this sacrificer now conquers by means of that very retreat, first heaven, then this intermediate space, and from there.
"By not stepping back, he drives away his rivals. This earth, indeed, is the foundation; thus he establishes himself upon this very foundation.
And so, Viṣṇu strode out across the sky.
By the *jagatī* metre, he has been excluded from that [world] who hates us and whom we hate;
in the intermediate space Viṣṇu strode out with the *triṣṭubh* metre, and by that he has been excluded from it who hates us and whom we hate; on earth Viṣṇu strode out with the *gāyatrī* metre.

"Then [he says]: 'Expelled from this food and from this support is he who hates us and whom we hate. For upon this [earth] all this food is supported; therefore he says, 'from this food and from this support. 1.9.3 [12]
Then he looks toward the east; for the east is the direction of the gods, therefore he looks toward the east. He looks: 1.9.3 [13].
He looks.

"We have gone to the light"—the gods are indeed the light; thus he says, "We have gone to the gods. "We have united with the light"—thus he says, "We have united with the gods. 1.9.3 [14] Then he gazes at the sun.
This is that goal, this is that foundation; he goes to that goal, to that foundation.
Therefore, he gazes at the sun.
He gazes upward.
"You are self-existent, the best ray"—this is indeed the best ray, namely the sun; therefore he says, "You are self-existent, the best ray. "You are the giver of splendor;
give me splendor"—thus indeed I say, Yājñavalkya used to say; for this is precisely what a Brāhmaṇa ought to desire.
"If one should desire to possess the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), [one should do this]," so indeed said Aupoditeya. "He will surely give me cows;
O giver of cows, give me cows!"—in this way, whatever desire he desires, that desire is fulfilled for him.
1.9.3. Then he turns back.
"Following the turning of the sun, I turn myself. Having gone to that course and that support, he turns himself according to the turning of that very [sun]. 1.9.3.
[17] Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire.
There are two reasons why he worships the Gārhapatya fire:
the Gārhapatya is indeed the house, and the house is the foundation; thus he establishes himself upon that foundation, the house.
And for as long as his human lifespan lasts here, it is for that very purpose that he worships it.
Therefore, he worships the Gārhapatya fire. He worships it, saying: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I become a good lord of the house through you, O Agni, as lord of the house."

"O Agni, may you be a good householder by me, the householder"—there is nothing hidden here in this. "May our household duties (*gārhapatyāni*) not be single-yoked; may our household duties be free from affliction"—this is what he says. "For a hundred winters"—this means "may I live for a hundred years. One should pay heed even when saying this, for there are indeed more than a hundred [years].
"A man lives for a hundred years; therefore, even when one says this, one should not take it seriously.
Then he turns around, saying, "I turn according to the turning of the sun," thereby [attaining] this goal and this support.
Having gone, he returns following its very path. 1.9.3 [20].
Then he utters the name of his son:
"May this son of mine continue this manly power," if he has a son.
It might even be that he should simply utter his own name.
1.9.3.[21] Then he stands in attendance upon the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "May my sacrifice be completed in the east," and he stands there silently. Then...
He releases the vow, saying:
"I am now who I truly am. For when he enters the vow, he becomes, as it were, non-human; therefore, it would not be appropriate for him to say, "Here I pass from truth to untruth. And that...
Furthermore, when one becomes a human being again, for that reason he should release his vow, thinking: "I am whoever I am; I am this very self."
